statement: Vanilla SF-AdamW is extremely sensitive to the momentum parameter beta1: test perplexity degrades from 25.12 at beta1=0.95 to 27.70 at 0.9, 41.01 at 0.5 and 67.20 at 0.1, all at the same LR of 2e-3.

comparator: Vanilla SF-AdamW (C = 1/(1-beta1)) at the same LR 2e-3, beta2=0.99, 124M LLaMA-style, SlimPajama-6B, 0.5M-token batch, 5000 steps.
effect: -1.52 perplexity (-6.1% relative) at beta1=0.95; -3.73 (-13.5%) at beta1=0.9. Gains persist for all of C in {50,100,200,500} at beta1=0.9 and 0.95, and C in {50,100} improves every momentum value tested.
locator: section 5 ('Our Refined SF Method', 'Empirical gains') and Appendix C.1 Table 5 (0.5M-token batch); Table 6 for the 2M-token batch
notes: Transfer 3: 124M / 0.5M-token batch is our operating point, the change is a scalar in the optimizer step, and the reported robustness to C (a whole order of magnitude works) is exactly what a campaign that cannot afford a sweep needs. Held below 4 because the run is 5000 steps and, critically, alpha_t ~ (C/T)(t/T)^(C-1) means the averaging window is defined relative to total steps T; with T~600 a C of 100-200 concentrates almost all weight on the last handful of iterates, so the tuned C does not carry over unchanged. Single seed per cell; these are the authors' own 'preliminary experiments'.
statement: Decoupling the averaging window from momentum in schedule-free AdamW by introducing c_t=(1-beta)C/t lowers test perplexity over vanilla SF-AdamW across a wide range of C at 124M scale: 25.12 -> 23.60 at beta1=0.95 (C=100) and 27.70 -> 23.97 at beta1=0.9 (C=50).

comparator: AdamW with cosine LR decay to 10% of peak, 124M model, 2M-token batch, 2500 steps (~5B tokens, ~2x Chinchilla).
effect: Vanilla SF-AdamW final loss is above AdamW+cosine at 2M-token batch; refined SF with C=200 matches (not beats) it. Table 6: vanilla beta1=0.98 gives 26.09 ppl, C=1000 gives 23.88.
locator: section 5 'Empirical gains' third bullet and Figure 9-right; Appendix C.1 Table 6; limitation restated in section 2.4
notes: Transfer 3 and registered as opposing evidence deliberately: the campaign's step budget is short and its batch is large for the model size, which is the direction in which SF is documented to degrade (the paper cites Zhang et al. and Morwani et al. for the same). This is the strongest single argument against swapping in schedule-free at our operating point without also tuning C. Scored 3 not 4 because 2M tokens/step is 4x our batch and 2500 steps is still 3-4x our horizon; single seed.
statement: At a 2M-token batch size, vanilla SF-AdamW with its best momentum (beta1=0.98) underperforms AdamW with a cosine schedule, and only matches it after adding the refinement parameter C=200.

comparator: Each other, after a per-scheme learning-rate sweep; LLaMA 20 blocks, d_emb 2048, ~1B params, DCLM 10% subset, 20,000 steps at 2^20 tokens/step, bf16, lambda=0.1.
effect: Best losses 2.815 (no WD) / 2.801 (independent WD) / 2.798 (standard WD); max spread 0.017 nats. The large differences between schemes appear only in how well the optimal LR transfers across widths, not in the achievable loss at one width.
locator: Appendix F.3.1 (Details for Figure 1), reporting best losses for the width-2048 / ~1B-param LLaMA runs on DCLM, 20B tokens
notes: Transfer 2 and registered as opposing evidence: our campaign never changes width, so the entire muP/LR-transfer payload is inapplicable, and this appendix number says the weight-decay scheme is worth ~0.01 nats at a fixed width once the LR is retuned - below or near our noise band. It argues against spending runs on weight-decay bookkeeping. Not scored higher because it is 1B params over 20B tokens / 20k steps (~30x our step budget) and the losses are averages of the last 100 training steps, not a clean held-out eval; also the input-layer/gain LRs were frozen at different values per arm, which is a confound between the no-WD and WD rows.
statement: At a single fixed model width, the best-over-learning-rate final loss is nearly identical whether AdamW uses no weight decay (2.815), independent weight decay scaling (2.801) or standard weight decay scaling (2.798) - a spread of at most 0.017 nats.

comparator: The steady-state theory of Kosson et al. that the relative update size depends only on eta*lambda, which the paper reformulates and then bounds in time.
effect: T_EQ ~ (1/(2*eta*lambda)) * ln(...); at eta=8e-3, lambda=0.1 the prefactor alone is 625 steps, so a few-hundred-step run never reaches the steady state in which only the product eta*lambda matters.
locator: Appendix D.1, Equation 31 (rho_inf^2 = eta/(2*lambda)) and Equation 32 (T_EQ); parameters eta=8e-3, lambda=0.1 from Appendix F.3
notes: Transfer 3: this is an analytic result parameterized directly by our own eta and lambda, and it says something the campaign can act on - in a 600-1000-step run weight decay is operating almost entirely in its transient regime, so it behaves as an initial-update scaler / implicit warmup (Appendix D.3) rather than as a norm regulator, and lambda should be tuned as a warmup-shaping knob and not by steady-state reasoning. Internal validity 2 because the authors explicitly state (Appendix D.1) that Equation 28 'does not accurately predict the behavior of the weight norm in neural network training' and that the model overestimates time-to-equilibrium; treat T_EQ as an order of magnitude, not a number. Also derived for AdamW, not Muon.
statement: The number of steps for AdamW weight norms to come within a factor sqrt(2) of their weight-decay equilibrium scales as 1/(2*eta*lambda) times a logarithmic factor, so with typical eta*lambda ~ 8e-4 equilibrium is an O(10^3)-step phenomenon.

comparator: LLaMA training at widths 128-2048, AdamW, 20k steps at 2^20 tokens/step, 10% linear warmup + linear decay baseline, best-LR sweep per arm.
effect: With no muP scaling, 10% and 50% linear warmup both give poor LR transfer; adding the multiplicative factor m^min(0, t/T_W - 1) or the decay-away factor of Equation 13 recovers transfer quality comparable to muP+independent WD, though it 'can require tuning and is less stable at higher learning rates'.
locator: section 6 ('The warmup effect of muP with independent weight decay') and section 7 with Figure 6 (three panels) and Figure 7; warmup forms in Equations 12 and 13
notes: Transfer 2: the width-transfer motivation is irrelevant to a fixed-width campaign, but the extractable mechanism - that warmup SHAPE (exponential, starting ~1/m below peak) matters more than warmup LENGTH, and that long linear warmup is not a substitute - is a cheap schedule change in train.py. Held at 2 because every experiment is a cross-width LR-transfer plot at 20k steps; there is no evidence at all that exponential warmup lowers loss at a single width and a short horizon, and burning warmup on a 600-step run costs a large fraction of the budget. Losses are last-100-step training averages.
statement: The practical benefit of muP's learning-rate scaling in AdamW is an implicit warmup effect on the relative weight updates, and an explicit additional exponential-shaped warmup factor can reproduce good learning-rate transfer without muP, whereas simply lengthening linear warmup from 10% to 50% of training does not.

comparator: None run. The paper's own AdamW alignment measurements (Figure 4, section 5.1) are the implicit contrast.
effect: No measurement. Stated as an expectation ('could result in', 'could potentially explain'); every experiment in the paper uses AdamW.
locator: section 9 (Discussion & Conclusion), final paragraph on matrix-level optimizers
notes: Transfer 2 because the campaign already runs a Muon+AdamW hybrid and 'shorten or drop warmup on the Muon-owned parameter group' is a zero-cost knob that buys back steps at the front of a 600-step run - but internal validity 1: this is an unsupported conjecture in a discussion section with no Muon run anywhere in the paper. Register it as a hypothesis to test cheaply, not as evidence. If tested, the AdamW-owned groups (embeddings, gains, 1-D params) may still need their warmup.
statement: The authors conjecture that matrix-level optimizers such as Muon produce a constant, low update alignment that does not vary over training, which would explain Muon's reduced need for learning-rate warmup and bypass the alignment dynamics that muP and weight decay are compensating for.

comparator: Best decay-based scheduler per model (WSD alpha=0.0 at 1B; Linear alpha=0.0 at 8B), AdamW, FineWeb-Edu, 80,000 steps, 4.2M (1B) / 12.6M (8B) token batches, eta_max=3e-4, 1000 warmup steps, WSD stable ratio 0.75.
effect: +0.071 nats (1B, 350B tokens) and +0.127 nats (8B, 500B tokens) validation loss relative to the best decay-based scheduler; the same models are best after SFT, but that inversion is irrelevant to a pretraining-loss objective.
locator: section 3.2, Table 1, column 'PT ValidLoss delta' (WSO rows, alpha_pre=1.0)
notes: Transfer 2 and registered as direct opposing evidence to the schedule-free / no-decay direction in 2507.09846: if the objective is val_bpb and nothing else, decaying the LR is worth ~0.07-0.13 nats and constant-LR schedules pay for their horizon-freedom in exactly the currency we are measuring. Not scored higher because it is 1B/8B params over 80k steps and 350-500B tokens (~100x our step budget), a single seed per cell, and the decay phase there is 25% of a very long run. Note this compares constant-LR to decayed AdamW, NOT to schedule-free AdamW, which is a different mechanism (iterate averaging) - so it weakens but does not refute 2507.09846.
statement: Pretraining with a warmup-stable-only schedule (constant LR, no decay phase) gives worse pretraining validation loss than the best decay-based scheduler: +0.071 at 1B params and +0.127 at 8B params.

comparator: WSD with alpha_pre=0.0 (the best 1B decay scheduler), same AdamW hyperparameters and 80k-step budget on FineWeb-Edu.
effect: 1B PT ValidLoss deltas: WSD 0.0/+0.004, Linear +0.016/+0.021, Cosine +0.016/+0.019 for alpha_pre 0.0/0.1. At 8B the ranking of WSD vs Linear flips (Linear 0.000, WSD +0.014), so the shape ordering is not stable across scale.
locator: section 3.2, Table 1, PT ValidLoss delta column, 1B block (all six decay rows)
notes: Transfer 2: says the decay-shape knob is a ~0.01-0.02-nat lever and its ordering is not even stable between 1B and 8B, so it is a poor use of a run at our operating point - decay to zero and stop tuning the shape. Held at 2 because 80k steps / 350B tokens is far outside our horizon and a 25% decay tail on an 80k-step run is a very different object from a decay tail on 600 steps, where the shape may matter more, not less. Single seed per cell; PT TaskAvg (the accuracy column) disagrees with the loss column repeatedly, which is a warning that these deltas are near this study's noise floor.
statement: Among decay-based schedulers the choice of decay shape and final-LR floor moves pretraining validation loss by at most ~0.02 nats: at 1B, WSD/Linear/Cosine at alpha_pre=0 land within 0.016 of each other, and decaying to zero beats decaying to 10% of peak by only 0.004 (WSD), 0.005 (Linear) and 0.003 (Cosine).

comparator: Pre-LN at its own best LR (2e-3, the same optimum as Peri-LN), Llama-3-style SwiGLU/RoPE transformers, Adam + cosine, 30B DCLM tokens, 14,400 steps, global batch 256 x seq 8192, weight decay 0.033, 5 training seeds per cell, LR swept 1e-4 to 5e-3.
effect: Eval loss 3.34 vs 3.43 (400M), 3.18 vs 3.29 (1.5B), 3.11 vs 3.20 (3.2B); Peri-LN also beats Post-LN by a wide margin (7.46/5.38/4.43). Benchmark average improves 49.69->51.57, 53.71->56.55, 56.69->58.56.
locator: section 4.3, Table 2, 'Loss' column (C4 eval loss, 10K random samples), all three model sizes; setup in section 4.1 and Appendix B.1 Table 3
notes: Best-controlled study in this batch: 5 seeds, full LR sweep per arm, three model sizes, effect consistent in sign and magnitude across all of them, and replicated under LayerNorm instead of RMSNorm (F.4) and at sequence length 2048 instead of 8192 (F.2). Transfer 3 because it is a pure train.py architecture edit with no data change and two extra RMSNorms per block - trivial GPU cost on an input-pipeline-bound host. Held below 4 because the smallest model is 400M non-embedding params at 14,400 steps / 30B tokens, ~20x our step budget and ~3x our width, and the mechanism (bounding exponential hidden-state variance growth) is explicitly a phenomenon that accumulates with depth and training time - 8 layers at 600 steps may simply not have grown the variance that Peri-LN exists to contain, in which case the gain shrinks toward zero. This is the single highest-value thing to test in this batch.
statement: Applying RMSNorm to both the input and the output of each transformer sub-module (Peri-LN) lowers held-out evaluation loss relative to Pre-LN by 0.09 at 400M, 0.11 at 1.5B and 0.09 at 3.2B parameters, each at its own best learning rate.

comparator: Pre-LN at its best LR, same 5 seeds, same 30B-token budget, model sizes 400M-3.2B.
effect: Example seed stds at 1.5B: ARC-Easy 1.22 -> 0.21, HellaSwag 1.53 -> 0.34, Winogrande 2.07 -> 0.44. Pre-LN spikes were 'particularly high in the early stages of training' and persisted at every LR tested; raising warmup from 10% to 30% did not reduce them.
locator: section 4.3 and Table 2 (per-task std across 5 seeds); section 4.2 and Figure 3(c); Appendix C.3 ('Gradient Spikes during Pre-Training'); Appendix F.3 (30% warmup does not fix Pre-LN spikes)
notes: Transfer 3 and separately valuable from the loss claim: our campaign's memory records a single-seed noise floor of sigma=0.00061 that is 72% of the decision gate, so an intervention that halves seed-to-seed variance changes what we can resolve at n=1, not just where the mean sits. Note also that the spikes are concentrated 'in the early stages of training', which is where our entire run lives - so the stability half of the Peri-LN case should transfer BETTER to a short run than the loss half. Held at 3 because the variance measurements are on downstream benchmark accuracy at 400M-3.2B, not on val_bpb at 124M, and 5 seeds is a small sample for a variance-ratio claim.
statement: Peri-LN reduces run-to-run variability and instability relative to Pre-LN: the standard deviation of benchmark scores across 5 training seeds is more than halved, gradient-norm spikes are rare rather than frequent, and diverged checkpoints occurred mostly under Pre-LN.

comparator: Pre-LN-only transformer at matched LR, 400M and 1.5B models, same 30B-token DCLM setup.
effect: Loss improvement and spike reduction over Pre-LN with gamma fixed to 1; learnable gamma 'slightly better'. Shown as curves for 400M and 1.5B; no numeric delta reported.
locator: section 4.4.1 ('Learnable Parameter gamma of RMSNorm') and Figure 4; gamma trajectories in Figure 7(b)
notes: Transfer 3: this isolates the cheapest possible version of the Peri-LN intervention - one parameter-free RMSNorm on each sub-module output, no new learnable tensors, no embedding-LN, nothing for the optimizer to have to tune within 600 steps. That last point matters more for us than for them: a freshly initialized learnable gamma has ~600 steps to find its value, so the gamma-fixed variant is arguably the better bet at our horizon even though it is the weaker one at theirs. Internal validity 3 rather than 4 because this ablation is reported as curves with no numbers and no seed count, unlike the main Table 2 result.
statement: Simply normalizing the output of each module - even with the RMSNorm learnable gain gamma frozen at 1, and with Peri-LN's embedding normalization removed - reduces gradient spikes and improves loss relative to a pre-normalization-only transformer; making gamma learnable gives a further slight improvement.

comparator: The same Peri-LN architecture without embedding LN, 30B DCLM tokens, matched LR.
effect: 'Slight improvement' in pretraining loss, larger at 400M than at 1.5B/3.2B. No numeric effect size is given anywhere; the claim rests on three loss-curve figures.
locator: Appendix F.5 ('Embedding Layer Normalization of Peri-Layer Normalization Transformers'), Figures 16 (400M), 17 (1.5B), 18 (3.2B)
notes: Transfer 3 because the stated scale trend points our way (124M is smaller than their smallest arm) and one RMSNorm on the embedding output is a one-line change with essentially zero throughput cost - but internal validity 2 because it is figures-only with no numbers, no seeds, and 'more pronounced in smaller models' is an eyeball reading across three plots. Relevant to the campaign's value-embedding path: this claim is about normalizing the embedding output, and interacts with wherever value embeddings are injected.
statement: Adding a normalization layer on the embedding output within the Peri-LN architecture yields a slight pretraining-loss improvement, and the authors observe the effect becomes more pronounced in smaller models.

comparator: The same Pre-LN/Peri-LN LR sweep at a 30B-token budget with the same 10% warmup fraction.
effect: Divergence at LR 5e-3 for 8B and 16B token budgets, no divergence at 30B, all with 10% warmup. The optimal LR range itself did not shift with token count.
locator: Appendix F.1 ('Amount of Training Tokens') and Figure 12; contrast with Appendix F.3 where 30% warmup did not fix Pre-LN gradient spikes
notes: Transfer 3 and important as a boundary condition: it says the maximum stable learning rate is a function of the ABSOLUTE number of warmup steps, not the warmup fraction, so shortening a run while holding warmup at 10% shrinks the usable LR ceiling. Our ~600-step run at 10% warmup gets ~60 warmup steps, an order of magnitude fewer than their shortest failing configuration, which argues that any aggressive-LR lever must be paired with an explicit warmup-step floor. Internal validity 2: the divergence is reported in passing, the attribution to warmup is the authors' unverified explanation (they ran no warmup-length control at 8B/16B), and the second-order reading is also consistent with the useful-LR range simply being narrower early. Also note the useful positive half: the optimal LR range did NOT shift with token count.
statement: With a fixed 10% warmup fraction, a learning rate of 5e-3 diverged in the 8B- and 16B-token runs but did not diverge at 30B tokens, which the authors attribute to the warmup phase being insufficient at the shorter budgets.

comparator: One-sample SGD (B=1), which the theorem recovers as a special case; and multi-pass batch SGD with/without replacement.
effect: One-pass variance bound O(min{M,(T_eff*gamma)^(1/a)}/(B*T_eff)); batching leaves the approximation exponent Theta(M^(1-b)) and the bias exponent unchanged and only rescales the stochastic term. Verified empirically only on synthetic Gaussian-sketched data (d=1e4, M=64, N=L=512, 100 repetitions).
locator: section 3, Theorem 3.1 and the discussion paragraphs 'What batch size changes' and 'Implications for choosing batch size'; empirical check in section 4 Experiment 1 and Figure 1(a)
notes: Transfer 1 - this does not transfer and I am saying so plainly. It is sketched linear regression with a power-law covariance spectrum and a source condition, plain SGD with no momentum, no adaptivity, no features; the authors themselves list extension to nonlinear or feature-learning models as open. The only reason to register it at all is that the one-pass structure literally matches our single-epoch-over-a-fixed-shard-set regime and the conclusion (batch size is a noise-control knob whose benefit saturates, and buying it with horizon is a bad trade when the bias term dominates) points the same way as 2607.20548's Figure 1. Do not use it as evidence for a batch-size decision; it is a framing, not a measurement.
statement: In one-pass (single-epoch) batch SGD the 1/B variance gain from a larger batch is partly cancelled at a fixed dataset size by the shorter optimization horizon T=N/B, so batch size should be increased only until the variance term stops being comparable to the approximation-plus-bias contribution.

comparator: AdamW and standard Muon (matrix params only, AdamW for the rest), supervised fine-tuning on 400k OpenOrca samples for 2 epochs, seq len 1024, effective batch 48-80, linear LR decay to 1e-7, 2x RTX A6000.
effect: Validation loss AdamW vs MuonAll vs Muon: 0.52592 / 0.54942 / 0.55058 (Qwen2-0.5B), 0.54377 / 0.57391 / 0.56029 (SmolLM2-360M), 0.000027 / 0.52772 / 0.52885 (GPT2-medium). MuonAll beats Muon on 2 of 3 but loses to AdamW on all 3, at higher wall-clock.
locator: section III (Algorithm 1) and section IV, Table IV (training/validation losses for Qwen2-0.5B, SmolLM2-360M, GPT2-medium); wall-clock statement in section V (Conclusion)
notes: Transfer 1: this is supervised fine-tuning of already-pretrained checkpoints, which the brief scores as out of scope, and the GPT2-medium row (AdamW validation loss 2.65e-5) is not a credible measurement - it indicates memorization or a logging bug and undermines confidence in the whole table. No seeds, no LR sweep beyond one hand-picked value per optimizer, and losses are on an SFT objective, not pretraining bpb. Registered only because 'put every parameter through Muon' is a mechanism the campaign might otherwise spend a run on, and the one available datapoint says it does not beat the Muon+AdamW hybrid and is slower - and slower directly costs steps at a fixed 300s. Note this paper also restates (section II) that Nesterov momentum helps Muon, contradicting 2607.20548 section 5.2.
statement: Routing one-dimensional parameters through Muon by embedding them as diagonal matrices (MuonAll), instead of leaving them to AdamW, produced higher validation loss than AdamW on all three models tested and did not beat plain Muon consistently, while costing more wall-clock time for the same number of tokens.

comparator: Dynamic Tanh (Zhu et al. 2025), fitted on the same simulated LayerNorm outlier data. No neural network is trained anywhere in the paper.
effect: Mean absolute residual against LayerNorm outputs on simulated outliers: <0.01 for ELN vs 0.33 for DyT (C=100, N=50, sigma=2, outliers injected in steps of 5). Fitted parameters alpha=0.049 (DyT), beta=301.1 (ELN).
locator: section 3 (Theorems 3 and 4, Equations 13 and 15) and section 4.2 with Figure 3; conclusion in section 5
notes: Transfer 1 and I am saying so plainly: there is not a single training run in this paper. The 'simulations' are a curve fit of two functional forms to synthetic Gaussian data passed through LayerNorm, and the authors explicitly leave 'how ELN compares to DyT in terms of performance and feasibility' to future work. The usual motivation for DyT-style replacements is throughput (no cross-channel reduction), and per this campaign's own finding that ~94% of charged time is the frozen Python packing loop, a faster normalization op buys close to nothing in wall clock here - so even the speed argument does not land at our operating point. Registered so the direction controller can see the mechanism exists and close it out, not to justify a run.
statement: Elementwise Layer Normalization, y = sqrt(C-1) * x / sqrt(beta + x^2), is the exact element-wise solution of the LayerNorm differential equation of which Dynamic Tanh is an approximation, and it reproduces LayerNorm's response to outliers far more closely than DyT in a synthetic fit.

comparator: vanilla Muon with per-size grid-searched lr_max (5e-3 at 0.13B C4, 3e-3 at 0.25B Pile), cosine schedule, 1M-2M token batches, 10k-50k iterations
effect: lower terminal loss at every size tested (0.25B Pile baseline Muon = 2.110); approximately 2x token speedup at the 100x-params (25k iteration) budget
locator: section 6.1 'Main Results' and Figures 1, 4; hyperparameters in appendix C.2
notes: Transfer 2: the 0.13B model matches our parameter count but the SHORTEST run in the paper is 10k iterations of which 1000 are warmup alone, i.e. the entire measured regime is long-horizon post-warmup, whereas our total budget is 600-1000 steps. Terminal-loss deltas are only shown in figures (no per-size table), so the effect size at 0.13B is not recoverable; only the 0.25B baseline number 2.110 is stated in text. n=1 per configuration, no seed repeats. Implementable in train.py (two extra Newton-Schulz calls in the Muon path) but requires choosing d_s, chi, beta_1, beta_2.
statement: Selectively amplifying the Muon update along the flat (non-top-eigenspace) directions - larger LR ratio chi>=2 plus larger Hessian-damping coefficient beta_2 - reaches lower terminal loss than a tuned vanilla Muon baseline at 130M-1.3B params.

comparator: vanilla Muon, LLaMA 0.25B on Pile, 1M-token batches, cosine schedule, ~10k iterations
effect: terminal loss 2.113 (beta_1,2=0.5) and 2.129 (beta_1,2=1.0) vs vanilla Muon 2.110; both worse despite being smaller than the beta_2=2.0 used on flat directions in Muon-LITE-H
locator: section 6.1, 'Ablation Studies'
notes: Transfer 3 because this is a cheap negative that governs an obvious first thing to try: globally increasing the Nesterov/gradient-correction term in a Muon update is not a free win, the gain requires subspace selectivity. Same 0.25B/long-horizon caveat as the positive claim, and n=1 per configuration, but the direction of the effect (baseline beats both uniform settings) is what matters. Blocker: we cannot cheaply verify the flat/sharp split at 124M.
statement: Applying the LITE gradient-correction (Hessian damping) coefficient uniformly to all directions rather than only to the flat subspace makes Muon WORSE than the untouched Muon baseline.

comparator: vanilla Muon, LLaMA-1.3B on Pile, global batch 8192, micro-batch 16, seqlen 1024, 8x A800-80GB
effect: 100.4k tokens/s (Muon-LITE) vs 101.5k tokens/s (Muon), i.e. ~1.1% slowdown
locator: appendix B.1, 'Computational Efficiency of Muon-LITE'
notes: Transfer 2: the 1% figure is measured in a regime (1.3B params, 8M-token global batch) where per-step gradient GEMMs dominate and the NS matrices are large. At 124M/d_model=512 the orthogonalization matrices are tiny and per-step cost is kernel-launch bound rather than FLOP bound, so the relative overhead here should be treated as a LOWER bound for our operating point, where the step is already dominated by many small kernels. Authors provide no small-model timing.
statement: The two extra Newton-Schulz calls per step that LITE adds to Muon cost about 1% throughput at 1.3B params on 8xA800.

comparator: Muon-LITE hyperparameters searched only on LLaMA 0.25B/Pile with the base LR fixed to vanilla Muon's optimum; no re-search at 0.13B, 0.5B or 1.3B, and no search at any horizon shorter than 10k iterations
effect: single search over r_s in {0.1,0.2}, beta_1 in {0.0,-0.25}, beta_2 in {0.5,1.0,2.0}, chi in {2.0,4.0} at 0.25B; selected chi=4 for emb/norm blocks, chi=2 for Muon blocks, (beta_1,beta_2)=(-0.25,1.0)
locator: appendix C.2, 'Hyper-parameter tuning for Muon-LITE'; section 6.1
notes: Transfer 2: useful because it means we could borrow their constants rather than run a grid we cannot afford, but internal_validity is only 2 - there is no control showing the transferred constants are near-optimal at the other scales, and no search was done at a short horizon at all. The horizon (not the model size) is the axis we differ on most, and it was never varied during the search.
statement: The LITE hyperparameters (chi, beta_1, beta_2, sharp-subspace ratio r_s=0.1) were grid-searched once at 0.25B and reused unchanged at 0.13B, 0.5B and 1.3B without re-tuning.

comparator: Muon, Adam and Stable-SPAM at matched tokens; LLaMA 60M/130M/350M on C4, seqlen 256, batch 512 sequences (131k tokens/step), 1.4B/2.6B/7.8B tokens, cosine LR with 10% warmup, per-method wandb LR sweep
effect: 130M eval perplexity: column-wise-normalized SGD 28.85 -> 22.57 with last-layer momentum only (Muon 22.20, Adam 23.13); at 350M 20.38 -> 16.32, beating Muon 16.70
locator: section 2.2 and Table 3; comparator numbers in Table 2 and Table 5
notes: Transfer 2: 130M matches our parameter count, but 2.6B tokens at 131k tokens/step is roughly 20k optimizer steps, ~20-30x our budget, and the paper's whole objective is optimizer-state MEMORY which is not a constraint for us on an H200. The usable content is the mechanism, not the algorithm: variance control concentrated at the output head buys most of what full-everywhere momentum buys. n=1 per cell, no seed repeats.
statement: Adding first-order momentum to ONLY the last (lm_head) layer of a column-normalized-gradient SGD recovers most of the gap to Muon at 60M-350M params.

comparator: same run with no last-layer momentum; variance estimated by treating a 512-sample batch as the 'true' gradient against the 32-sample training batch, smoothed over a 50-iteration window, LLaMA 130M on C4
effect: lm_head variance highest for most of training; applying momentum to lm_head drops its variance to a very low level AND also reduces the embedding layer's variance
locator: section 2.2, Figure 3(a); Figure 3(b) for the effect of adding lm_head momentum
notes: Transfer 3: this is a measurement at our parameter scale, includes early training, and speaks directly to where signal-path/value-embedding interventions should be aimed - the head and the embedding, not the middle blocks. internal_validity only 2: the 'true gradient' is a 512-sample proxy, one model, one seed, no error bars, and variance is reported only as smoothed curves.
statement: Measured layer-wise stochastic gradient variance during 130M pretraining is largest at the lm_head, second largest at the embedding, and lower for all intermediate layers.

comparator: same 1B LLaMA on C4, 13.1B tokens, identical batch/schedule, per-method LR tuning
effect: qualitative curve ordering: Muon fastest at the beginning; SCALE, Stable-SPAM and APOLLO reach it only at the end (final: Stable-SPAM 13.97, APOLLO-Mini 14.13, Muon 14.18, SCALE 14.25)
locator: appendix A.3, Figure 4 (LLaMA 1B eval perplexity curves)
notes: Transfer 3: the claim is specifically about the EARLY portion of training, which is the only portion our 300s budget ever reaches, and it argues against swapping Muon out for an optimizer whose advantage is asymptotic. internal_validity 2: read off a single curve figure with no seeds and no early-checkpoint table, so the size of the early gap is not quantified.
statement: Muon converges fastest in the early stage of training while memory-efficient and Adam-family competitors only catch up in the final stage.

comparator: torch operations on a single square matrix, no fusion, no torch.compile, single A40 GPU
effect: per-matrix time on one A40: NS 6.03/7.00/14.41 ms at d=1024/2048/4096 vs column-wise 0.10/0.12/0.17 ms, row-wise 0.09-0.13 ms, sign 0.03 ms; exact SVD 79.8-1958.7 ms
locator: section 2.1, Table 1
notes: Transfer 2: the absolute numbers do not transfer (A40, uncompiled, per-matrix microbenchmark, and our d_model is 512 which is below their smallest size), but the shape does - NS time is nearly flat from d=1024 to 2048, i.e. launch-bound, which matches our own profile where the step is dominated by many tiny kernels. Relevant as a warning that per-parameter-block NS is a fixed per-step tax that does not shrink with our small matrices.
statement: Newton-Schulz orthogonalization costs 1-2 orders of magnitude more time per matrix than column-wise or sign normalization.

comparator: 206M 12-layer RoPE transformer with RMSNorm and QK-norm, FineWeb-Edu 10B, seqlen 1024, batch 64, 100k steps, NAdamW paired optimizer for non-matrix params; MuonMax/EF-MuonMax got 30 tuning trials each while vanilla Muon used init2winit defaults
effect: validation CE 3.01 (vanilla Muon) vs 3.27 (MuonMax) vs 3.43 (EF-MuonMax); ordering reverses on CIFAR-10 where MuonMax 0.265 beats vanilla Muon 0.287
locator: section 5 'Results' and Table 1; setup in appendix F.2
notes: Transfer 3: opposing evidence that directly closes off a family of 'improved Muon' substitutions, on a FineWeb-Edu LM close in architecture to ours, and the tuning asymmetry runs AGAINST the winner (vanilla Muon was less tuned and still won), which strengthens it. Docked from 4 because 100k steps at 65k tokens/step is a two-orders-of-magnitude longer horizon than ours and the task-dependence (CIFAR ordering flips) shows the ranking is not universal.
statement: On language-model pretraining vanilla Muon reaches a lower validation cross-entropy than the norm-regularized MuonMax variant and than error-feedback MuonMax.

comparator: MuonMax with the same paired optimizer and the same 30-trial (LM) / 60-trial (vision) sweep
effect: EF-MuonMax is worse than MuonMax in both settings: LM val CE 3.43 vs 3.27, CIFAR-10 val CE 0.388 vs 0.265
locator: section 5 'Discussion'; Table 1; section 6
notes: Transfer 2: mechanism-level negative - treating the Muon LMO as a compression operator whose residual should be fed back is not worth the extra full-size error buffer and extra state traffic. Only two tasks, one seed each, and the LM run is 100k steps; the authors themselves frame this as analogous to AMSGrad never displacing Adam.
statement: Adding error feedback to Muon restores a convex-Lipschitz convergence guarantee but does not improve empirical performance on either task tested.

comparator: n/a - theoretical scope statement
effect: counterexample 3.3 excludes the regularized Muon variant; counterexample 3.4 excludes beta >= 1/2, i.e. excludes the standard beta=0.95
locator: section 7 'Limitations'
notes: Transfer 1: registered specifically so the paper's title is not mistaken for a reason to abandon or modify Muon at our operating point. The negative theory says nothing about beta=0.95 with a warmup+decay schedule and Newton-Schulz-approximated polar factors, which is what we actually run. No experimental content.
statement: The paper's Muon non-convergence counterexamples do not cover the settings used in practice: one requires decreasing stepsizes and the other only holds for momentum beta in [0, 1/2), and neither covers a momentum schedule or approximate polar factors.

comparator: fixed 4M-token global batch baseline; InternLM2 122M-1B for the fitting, AdamW at constant LR 6e-4 with 1000-step warmup, batches 64k-7.5M tokens, 50-120B tokens per configuration
effect: both B_min and B_opt scale monotonically with decreasing target loss across five model sizes from 122M to 1B; the derived dynamic schedule starts at 2M tokens/batch versus a 4M fixed baseline and wins
locator: section 3.3, Equation 15 and Figure 3; fitting setup in section 4.3.1
notes: Transfer 3: the mechanism is specifically about WHERE in training you are, and our entire 300s run sits in the earliest phase where their curve says the data-optimal batch is at its smallest - which argues for trading batch size for step count at fixed tokens. Docked from 4 because the validation runs are 500B-token Qwen3 MoE/dense at 4-6M batch, the loss-step pairs used for fitting are interpolated through a scaling law L(S)=L0+A*S^-alpha rather than measured directly at every point, and our 524288-token batch may not be freely adjustable given the frozen prepare.py.
statement: The batch size that minimizes data consumption to reach a target loss (B_opt) increases monotonically as the target loss decreases, i.e. it is smallest at the start of training.

comparator: the standard critical-batch-size formulation of McCandlish et al.; InternLM2 models 122M-1B, AdamW constant LR 6e-4, batches 64k-7.5M tokens
effect: the ordering E_1 < E_2 for B_1 < B_2 holds only above a threshold loss and inverts below it; the classical Critical Batch Size framework fails in the stable phase
locator: section 3.1 and Figure 1
notes: Transfer 3: we operate entirely above the crossover (high loss, very early training), which is exactly the region where their data says smaller batch / more steps is data-optimal. Docked from 4 because the crossover point is shown only in a figure without axis values, no seeds are reported, and their constant-LR stable phase differs from a short warmup+decay schedule where the decay phase is a large fraction of the run.
statement: Under a constant-learning-rate (WSD stable) phase, loss-versus-tokens curves for different batch sizes intersect: the smaller batch is ahead at higher target losses and behind after a crossover, which contradicts the monotonic critical-batch-size relation E = E_min + B*S_min.

comparator: same dynamic batch schedule with constant LR 3.2e-4, Qwen3 MoE, 500B tokens, weight decay 0.1, 1000 warmup steps
effect: no performance improvement from LR ~ sqrt(B) versus constant LR while batch grew 2M -> 6M tokens; authors attribute this to higher LR re-injecting the gradient noise the larger batch was meant to suppress
locator: section 5.1 'The Effect of learning rate', Figure 9
notes: Transfer 2: useful as a negative on the common reflex to co-scale LR with batch, but demonstrated only at 500B tokens on a large MoE with downstream benchmark curves rather than validation loss, n=1 per arm, and only one scaling exponent (sqrt) was tested. If we vary batch size at fixed 300s, this says do not automatically move LR with it - but it does not tell us the right LR at 600 steps.
statement: Scaling the learning rate as sqrt(batch size) while increasing the batch size gave no improvement over holding the learning rate constant.

comparator: micro-batch expansion to the identical global batch, Qwen3 MoE, same LR and weight decay
effect: immediate downstream performance drop on raising seqlen 4K -> 6K (switches at 250B and 375B tokens) at batch-size parity; the model eventually recovers but the authors judge the approach undesirable
locator: section 5.2 'The Effect of sequence length', Figure 10
notes: Transfer 2: our sequence length is fixed by the frozen prepare.py, so this is only relevant as a guard against proposing seqlen changes as a batch/throughput lever. Evidence is a single large-scale A/B measured on downstream benchmarks, not validation loss, with no seeds; the mechanism cited (train-distribution perturbation from changed sample structure) would apply differently under our fixed packing.
statement: Reaching a larger global batch by extending sequence length caused an immediate performance drop, whereas reaching the same batch by micro-batch expansion did not.

comparator: WSD with the same 300-step warmup, same decay fraction alpha=0.2 and the same base LR 0.0015 selected on a 10000-iteration pilot; LLaMA-style 12-layer 124M / 24-layer 213M, SlimPajama, GPT-2 BPE, seqlen 512, batch 200 sequences, AdamW
effect: 124M: WSqD matches WSD at T=15000 and the gap only reaches ~0.003 nat at T=15000 and ~0.005 nat at T=60000; 213M: gap grows 0.003 nat at T=15000 to 0.011 nat at T=60000; relative compute advantage 1.01x at the initial horizon rising to ~1.05x at 60000 iterations
locator: appendix C.3 (124M model, Figure 11) and section 3.2 / appendix C.1 (213M, Figure 9)
notes: Transfer 2 and stance OPPOSES: this is the closest study in the batch to our parameter count (their appendix C.3 model is literally 124M) and it says the schedule's benefit is a long-horizon effect that is absent at their SHORTEST horizon - which is still 15000 iterations, ~20x ours. It is direct evidence against spending a slot on inverse-sqrt base schedules. Also the entire motivation (post-hoc horizon extension without re-tuning) is irrelevant when our horizon is fixed at 300 charged seconds.
statement: An inverse-square-root base phase (WSqD) only MATCHES flat-stable WSD at the shortest horizon tested and its advantage grows with horizon, at both 124M and 213M params.

comparator: same schedule, same LR 0.0015, three independent (init, data-shuffle) seed pairs, 213M LLaMA on SlimPajama
effect: max-minus-min full-validation final loss across 3 seeds <= ~0.01 nat at every horizon; the WSqD-vs-WSD mean gap at T=15000 is 0.003 nat, i.e. inside that band, though the sign of the gap was consistent across all three seeds
locator: appendix C.1 'Sensitivity to random seeds', Figure 9
notes: Transfer 3: a directly usable noise-floor calibration from an independent group, at a scale near ours, and it matches our own finding that single-seed differences below ~1e-3 nats are not resolvable. Practical consequence: any lever whose claimed effect is a few thousandths of a nat needs n>=3 and sign-consistency across seeds, exactly as they did, or it should not be believed. Docked from 4 only because the measurement is at 213M and 15k-60k iterations, and seed noise typically grows at shorter horizons.
statement: Varying model-initialization and data-shuffling seeds changes the final validation loss by at most about 0.01 nat at 213M params, which is larger than the schedule effect the paper reports at its shortest horizon.

comparator: per-horizon grid over six peak LRs, 213M LLaMA on SlimPajama, AdamW, decay fraction 0.2, 300-step warmup
effect: WSqD optimum stays at eta_max = 0.0015 at all four horizons; WSD's optimum moves to smaller values as T increases
locator: section 3.3, Figure 4 (sweep over eta_max in {0.0005,...,0.003} at T in {15000,30000,45000,60000})
notes: Transfer 3: the actionable direction is the contrapositive - a peak LR inherited from any longer-horizon recipe is too SMALL for our 600-1000-step run, so the LR sweep at our horizon should be centered above published values rather than at them. Not 4 because the horizons swept (15k-60k) are all far above ours and the drift is only demonstrated for AdamW with WSD, not for a Muon+AdamW hybrid.
statement: The optimal peak learning rate for a WSD schedule drifts toward SMALLER values as the training horizon grows, whereas the horizon-free WSqD schedule's optimum stays fixed.

comparator: WSqD with T_0 in {500,5000,10000}, peak LR selected on a 10000-iteration search, 213M LLaMA on SlimPajama
effect: T_0=500 degrades final loss at all four horizons; performance becomes insensitive to T_0 once it is moderately large; recommended default T_0 = T_1 (pilot horizon = 10000 iterations)
locator: section 3.4 'Ablation study of shift parameter T_0', Figure 5 (T_0 in {500, 5000, 10000})
notes: Transfer 2: only relevant if we ever try a decaying base phase at 600-1000 steps, in which case their rule implies T_0 on the order of the run length itself, making the base phase nearly flat - i.e. collapsing back toward WSD. That is a useful structural warning: at our horizon the schedule family degenerates. Evidence is 3 values of T_0, one seed, at 213M.
statement: Setting the inverse-square-root shift parameter T_0 too small makes the base learning rate decay too aggressively in early training and degrades final performance; the authors recommend T_0 equal to the pilot horizon length.

comparator: Adam and Muon with grid-searched LR, no weight decay, momentum 0.95
effect: reported wins are lower final train/test loss on a 50-dim-in/50-dim-out Gaussian-random-field regression (two-layer MLP, hidden 100, 1000 steps) and higher CIFAR-10 test accuracy over 100 epochs; no perplexity or bpb number anywhere in the paper
locator: section 4.1 'Datasets and Models' and section 4.2, Table 1, Figures 1-2
notes: Transfer 1, registered so the direction controller does not pick this up from its abstract. The modification itself is cheap (one extra accumulated scalar, no extra tensor state, no extra Newton-Schulz) and would be trivially implementable in train.py, but there is zero evidence at any language-model scale, the optimal LR moves by 2 orders of magnitude (Muon 5e-3 -> AdaGO 0.5 on regression), and it introduces two new hyperparameters (epsilon, gamma) we cannot afford to sweep. Not usable without our own screening run.
statement: AdaGO (an AdaGrad-norm scalar adaptive stepsize applied on top of Muon's orthogonalized update) is evaluated only on a 2-layer MLP regression task and a 5-layer CNN on CIFAR-10, with no transformer or language-modeling experiment.

comparator: per-optimizer best configuration tuned at the near-Chinchilla 2.1B-token horizon, then lambda swept over {0, 0.1, 0.5}; Llama-like 124M, FineWeb 100B subset, GPT-2 tokenizer, seqlen 512, batch 256x512=131k tokens, cosine to 0.01*gamma_max
effect: lambda=0.5 beats lambda=0.1 for all durations from 1B up to 8.4B tokens and loses only at 16.8B; lambda=0 leaves a large gap to 0.1 that widens with horizon; Signum and Lion at lambda=0.5 beat AdamW at the same LR
locator: section 4.1 'Weight decay ablation', Figure 7(a,b); appendix D.1 'Weight decay ablation', Figure 23
notes: Transfer 3 and this is the single most on-point lever in the batch: same parameter count, same data family, same tokenizer, and the effect is explicitly a SHORT-HORIZON effect that reverses with more tokens. Docked from 4 because their shortest run (1B tokens = 8k iterations at this batch) is still ~10x our step budget, so the monotone trend has to be extrapolated one further decade toward us; the direction of extrapolation, however, is favorable. Study is unusually strong internally: 2900 models, ~30000 GPU-hours, per-optimizer tuning. Blocker: see the Muon-specific exception.
statement: At 124M params, holding the tuned learning rate fixed and raising decoupled weight decay from 0.1 to 0.5 gives better final validation loss for short training durations, with lambda=0.1 only overtaking it at the longest horizon.

comparator: same 124M setup and the same {0, 0.1, 0.5} sweep applied to D-Muon, where weight decay reaches all parameter groups and the normal 'large lambda for short runs' pattern reappears
effect: Muon runs with lambda=0.5 lose to lambda in {0, 0.1} at 1, 2.1, 4.2 and 6.3B tokens; MARS, which also treats 1D and 2D parameters differently, shows the same pattern with a faster-narrowing gap
locator: appendix D.1 'Weight decay ablation' (text) and Figure 23; section 4.1 Figure 8
notes: Transfer 3 and this is the critical caveat for us because we run a Muon+AdamW hybrid: raising the weight decay hyperparameter is only a short-horizon win if the decay actually reaches the matrix parameters. If our Muon path excludes 2D params from decay, cranking lambda will load all the regularization onto the AdamW-owned groups (embeddings, norms, head) and can hurt. Same horizon caveat as the parent claim.
statement: For plain Muon, which does not apply weight decay to its 2D matrix parameters, lambda=0.5 UNDERPERFORMS lambda in {0, 0.1} even on the short training runs where large weight decay helps every other optimizer.

comparator: basic Muon (jordan2024muon) with weight decay only on embeddings, scalar params and the final layer, same tuning protocol, 124M/210M/720M Llama-like models on FineWeb
effect: major improvement of D-Muon over Muon at all three model sizes; basic Muon degrades further as model size grows while D-Muon is consistent across every setting tried; D-Muon's tuned LR at 124M large-batch is 0.002 vs Muon's 0.01 Muon-LR/0.001 AdamW-LR split
locator: section 4.1 Figure 8(a,b,c) and section 3 Figure 4; 720M discussion in section 4.3
notes: Transfer 3: a concrete, cheap, implementable change to the Muon path (decay the 2D matrices too, share the LR treatment) validated at exactly our parameter count on FineWeb data. Docked from 4 because every horizon tested is >=8k iterations and because the comparison also bundles a learning-rate parameterization change alongside the weight-decay change, so the attribution to weight decay alone rests on the authors' cross-reference to Figures 7 and 23 rather than an isolated A/B.
statement: D-Muon, which applies decoupled weight decay to all parameter groups including the 2D matrices, substantially outperforms basic Muon at 124M, 210M and 720M params, and the gap is attributed to the weight decay.

comparator: AdamW at 124M and 210M with the same peak LR and schedule shape, sweeping gamma_end over 1e-1 to 1e-6 times gamma_max
effect: decaying only to 0.1*gamma_max is much worse than any deeper decay tested; best endpoint at 210M is 0.01*gamma_max for cosine and WSD and 0.001*gamma_max for linear; at 124M the best shifts further to 1e-4*gamma_max for linear and 1e-6*gamma_max for WSD; differences beyond 0.1x are described as relatively small
locator: section 4.2 'Decay the learning rate sufficiently', Figure 15; appendix D.1 Figure 30 for the 124M model; sweep values in Table 7
notes: Transfer 3: costs nothing to implement, is tested at our parameter count, and the optimal endpoint is explicitly reported to depend on model size (deeper decay preferred at 124M than at 210M), which is the direction that favors us. Docked from 4 because horizons are 8k-128k iterations; at 600-1000 steps the decay phase is a much larger fraction of the run, so the endpoint interacts with the schedule shape differently, and the authors themselves note the gains beyond 0.1x are 'relatively small'.
statement: Decaying the learning rate to 0.01x the peak or lower gives significantly better final loss than the common 0.1x endpoint, at both 124M and 210M params.

comparator: Muon at 124M, batch 256x512=131k tokens, 16k steps, otherwise best-found configuration
effect: no final-loss improvement for T_NS in {10, 20} over T_NS = 5; 5 selected as best in the 124M hyperparameter table
locator: appendix D.1, Figure 37 'Muon's dependence on the number of Newton-Schulz iterations' (sweep T_NS in {1,5,10,20}); tuned value bolded in Table 12
notes: Transfer 4: demonstrated at exactly 124M with a FineWeb-tokenized GPT-2-vocabulary setup, implementable as a one-line change, and it is a pure throughput lever - in our CPU-contended, launch-bound regime every removed NS iteration is removed kernel launches per matrix per step, which converts directly into steps. The one gap: they do not report whether T_NS=1 is as good as 5 (the sweep includes 1 but the text only states 'beyond 5 does not improve'), so the downside direction is unverified and worth screening ourselves at n=1 on step count.
statement: Increasing Muon's Newton-Schulz iteration count beyond 5 does not improve final loss and only costs wall-clock time.

comparator: each optimizer's own best 16.8B-token configuration with only T_warmup varied; 124M Llama-like on FineWeb, batch 256x512
effect: sweep over T_warmup in {1.56%, 6.25%, 25%} of T (= {2k, 8k, 32k} steps at 128k total): 2000 steps best for most optimizers; exceptions Signum, Lion, Sophia and SF-AdamW prefer the longer 8k warmup; the 25%-of-Chinchilla rule is contradicted
locator: section 4.1 'Warmup ablation', Figure 10; appendix D.1 'Warmup ablation', Figure 22
notes: Transfer 3: the DIRECTION (small warmup fraction, and optimizer-dependent) transfers; the absolute count does not - 1.56% of our 600-1000 steps is only ~10-16 steps, well below anything they tested, so the linear extrapolation is unsafe and we should treat this as 'sweep warmup low, and expect the answer to differ between the Muon-owned and AdamW-owned parameter groups'. Sweep had only 3 (for AdamW, 5) points and one seed per point.
statement: At 124M params a short warmup of about 1.5% of total iterations was best for most optimizers, and the published recommendation of warming up over 25% of the Chinchilla-optimal duration was clearly worse.

comparator: identical OLMo2 baselines with RMSNorm, identical corpus (OLMo-mix-1124), same token budgets
effect: c4_en validation loss 3.011 -> 3.008 for OLMo2-550M at 400B tokens and 2.884 -> 2.879 for OLMo2-1B at 500B tokens; the MoE gain is larger (2.922 -> 2.900 at 1.3B/500B) and the authors attribute the dense shortfall to dense parameters already being sufficiently trained
locator: section 4.1 'Dense Models' and Table 1 (OLMo2-550M and OLMo2-1B rows)
notes: Transfer 1 and stance OPPOSES: every number in this paper comes from 400B-1000B token runs, the dense-model effect is 0.003-0.005 nats there, and the authors explicitly report the advantage GROWING with tokens - so the expected effect at 0.3-0.5B tokens is at or below zero. It also adds a per-normalization-layer matvec (x . beta^T), a tanh and two extra learnable vectors at every norm site including QK-norm, which in our launch-bound step is a real throughput cost for no demonstrated short-horizon benefit.
statement: On DENSE language models SeeDNorm's validation-loss improvement over RMSNorm is a few thousandths of a nat and the authors state the training-loss improvement widens as the token count increases.

comparator: OLMoE-1.3B baseline with RMSNorm, all ablations trained for 500B tokens on OLMoE-mix-0924
effect: alpha initialized to 10 gives c4_en loss 3.154 versus 2.900 at alpha=1 and 2.912 at alpha=0.1 (baseline RMSNorm 2.922), i.e. a large-init gain is much worse than doing nothing; replacing tanh with GeLU or Swish makes the model fail to converge, while sigmoid, tanh and hardtanh all converge and beat the baseline
locator: section 4.3 'Initialization of alpha' and 'Activation Function in SeeDNorm', Figure 4 and Table 4
notes: Transfer 2: the transferable content is the guardrail, not the method - any lever that makes a normalization gain depend on the activations must bound the gain path (saturating nonlinearity) and start it small, or it destabilizes training. Docked heavily because all ablations are 500B-token MoE runs at 1.3B params, n=1 per cell, and the sensitivity ordering could differ at 600 steps where the gain parameters have barely moved from init.
statement: For an input-dependent normalization gain, the initialization of the rescaling magnitude is stability-critical and an unbounded activation in the gain path prevents convergence entirely.

comparator: OLMoE-1.3B with RMSNorm, 500B tokens, identical corpus and hyperparameters
effect: c4_en loss 2.968 vs 2.922 baseline and PPL 19.45 vs 18.63; all five downstream accuracies drop (ARC-C 30.4 vs 32.3, ARC-E 61.9 vs 62.2, HellaSwag 53.2 vs 55.2, MMLU-Var 30.5 vs 32.4, PIQA 70.6 vs 72.6)
locator: section 4.1 'MoE Models' and Table 1 (OLMoE-1.3B-DyT row)
notes: Transfer 2: relevant only as opposing evidence against the tempting throughput lever of deleting RMSNorm's reduction (a real cost in a launch-bound step) in favor of a pointwise saturating activation. Not higher because it is a 500B-token MoE result at 1.3B params with n=1 and the ranking could plausibly differ in a 600-step run where normalization is doing more of the early conditioning work, not less.
statement: Replacing RMSNorm with DyT, a saturating activation that removes the normalization statistics, slows convergence and degrades both validation loss and every downstream task on a language model.

comparator: full-precision full-memory training of the same LLaMA models on C4 without data repetition, seqlen 256, global batch 512, LR tuned per model size, linear warmup 10% then cosine to 10% of peak; 10K/60K/100K steps for 60M/350M/1B
effect: LLaMA-60M perplexity 30.97 (full) -> 31.98 (r=1/128), 32.15 (r=1/256), 32.46 (r=1/512); but LLaMA-350M 18.80 -> 18.26/18.29/18.47 and LLaMA-1B 15.56 -> 15.00/15.00/15.10, i.e. an improvement at the two larger sizes
locator: appendix A, Table 2 (pretraining perplexity by model size and compression ratio); section 4.2
notes: Transfer 2 and stance OPPOSES: the only data point near our capacity (60M, 10K steps) shows a consistent DEGRADATION that worsens monotonically with compression, and the paper's headline 'quality preserved or improved' rests entirely on the 350M and 1B runs. This is a scale-dependence warning for any sequence-dimension activation approximation in the attention input path: the redundancy the method exploits appears not to be there yet at small capacity. n=1 per cell, perplexity only.
statement: Approximating the QKV projection weight gradients by compressing the saved input activations along the sequence dimension degrades perplexity at 60M params while improving it at 350M and 1B.

comparator: full-memory training on A100s; FlashAttention-v2 used throughout and the output projection deliberately left untouched to avoid perturbing gradients into FlashAttention
effect: QKV projection activation memory reduced up to 512x (LLaMA-1B: 3 GB -> 18 MB), which the authors note is ~20% of attention-block peak memory; all PAMM-trained weights use a reduced rate eta_tilde = 0.25 * eta 'for stability'; authors state implementing PAMM in CUDA to achieve its theoretical speedup is a future direction
locator: section 6 'Conclusion' (CUDA implementation listed as future work), appendix A (learning-rate scaling alpha=0.25), section 5 'Limitations'
notes: Transfer 0: memory is not a binding constraint for a 124M model on an H200, and the intervention as published adds Python/PyTorch-level compression work per layer per step with no fused kernel, which in our CPU-contended, launch-bound regime costs steps and therefore costs val_bpb. The forced 4x learning-rate reduction on those weights is an additional disqualifier at a 600-step horizon where every step of effective learning rate counts.
statement: The QKV activation compression method delivers activation-memory savings only; no wall-clock speedup is demonstrated and it requires a reduced learning rate on the affected weights for stability.

comparator: No trained baseline: this is the argmin of the RHS of a published LMO convergence bound (eq. 2) with all constants C_1=C_2=C_3=1. The only empirical support is a 160M PlainLM on <=5B SlimPajama tokens.
effect: eta*_T(b) proportional to b^{1/2} T^{-1/2}; practical rule eta_1 = eta_0 (T_0/T_1)^{1/2} when b and momentum are held fixed
locator: Theorem 1 (section 3.1, eq. 6-7) and Appendix A Table 2 regime (A)
notes: Transfer 2, not higher: the derivation assumes a CONSTANT learning rate, no warmup, no weight decay, no schedule and matched initialization, so 'eta*' is not the same object as our peak LR under a warmup+cooldown schedule. It is also a large-horizon asymptotic and Figure 1 shows a burn-in phase before the trends hold, which is exactly the 600-1000-step regime we live in. Directly contradicted empirically by 2604.27077, which fits -1/3 and calls the -1/2 exponent 'too large'. No seeds or uncertainty anywhere; the numerical verification is a grid over the bound, not over training runs.
statement: For LMO-type optimizers (Muon, signSGD/Adam surrogates, normalized SGD), minimizing a convergence-bound proxy at fixed batch size and fixed momentum gives an optimal learning rate scaling as T^{-1/2} with token budget, i.e. the transfer rule eta_1 = eta_0 (T_0/T_1)^{1/2}.

comparator: Same proxy-bound minimization as above; no training run tests momentum scaling in this paper.
effect: risk_T proportional to alpha^{1/2} b_max^{-1/2} (non-vanishing) at fixed alpha; restored to T^{-1/4} by alpha*_T(b) proportional to b T^{-1/2}, i.e. beta = 1-alpha driven toward 1 as the horizon grows
locator: Corollary 1 part 2, section 3.2; Theorem 2 (eq. 8)
notes: Transfer 2. Our batch IS hardware-capped at 524288 tokens/step, so the capped regime is the one that applies, and this is the paper's one argument that momentum is a real (not cosmetic) knob for us. But it is a bound, not a measurement; the prescription is asymptotic in T while our T is small; and the direction it prescribes (raise beta as steps grow) is the opposite of what a 600-step run's short averaging window might want. Blocker: no empirical validation of momentum scaling at any scale in this work.
statement: When batch size is capped by hardware, tuning only the learning rate at a fixed momentum leaves a non-vanishing noise floor proportional to alpha^{1/2} b_max^{-1/2} in the LMO proxy bound, and letting the momentum parameter alpha decrease with the token budget removes that floor.

comparator: Proxy bound at optimally tuned (eta, b) for arbitrary fixed momentum vs optimally tuned momentum; no measured loss.
effect: risk*_T(alpha) proportional to (1+alpha)^{1/4} T^{-1/4}; best possible gain from re-tuning alpha is 1.19x in the rate constant
locator: Corollary 1 part 1, section 3.2
notes: Registered as opposing evidence against spending budget on momentum tuning. Transfer 2 with a caveat that cuts the other way: the corollary's premise (batch free to grow) is FALSE for us, and the companion corollary (previous claim) says momentum matters more under a batch cap. So this bounds the payoff only in the regime we are not in. It also bounds a rate constant of a loose upper bound, which need not track val_bpb at all. Use it as a prior against momentum-sweeping, not as proof.
statement: If batch size can be tuned freely, re-tuning momentum changes the LMO proxy's asymptotic rate constant by at most a factor 2^{1/4} (about 1.19), so momentum tuning is close to irrelevant in that regime.

comparator: 160M PlainLM on SlimPajama, Adam betas fixed (0.9,0.95), 8% warmup then constant LR, grid over eta at each of 3 batch sizes; baseline is the other grid points, not a separate recipe.
effect: At T=5B tokens: eta*=0.001 at b=32, 0.003 at b=128, 0.01 at b=512. At b=32: eta* shifts from 0.003 to 0.001 after 2.5B tokens; at b=128 the switch point is not reached by 5B tokens.
locator: Figure 3 (section 4), empirical support experiment
notes: Transfer 3: 160M is the closest parameter scale in this batch to our 124M, and the two directions are usable priors. But n=1 per grid point with no seeds or error bars, only 3 batch sizes, constant-LR (not our cooldown recipe), and the token budgets (2.5-5B) are 8-16x ours, so the 'decreases with horizon' half is measured entirely outside our horizon range and the switch point at b=128 was never even reached. The 'larger batch wants larger LR' half is the more usable one for us since our per-step batch is very large.
statement: In a 160M-parameter transformer grid search with 8% warmup and a constant learning rate, the best constant learning rate increased with batch size and decreased with token budget at fixed batch size.

comparator: WSD sweeps with cooldown fraction in {0,0.05,...,0.95}, peak rate tuned separately at every point, mean over 512 runs (8 for the deep linear net), against the same optimizer at cf=0.
effect: Cooldown gain (loss at cf=0 divided by best-cf loss) on the anisotropic quadratic: 1.0x for SGD, 1.7e6x for signSGD, 3.8e5x for normalized SGD; 5.8e6x for signSGD on a deep linear net. Measured floor exponent eta^{2.00+-0.01}; closed-form floor constant matches simulation within 0.7%.
locator: Proposition 2 and Remark 3 (section 4); Table 1 (section 5); Table 3 WSD sweeps (section 10)
notes: Internal validity 4 because the stationary law is solved exactly and simulation matches the closed form across the whole parameter range with >=1e5 post-burn-in steps and >=100 chains. Transfer only 2: every model is a quadratic, a quartic, a deep linear net or a 2-layer MLP -- there is no transformer and no language modelling anywhere. It matters to us only because Muon (spectral-norm normalized) and AdamW are both in the 'cannot self-anneal' class by the paper's criterion, which predicts our recipe genuinely needs decay to ~0. It gives no guidance on HOW to decay (see the interior-fraction claim).
statement: Under gradient-proportional (multiplicative) noise, sign-based and normalized updates sit on a last-iterate loss floor of order eta^2 that only driving the learning rate to zero removes, whereas plain SGD self-anneals and its optimal cooldown fraction is 0.

comparator: Two-layer ReLU 64-128-10 on scikit-learn digits (1500 images, minibatch 32), WSD sweep with peak rate tuned per point, 5 seeds, min-max bands, versus the same optimizer at cf=0.
effect: Adam cf*=0, ending 3.5x worse at strong cooldown; SGD cf*=0, 2.4x worse at cf=0.95; only signSGD improved (7.7e-2 to 6.6e-2). Adam's per-step update norm as a fraction of a full sign step fell from 0.33 to 0.02 while the gradient norm dropped 500x.
locator: Figure 2 and 'A real-data check' paragraph, section 10
notes: Registered as opposing evidence: it shows the 'normalized optimizers need cooldown' rule is not automatic for Adam. Transfer scored 1, not higher, because the workload is a 1500-image multi-epoch MLP sitting near interpolation, where the measured noise exponent is 0.56 and gradients collapse 500x; single-epoch 124M LM pretraining on FineWeb is nowhere near interpolation, gradients do not collapse like that, and the cooldown-helps result is empirically settled for LLM pretraining. Keep it visible as a mechanism warning (measure whether our Adam/Muon update norms are actually staying order-1 late in the run) rather than as a reason to cut cooldown.
statement: On the paper's one real-data workload, Adam's optimal cooldown fraction was 0 and strong cooldown made the final training loss 3.5x worse, because Adam's measured update magnitude shrank with the gradient instead of staying order-1.

comparator: Same WSD sweep protocol (cf grid of 20 values, peak rate tuned per point) within the same optimizer.
effect: Broad plateau over cooldown fraction in [0.4, 0.95] on the anisotropic quadratic and [0.8, 0.95] on the real-data signSGD run; the authors state the argmin within the plateau is not determined and Table 3 should be read for the cf=0 vs plateau contrast only.
locator: 'Dissociation across models' paragraph, section 10; Table 3 caption
notes: Transfer 2: usable as a prior that fine-grained cooldown-fraction sweeps are low-yield relative to the noise floor of our A/B harness, but demonstrated only on toy landscapes. The plateau shape may well be narrower on a real transformer. This is a reason NOT to spend runs on cooldown-fraction knob-tuning.
statement: For sign-based and normalized optimizers the optimal cooldown fraction sits on a broad plateau near full decay rather than at a sharp argmin.

comparator: The paper's own full WSD sweeps versus reported practice in LLM pretraining (cited refs 7, 15, 2).
effect: Every optimum found is either 0 (SGD, multiplicative noise) or maximal / a plateau near full decay (normalized methods, or any method under additive noise). Interior optima are attributed to non-stationarity, feature learning or finite-data effects, none of which the model contains.
locator: Section 11, 'Not the interior WSD fraction'
notes: Boundary claim, stated by the authors as an explicit limitation, which is why internal validity is high. Transfer 2 and the value is negative: it tells us not to import this line of theory to choose a cooldown fraction for our run, and that the mechanism explaining an interior optimum is not yet in any stationary model. Useful for pruning a whole class of proposed schedule interventions rather than for launching one.
statement: No model in this study -- across quadratic, quartic, deep linear and a real MLP workload, and across noise structures and optimizers -- produces an interior optimal cooldown fraction, so the roughly 0.2-0.35 fractions used in real pretraining lie outside stationary landscape-and-noise geometry.

comparator: Same BLaLM (mLSTM token mixer) architecture, BabyLM strict track (100M words, 10 epochs, context 512, effective batch 64), a SINGLE shared learning rate of 4e-4 for both optimizers, cosine decay with 10% warmup.
effect: Validation perplexity 7.95 +- 0.15 (Muon hybrid) vs 11.21 +- 0.11 (AdamW), 3 runs each; zero-shot average 36.24 +- 1.16 vs 35.75 +- 1.74 (a much smaller and overlapping gap).
locator: Section 6.3 Experiment 3, Table 4
notes: Internal validity 2: 3 seeds is decent but both optimizers were run at one shared LR with no per-optimizer tuning, and their own Table 5 shows perplexity moving from 9.83 to 7.64 across the LR range for Muon alone, so the 11.21 vs 7.95 gap is not separable from LR mis-specification for AdamW. Transfer 2: this confirms the hybrid we ALREADY run rather than offering a new lever, the backbone is an mLSTM not softmax attention, and the regime is 10 epochs over 100M words rather than a single epoch over FineWeb. Value is confirmatory only; do not treat it as a proposal.
statement: A Muon-on-matrices plus AdamW-on-scalars hybrid reached lower validation perplexity than AdamW on all parameters under a 100M-word, 10-epoch budget, with lower run-to-run spread.

comparator: Base BLaLM (mLSTM) at a fixed LR of 4e-4 with Muon, same 10-epoch budget, best-checkpoint selection by downstream average.
effect: Validation perplexity 20.01 -> 12.37 (strict-small, 10M words) and 7.95 -> 6.48 (strict, 100M words); note the zero-shot average went DOWN in both tracks (37.27 -> 36.41 and 35.08 -> 34.57).
locator: Section 6.5 Experiment 5, Table 6 (row '- ShortConv')
notes: Internal validity 1: n=1 per configuration, LR frozen at 4e-4 for every arm, and the strict-small base at that LR (20.01) is anomalously worse than the same base model at every other LR in Table 5 (15.73-16.61), so the 20.01 -> 12.37 delta is largely against a broken baseline. Checkpoints were also selected on downstream average, not perplexity. Transfer 2: short convs on Q/K are cheap and implementable on our attention path, and our objective is perplexity-like so the downstream regression does not count against it here, but the mechanism was only ever shown to help a linear-attention (mLSTM) mixer where it supplies local mixing our sliding-window attention already provides. Costs a per-step conv, which is charged against step count.
statement: Adding depthwise 1D short convolutions on the query and key projections before the token mixer lowered validation perplexity in both BabyLM tracks.

comparator: Same BLaLM/Muon setup across LR values; the comparator is the other LR grid points.
effect: Strict-track validation perplexity 9.83 (2e-4), 8.46 (3e-4), 8.06 (4e-4), 7.74 (5e-4), 7.76 (6e-4), 7.64 (7e-4), 7.70 (5.5e-4); the downstream-average optimum sat at 5.5e-4, i.e. perplexity and downstream disagree about the best LR.
locator: Section 6.4 Experiment 4, Table 5 (strict track PPL column)
notes: Internal validity 1: n=1 per LR, and the strict-small column reports the identical perplexity 16.41 at three different LRs, which is a reporting or checkpoint-selection artifact that undermines the whole table. Transfer 2, direction only: it suggests that in a data-limited regime the perplexity-optimal LR can sit at or above the top of a conventional sweep, and it warns that selecting LR on a downstream metric picks a different point than selecting on perplexity -- relevant because our sole objective IS the perplexity-like metric. Do not import the absolute LR values: different optimizer scaling, different architecture, batch 64x512 tokens versus our 524288.
statement: In a Muon learning-rate sweep under a 100M-word 10-epoch budget, validation perplexity fell monotonically across the entire swept range from 2e-4 to 7e-4 without reaching an interior optimum.

comparator: Same LLaMA-architecture models, 6.6B-token Pile subset, single H200, bf16, cosine + 10% warmup, batch 130k tokens, 3 seeds averaged; the two arms differ only in which optimizer touches the embedding table.
effect: Test perplexity 192.7 / 117.8 / 98.84 at 270M / 0.6B / 1.3B for SinkGD applied to all 2D weights including embeddings, versus 34.30 / 32.85 / 28.71 for the identical method with AdamW retained on the embedding layer. Attributed to sparse, high-variance Zipfian embedding gradients; the authors note the failure persists even with the LR retuned.
locator: Section 2.3 and Figure 1 (motivating experiment); Table 2 rows 'SinkGD-Pure' vs 'SinkGD-Hybrid'
notes: Transfer 3, the highest in this batch for an optimizer claim: 270M is close to our 124M, the run is a single-H200 from-scratch pretrain, and the conclusion applies directly to our parameter-group split, where AdamW handles the token embedding and value-embedding tables while Muon handles matrices. It is strong evidence against any 'unify the optimizer across all 2D parameters' proposal, including extending Muon-style orthogonalization to the embedding or VE tables. Held below 4 because 6.6B tokens is >10x our token budget and the failing method (SinkGD) is not Muon, so the result is about stateless normalization generally rather than Muon specifically.
statement: Applying a stateless normalizing optimizer to the embedding matrix instead of keeping a stateful adaptive optimizer there is catastrophic for perplexity at every scale tested.

comparator: Same models, data, budget and 3-seed protocol as above; arms differ only in whether dense 2D weights get the sign rule or the normalizing rule.
effect: Test perplexity 116.0 / 179.0 / 216.0 at 270M / 0.6B / 1.3B for the sign rule applied to all parameters, versus 29.95 / 26.71 / 24.33 when dense 2D weights keep a matrix-aware normalizing rule. The pure-sign arm gets monotonically worse with scale.
locator: Table 2 row 'SAGE-Pure' vs 'SAGE-Hybrid'; section 4.1 Optimizers and Baselines
notes: Transfer 3: it supports keeping a matrix-aware rule (our Muon) on dense weights and is a clean prune of the 'replace Muon with a cheaper sign-based update to buy throughput' direction, which is otherwise attractive at a 300-second budget because Newton-Schulz costs FLOPs. 270M/single-H200 makes the scale credible. Held below 4 because the comparator normalizer is SinkGD, not Muon, and the token budget is 6.6B.
statement: Applying the sign-based update to dense 2D weights as well as embeddings, instead of a matrix-aware normalizing rule, is far worse than the hybrid and degrades further as model size grows.

comparator: AdamW and other baselines at 'the learning rates favored by their original works' plus a sanity check at larger LRs; SAGE and unpublished hybrids got a fresh grid search. Same 6.6B Pile tokens, 3 seeds.
effect: Test perplexity 29.95 vs 37.35 (270M), 26.71 vs 31.74 (0.6B), 24.33 vs 27.81 (1.3B) against AdamW; also beats Lion-Hybrid (32.10 / 28.73 / 28.40) and SinkGD-Hybrid (34.30 / 32.85 / 28.71).
locator: Table 2, section 4.2 'Performance at Scale'
notes: Internal validity only 2 despite 3 seeds: the baselines were not tuned on a matched grid, and Lion-on-everything (30.24 at 270M) beating AdamW (37.35) is a strong smell that the AdamW arm was under-tuned, which inflates every reported margin. Transfer 2: the paper NEVER compares against Muon and says so in its own Limitations, so the delta against our actual baseline is unmeasured; the dense-layer half is not a drop-in for us. Only the embedding-side mechanism is worth extracting, and see the LR-headroom claim for that.
statement: A hybrid using a normalizing rule on dense weights and a bounded sign-with-damper rule on embeddings and 1D parameters reached lower test perplexity than AdamW at every scale tested from 270M to 1.3B.

comparator: Lion-Hybrid with an identical structure and the same learning rates, same 270M-1.3B models and 6.6B-token budget.
effect: Grid over {1e-4, 2e-4, 5e-4, 1e-3, 2e-3}: Lion-Hybrid peaks at 1e-4 and 'collapses shortly after', the damped variant peaks at 1e-3. Figure 3 shows the damper is sparse -- most dimensions stay clipped at scale 1.0 and only a few high-variance dimensions are damped, with damping becoming sparser after the first ~500 steps.
locator: Section 4.4 'Learning Rate Tuning and Stability'; Lemma 3.2; Figure 3
notes: Transfer 2. The mechanism -- a cheap per-dimension bounded damper on the embedding/VE parameter group to buy learning-rate headroom -- is implementable in train.py at O(d) memory and negligible FLOPs, and higher usable LR is a plausible lever at 600-1000 steps. But the headroom was demonstrated against Lion, not against AdamW or Muon, so it is not established that our current embedding optimizer is the one leaving LR headroom on the table. No seed count is given for the LR grid, and the damper's benefit is entangled with the SinkGD dense-layer rescaling the paper says was 'critical for stability'.
statement: Bounding the per-dimension embedding update magnitude at 1.0 with an O(d) L1-EMA relative damper kept training stable at a roughly 10x higher learning rate than the undamped sign baseline, which collapsed just above its optimum.

comparator: LLaMA2-130M, C4, 10000 steps, global batch 512, sequence length 1024 (~5.2B tokens), bf16, 1000 warmup steps, cosine to 10%, weight decay 0.1, a SINGLE fixed learning rate of 1e-3 shared by all optimizers.
effect: Rate improves from O(T^{-1/4}) to Otilde(T^{-1/3}) (and from Otilde(T^{-1/2}) to Otilde(T^{-2/3}) under PL); on LLaMA2-130M / C4, Muon-VR2 gives a faster drop and lower final train and validation loss than AdamW, Muon-EMA and Muon-VR1. No numeric losses are reported.
locator: Theorem 4.3 and Table 1; section 5 'LLaMA2 on C4' and Figure 2
notes: Internal validity 2: the LM result is curves only with no numbers, no seed count and no per-optimizer LR tuning (the CIFAR-10 arm got 5 seeds and a 7-point LR grid; the LM arm got neither). Transfer 2: 130M and 12 layers is close to our scale, but 10000 steps and 5.2B tokens is 10x our horizon, and the entire proposition is about the asymptotic-T regime where a T^{-1/3} vs T^{-1/4} distinction can be read. See the paired throughput claim -- at a fixed 300s wall clock this variant is very likely net-negative.
statement: A two-batch variance-reduced Muon variant attains an Otilde(T^{-1/3}) ergodic rate, versus O(T^{-1/4}) for standard Muon, and reached lower training and validation loss than AdamW and both standard Muon variants on a 130M language model.

comparator: VR2 versus VR1/EMA on the same task, compared on wall-clock time rather than on step count.
effect: VR2 needs grad f(X_t; xi_t) and grad f(X_{t-1}; xi_t), i.e. two backward passes per optimizer step; the authors show the cost in wall-clock (Fig 1c) and call the overhead potentially prohibitive at scale, positioning VR1 as the pragmatic alternative with 'minimal degradation'.
locator: Section 3 (Option VR2, eq. 5, 'one gradient evaluation per step versus two'); Remark 5.1; Figure 1c (test accuracy vs wall-clock time)
notes: Registered as opposing evidence and scored transfer 3 because the objection bites hardest exactly at our operating point: our objective is val_bpb within 300 CHARGED SECONDS, so roughly doubling per-step gradient cost roughly halves step count, and step count dominates val_bpb at fixed wall clock. The per-iteration win in Figure 2 is measured against steps, not seconds; the authors' own wall-clock figure and Remark 5.1 are the honest reading. Their caveat that a larger batch mitigates the noise VR2 targets also applies to us, since our per-step batch is already 524288 tokens.
statement: The variance-reduced Muon variant that achieves the improved rate requires two gradient evaluations per step, and the authors state its computational overhead can be prohibitive and recommend the one-gradient approximation when compute efficiency is the priority.

comparator: Worst-case rates under identical L-smoothness, unbiased-gradient and bounded-variance assumptions; not a training comparison.
effect: Muon-EMA: O(T^{-1/4}) with O(1) batch. Muon-VR1 (equivalent, after rescaling M_t, to the practical Muon update M_t = mu*C_t + grad f): also O(T^{-1/4}). Only VR2 reaches Otilde(T^{-1/3}).
locator: Table 1 (rows 'Ours / Option EMA' and 'Ours / Option VR1'); Theorems 4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.5
notes: Opposing evidence against treating the Nesterov/momentum-form detail of our Muon as a promising lever: theory says it buys no rate, and the paper's own LM curves put VR1 close to EMA. Transfer 2 -- these are worst-case upper bounds under assumptions (bounded variance, L-smoothness) that language modelling violates, so they cannot rule out a real empirical difference, but they argue the expected effect size is small relative to our noise floor. Useful for pruning, not for launching.
statement: The Nesterov-style one-batch momentum form of Muon used in practice has the same O(T^{-1/4}) worst-case convergence rate as plain EMA momentum Muon; only the two-batch variance-reduced form improves the rate.
