statement: When AdamW's second-moment memory is much longer than its momentum memory (beta1^2 < beta2), a single heavy-tailed gradient outlier can inflate the denominator long enough to suppress subsequent updates, and there exists a construction where the average gradient norm then stays bounded away from zero.

comparator: Muon without Nesterov (C_t = M_t) under the same smoothness and bounded-variance assumptions, same schedules (constant / cosine / polynomial / diminishing) and batch rules
effect: with Nesterov the bound gains a sixth term C6 * sum(eta_t/sqrt(b_t)) / sum(eta_t) with C6 = 2(1-beta)*sigma*sqrt(n), so the batch-noise constant becomes D4 = (C5+C6)/(1-beta) >= D3 = C5/(1-beta); the asymptotic rate is identical (O(1/T + eta + 1/sqrt(b))) for both variants under every learning-rate and batch-size combination examined
locator: Theorem 3.1(i) vs 3.1(ii); Corollary 3.1(i) constants D3 = C5/(1-beta) vs D4 = (C5+C6)/(1-beta), C6 = 2(1-beta)*sigma*sqrt(n)
notes: Registered as opposing evidence on the campaign's live contradiction about whether Nesterov helps Muon: theory gives Nesterov no advantage here and a strictly larger noise constant. Internal validity 2 because comparing two upper bounds proves nothing about actual performance (the bound could simply be loose for the Nesterov variant), and there are no experiments at all in this paper. Transfer 2: the toggle is one line in our Muon update and the claim is about exactly our algorithm, but the evidence class (asymptotic bound, no measurement) cannot resolve a sub-gate effect. Contrast with 2509.01440, which always uses Nesterov for Muon-like methods and finds Nesterov best for Signum.
statement: In this convergence analysis, Muon with Nesterov momentum carries an extra additive noise term in its upper bound that is absent without Nesterov, so the derived bound with Nesterov is never tighter than without it at any horizon.

comparator: the four schedules of eq (4) and the two batch rules of eq (5), all under the same smoothness / bounded-variance assumptions
effect: identical O(1/T + eta + 1/sqrt(b)) bound for constant, cosine and polynomial-decay LR at constant batch; O(1/sqrt(T)) requires eta=O(1/T) with b=O(T), and O(1/T) requires b=O(T^2) or an exponentially growing batch
locator: Corollary 3.1(i),(iii),(v) and Table 1 rows (R1),(R2)
notes: Boundary claim: it says this class of theory cannot rank schedule shapes for Muon, so schedule proposals in our campaign must be justified empirically, not by convergence-rate arguments. Transfer 2, with a hard blocker on the part that does discriminate -- the rate improvements all come from growing the batch size (b=O(T) or b*delta^t), which is impossible for us because prepare.py is frozen at 524288 tokens/step. No experiments in the paper; constants D1..D4 are unquantified, so the bound cannot be evaluated at T~1000.
statement: For Muon at fixed horizon T, constant, cosine-annealing and polynomial-decay learning rates all yield the same convergence upper bound O(1/T + eta + 1/sqrt(b)); only coupling eta and batch size to T changes the rate.

comparator: AdamW on the same model, batch 512, single H100, mean over runs
effect: single H100, ViT-B/16 full recipe: AdamW 2557 img/s (1.00x), MUD 2241 (0.88x), Muon 1980 (0.77x) on ImageNet-100; on Pl@ntNet AdamW 2247, MUD 2251 (1.00x), Muon 2020 (0.90x); the authors also state the overhead is generally larger in language models than in this vision setting
locator: appendix A, Table 3
notes: Transfer 2 and registered as a boundary because it is the cost side of every Muon/NS mechanism we might propose in a wall-clock-bounded frame: 10-23% throughput is 10-23% fewer steps at fixed 300s, which at our operating point is a first-order loss. Discounted heavily -- it is ViT-B/16 image classification on H100, not a 124M LM on H200 under torch.compile, the two datasets disagree by 13 points on the same measurement, and no variance is reported. The one transferable inference is directional and must be re-measured locally: cheaper orthogonalization (fewer NS steps, MUD-style) trades quality for throughput and did not pay off in their setting.
statement: Muon's approximate orthogonalization costs a measurable fraction of single-GPU training throughput (up to ~23% on ViT-B/16), and a cheaper approximate-orthogonalization alternative did not recover enough throughput to offset its weaker quality.

comparator: AdamW at its own swept lr (3e-4 best of four) vs Muon at its own swept lr (1e-3 best of three), ViT-B/16, batch 512, 15000 steps, cosine to 0.05*lr_max, four augmentation recipes
effect: Pl@ntNet macro top-1: Muon leads AdamW by +21.40 under the full recipe but only +4.67 under No Mix; AdamW is actively hurt by the full recipe (top-1/macro 63.58/16.30 full vs 71.04/28.90 with mixing removed) while Muon is best under the full recipe (80.39/37.70) and degrades as components are removed (73.93/31.52)
locator: section 3, Table 1 and Figure 1 (Pl@ntNet-300K and ImageNet-100, ViT-B/16)
notes: Boundary claim about the portability of optimizer verdicts, not about vision. Transfer 2: our data pipeline is frozen so the specific recipe levers (Mixup/CutMix/label smoothing/RandAugment) are inapplicable and the domain is image classification, but the structural lesson bites -- a 4x swing in the Muon-vs-AdamW gap from a data-side change means published Muon-family margins measured on other data recipes cannot be assumed at our fixed FineWeb-like shards. Internal validity 3: clean 4-cell factorial with per-optimizer lr sweeps, but single seed for the classification tables (3 seeds only for the segmentation table).
statement: The size of Muon's advantage over AdamW depends strongly on the data recipe, to the point that the recipe which maximizes Muon's result is the one that makes AdamW worse.

comparator: AdamW scaling law fitted at 1.2B Qwen3-style params over Chinchilla ratios 1x-8x, DCLM+StarCoder+ProofPile2 mixture
effect: 20-30% token-equivalent speedup for MuonH vs ~10% for MuonW, over the AdamW scaling law fit across Chinchilla 1x-8x
locator: section 3.2 'End-to-end speedup', figure 2
notes: transfer=2: demonstrated only at 1.2B and at Chinchilla-optimal-or-longer horizons, and the speedup is explicitly described as GROWING with training duration, i.e. the opposite of our ~1000-step regime. The mechanism itself is cheap and self-contained (two Frobenius norms per matrix per step, O(N^2), no SVD) so it is implementable as a train.py edit without a new knob. No seed counts or error bars are reported for the speedup fits; the token-equivalent metric is a scaling-law extrapolation, not a paired run.
statement: Wrapping Muon in Hyperball (fix each matrix's Frobenius norm to its init value R and take a step of length eta*R along the Frobenius-normalized update, then reproject) sustains 20-30% token-equivalent speedup over an AdamW scaling law at 1.2B params, where plain Muon with decoupled weight decay gives only about 10%.

comparator: public modded-nanogpt Track 3 logs, fixed 124M-scale model and data, tuned MuonW and NorMuonW baselines
effect: MuonH and MuonW both reach the ~3.279 band at 3325 steps (0.0008 loss difference); AdamH 4875 vs AdamW 5625 steps (-13.3% steps)
locator: section 3.2, figure 4 (modded-nanogpt Track 3 log comparison)
notes: transfer=3: this is the closest setting in the paper to ours (nanogpt-scale model, few-thousand steps, step-count objective) and it says the Hyperball lever is an Adam lever, not a Muon lever. internal_validity=2 because these are single public leaderboard entries with no seeds and heterogeneous tuning effort across entries. Directly opposes the headline 1.2B claim above when read at our operating point; register both.
statement: On the modded-nanogpt Track 3 benchmark, which fixes model and data and scores optimizers by step count, Hyperball buys essentially nothing for Muon (MuonH 3.2782 in 3325 steps vs MuonW 3.2790 in 3325 steps) even though it saves ~13% of steps for Adam (AdamH 3.2741 in 4875 steps vs AdamW 3.2790 in 5625 steps).

comparator: paired 1.2B AdamW runs differing only in the (eta,lambda) split at fixed product
effect: two 1.2B AdamW runs at (eta,lambda)=(0.002,0.2) and (0.004,0.1), same product 4e-4, have nearly overlapping train loss curves while layer-9 Q/K norms roughly double in the larger-eta run
locator: section 4.3, Phenomenon 3, figure 10; theorem 4.6 and eq. (39)/(43)
notes: transfer=2: the theory assumes stationarity reached from an 'infinite history' and constant hyperparameters, which a ~1000-step run with warmup and decay never reaches; the equilibrium radius R* is approached on a 1/(eta*lambda) timescale that likely exceeds our whole run. Useful mainly as a warning that separately sweeping our AdamW lr and wd is largely a one-dimensional sweep, and as a caution that any wd change should be read as an angular-step change. n=2 runs, no seeds.
statement: For AdamW on scale-invariant matrix blocks, holding the product eta*lambda fixed leaves the training loss nearly unchanged while the equilibrium weight norm scales proportionally to eta, so learning rate and weight decay are redundant along the curve eta*lambda = const.

comparator: WD vs no-WD 1.2B AdamW runs sharing warmup+decay schedule; MuonH vs MuonW at 1.2B
effect: qualitative crossover: larger effective angular step raises early loss (hill-direction oscillation) and lowers final loss after decay; no crossover-step number is given
locator: section 3.2 ('Hyperball starts slightly worse but overtakes WD as the learning rate decays'); section 4.3 Phenomenon 4, figure 11
notes: transfer=2: this is the single most important caveat for our operating point. Any lever whose payoff is 'oscillate more now, collect after the decay' is scored against a 300s / ~1000-step budget where the decay phase is a few hundred steps and the crossover may simply not arrive. Explains mechanistically why the 1.2B Hyperball win does not reproduce as a step saving on nanogpt Track 3. No measurement of where the crossover sits as a fraction of training.
statement: Norm-controlled training (Hyperball, and weight decay versus no weight decay under an identical learning-rate schedule) starts at a HIGHER loss than its comparator and only crosses over to a lower loss once the learning rate decays.

comparator: single-matrix microbenchmark on one NVIDIA A40, torch tensors, d_in = d_out = d in {1024,2048,4096}
effect: NS orthogonalization is ~60x the per-matrix cost of column-wise normalization at d=1024 and ~200x the cost of sign; exact SVD is a further ~13x on top of NS
locator: section 2.1, table 1 (timing of normalization methods)
notes: transfer=3: our hidden matrices are near d=512-2048 and the ns_steps knob is already exposed, so this directly prices the ns knob. internal_validity=3 not 4: the number of NS iterations is not stated, dtype is not stated, and it is a microbenchmark not an end-to-end step time, so it cannot be converted into our steps/second without measurement. Caveat for us specifically: our scope is input-pipeline bound with GPU capacity comparatively free, so a 6 ms/matrix optimizer cost may be absorbed rather than charged - measure before assuming it costs steps.
statement: Newton-Schulz singular-value normalization of a d x d matrix costs about 6.03 ms at d=1024 and 14.41 ms at d=4096 on an A40, versus 0.10 ms for column-wise, 0.09 ms for row-wise and 0.03 ms for sign normalization; exact SVD costs 79.77 ms at d=1024.

comparator: Muon (Moonlight implementation) on LLaMA 60M-350M, C4, seq len 256, batch 512, 1.4B-7.8B tokens, cosine + 10% warmup, learning rates swept per method
effect: eval perplexity: singular-value-normalized SGD 34.15 / 25.25 / 18.73 at 60M / 130M / 350M vs Muon 28.86 / 22.20 / 16.70 (a 3.05 ppl gap at 130M); all four momentum-free normalizations lose to Muon
locator: section 2.1, table 2 (steepest-descent under four norms vs Muon and Adam)
notes: transfer=3: same parameter scale as ours (60M-350M brackets our 124M) and the comparison is the momentum term of the exact update we run. Argues that momentum settings (our 0.85->0.95 ramp) are a first-order lever and that any change that weakens the momentum buffer should be expected to cost more than the orthogonalization itself. Caveat: their token budgets (~20 tokens/param) are ~5x ours, and the momentum-free arm may simply need a different learning rate than the swept range allowed.
statement: Orthogonalized (singular-value / Newton-Schulz normalized) steepest descent WITHOUT momentum is substantially worse than Muon at LLaMA pretraining scale, so Muon's advantage is not attributable to the orthogonalization alone.

comparator: Muon (Moonlight implementation) on LLaMA models, C4, identical token budgets, per-method learning-rate sweeps via wandb
effect: eval perplexity 22.57 vs Muon 22.20 at 130M, and 16.32 vs Muon 16.70 at 350M; full SCALE at 1B is 14.25 vs Muon 14.18
locator: section 2.2, table 3; section 4, table 5
notes: transfer=3: a MECHANISM, not a knob - it swaps the expensive NS map for a 0.10 ms column normalization, so it is the natural companion experiment to the NS-cost claim, and it is a self-contained train.py edit. Downgraded from 4 because the win is only at >=130M (see the opposing 60M claim), the comparison is at ~20 tokens/param rather than our ~4, and no seeds or repeats are reported - the 22.57 vs 22.20 and 16.32 vs 16.70 gaps are within plausible single-run noise.
statement: Replacing Newton-Schulz orthogonalization with column-wise (output-dimension) gradient normalization, while keeping first-order momentum only on the output layer, matches or beats Muon at 130M and 350M LLaMA pretraining.

comparator: same LLaMA 60M / C4 / 1.4B-token setup, per-method LR sweep
effect: 60M eval perplexity 30.81 (column-wise + last-layer momentum) vs 28.86 (Muon), i.e. +6.8% relative; the singular-value + last-layer-momentum variant is also worse at 60M (31.20)
locator: section 2.2, table 3 and section 4, table 5 (60M column)
notes: transfer=3: 60M is the nearest scale below our 124M, and the reported trend is monotone in model size AGAINST the substitution at small scale, which is exactly where we sit. Registers the boundary on the previous claim: do not read 'column normalization replaces NS' as scale-free. The paper offers no mechanism for the size dependence, so the direction of the trend at 124M is an interpolation.
statement: At the smallest model size tested (60M), column-wise normalization with last-layer-only momentum is clearly worse than Muon, and the gap closes only as model size grows.

comparator: large-batch (512) gradient estimate as a proxy for the true gradient vs training-batch (32) gradients, SGD with column-wise normalization, LLaMA 130M
effect: lm_head gradient variance is highest across training; adding momentum only there drops its variance to a very low level and also lowers the embedding layer's variance
locator: section 2.2, figure 3 (a)-(b) and theorem 2.1 / remark 2.1
notes: transfer=3: 130M is our scale and the layer partition (embeddings/lm_head on AdamW, hidden matrices on Muon) is exactly the split our hybrid already uses, so this is direct mechanistic support for the current parameter partition and an argument that momentum/beta1 on the AdamW group is a higher-leverage knob than momentum on the Muon group. Variance is estimated with a 512-example batch as ground truth, which is itself noisy; theorem 2.1 assumes no normalization for tractability.
statement: In LLaMA 130M pretraining the stochastic-gradient variance of the output layer (lm_head) is the largest of any layer for most of training, followed by the embedding layer, which is why applying first-order momentum to only those layers recovers most of the benefit of full momentum.

comparator: 12-layer RoPE transformer, d=1024, QK-norm, 206M params, FineWeb-Edu 10B, seq 1024, batch 64, 100K steps, cosine + 10% warmup, NAdamW paired optimizer
effect: validation CE 3.01 (vanilla Muon) vs 3.27 (MuonMax) vs 3.43 (EF-MuonMax) on LM; on CIFAR-10 the order flips to MuonMax 0.265 < vanilla Muon 0.287 < EF-MuonMax 0.388
locator: section 5 'Results', table 1; appendix F.2
notes: transfer=2: model scale (206M) and data (FineWeb-Edu) are close to ours, but 100K steps at 65K tokens/step is a 100x longer horizon than our ~1000 steps, and the tuning is badly asymmetric - vanilla Muon inherited hyperparameters from a 400-run init2winit sweep while MuonMax got 30 trials, so part of the 0.26 CE gap is tuning budget, not algorithm. Actionable reading: do not spend our budget migrating to a regularized/normed Muon variant on the strength of vision results. Single run per configuration, no seeds.
statement: On a 206M nanoGPT-style transformer trained on FineWeb-Edu, vanilla Muon reaches a lower validation cross-entropy (3.01) than the max-norm regularized variant MuonMax (3.27) and than error-feedback MuonMax (3.43), reversing the ordering the same authors observe on CIFAR-10.

comparator: MuonMax with an identical norm choice and identical 30-60 trial hyperparameter sweep per method
effect: EF-MuonMax is worse than MuonMax on both tasks: 0.388 vs 0.265 validation CE on CIFAR-10 and 3.43 vs 3.27 on LM
locator: section 4.2 (theorem 4.2), section 5 'Discussion', table 1
notes: transfer=2: the specific EF mechanism is not something we would adopt, but the claim is a strong prior against the whole class of 'make Muon provably converge' modifications, which is the class most of the optimizer_numeric literature produces. The authors themselves draw the AMSGrad-vs-Adam analogy. Scored 2 not 3 because both demonstrations are far from our horizon and the negative result is only two tasks.
statement: Adding error feedback to Muon restores a provable anytime convergence rate on convex Lipschitz functions but degrades measured performance on both image classification and language modeling.

comparator: non-Euclidean subgradient descent on a convex Lipschitz counterexample adapted from Karimireddy et al.
effect: non-convergence for all learning-rate schedules; the almost-every-initialization strengthening only for beta in [0,1/2)
locator: section 1.1 contributions, counterexamples 3.3/3.4, proposition 3.2; section 7 'Limitations'
notes: transfer=1: pure worst-case theory with no measurable prediction at 124M/1000 steps, and the authors state their own experiments contradict acting on it. Registered because it explicitly carves out the practical regime (beta=0.95, beta ramps, NS approximation) as UNCOVERED - which means it is not evidence against our 0.85->0.95 momentum ramp, and the limitations section even notes that the interesting stochastic convergence proofs are the ones with beta_t increasing toward 1, weakly consistent with a ramp.
statement: Muon reduces exactly to signed momentum on functions of a matrix diagonal and provably fails to converge on convex Lipschitz functions, but the counterexample that holds for almost every initialization requires momentum beta in [0, 1/2), excludes any beta scheduler, and assumes exact rather than Newton-Schulz orthogonalization.

comparator: 160M transformer (PlainLM), SlimPajama, Adam betas (0.9,0.95), 8% warmup then CONSTANT learning rate, grid search over eta at each batch size, up to 5B tokens
effect: at b=32 the optimal eta shifts from 0.003 to 0.001 after 2.5B tokens; at T=5B tokens the optimal eta is 0.001 at b=32, 0.003 at b=128 and 0.01 at b=512 (roughly a sqrt(b) trend)
locator: section 4, figure 3 (160M PlainLM on SlimPajama); theorem 1 part 2
notes: transfer=3: 160M and a real LM objective, and the direction is the one that matters for us - our ~500M-token budget sits at the extreme short-horizon end of their curve, so the prediction is that our optimal learning rate is HIGHER than any recipe tuned at Chinchilla-scale horizons. internal_validity=2: a coarse log grid, single runs, constant-LR (no decay) so it does not directly price a decayed schedule, and the paper calls it 'qualitative empirical support'.
statement: At a fixed batch size the empirically optimal constant learning rate decreases as the token budget grows, and at a fixed token budget it increases with batch size, matching the theoretical prediction eta* proportional to sqrt(b)/sqrt(T).

comparator: minimization of the Pethick et al. LMO bound (which covers Muon as the spectral-norm instance) treated as a proxy objective; no LM experiment for the momentum law
effect: alpha*_T(b) proportional to b*T^(-1/2) with the accompanying eta*_T(b) proportional to b*T^(-3/4)
locator: section 3.1, theorem 2 (eq. 8); appendix B.2
notes: transfer=2: it applies to Muon by construction (Muon is the spectral-norm LMO) and our batch is hardware-fixed while T is tiny, which is exactly the fixed-b regime the theorem addresses - so it predicts our Muon beta should sit BELOW the usual 0.95 and possibly below the 0.85 our ramp starts at. Scored 2 not 3 because it is a bound-minimization with all constants set to 1, the bound is on expected dual-norm gradient not on loss/bpb, and the asymptotics are 'large T' while T here is small. Testable as a self-contained train.py edit (momentum ramp endpoints).
statement: Minimizing the LMO convergence bound at fixed batch size gives optimal momentum alpha = 1 - beta proportional to b * T^(-1/2), i.e. the optimal beta is FURTHER from 1 (less momentum) the shorter the token budget.

comparator: proxy-bound minimization over (eta, b) at each fixed alpha, LMO methods, large-T asymptotics
effect: risk*_T(alpha) proportional to (1+alpha)^(1/4) * T^(-1/4), so the whole range of alpha spans a 1.19x constant
locator: section 3.2, corollary 1 part 1; appendix B.4 part (1)
notes: transfer=2: directly opposes the preceding claim's implication that momentum is worth spending experiments on. Both come from the same proxy, and the paper's own resolution is the batch-cap boundary (registered separately). At our operating point batch size is NOT free, so this corollary's premise fails - which is why it is registered as opposing evidence rather than as a reason to skip momentum work. The bound is on gradient norm, not loss, so a 1.19x rate constant does not translate to a bpb delta.
statement: When batch size and learning rate are free to be re-tuned, re-tuning the momentum can change the achievable rate constant by at most a factor 2^(1/4) (about 1.19).

comparator: same proxy bound, minimized under the constraint b <= b_max
effect: risk_T proportional to alpha^(1/2) * b_max^(-1/2) (a floor) at fixed alpha, versus T^(-1/4) when alpha is allowed to scale
locator: section 3.2, corollary 1 part 2; appendix B.4 parts (2)-(3)
notes: transfer=2: this is the condition under which the '1.19x, don't bother' corollary does not apply, and our batch IS capped (524288 tokens/step, fixed). It says momentum is worth touching precisely in our situation. Still only a bound-minimization with unit constants and no LM experiment; the 'floor' is asymptotic in T, and our T is small enough that the asymptotic regime may not be entered at all. Registered as boundary so the tension with the previous claim stays visible.
statement: If batch size is capped by hardware, tuning only the learning rate at a fixed momentum leaves a non-vanishing noise floor proportional to sqrt(alpha / b_max), and only letting alpha decrease with the token budget restores the T^(-1/4) rate.

comparator: Muon (beta=0.95) and Adam (0.9,0.95) as hybrid methods with Adam on non-matrix params, per-task learning-rate grid search, no weight decay
effect: lower final train and test loss than Muon and Adam on a 2-layer GeLU MLP regression (1000 steps) and lower train loss plus higher test accuracy on a 5-layer CIFAR-10 CNN (100 epochs); no numeric values are reported, only curves
locator: section 2 (algorithm 2), section 4.2, figures 1 and 2
notes: transfer=1: there is NO language-model experiment anywhere in the paper - the authors list 'testing AdaGO on LLM training' as future work - and the models are a 100-hidden-unit MLP and a small CNN, orders of magnitude from 124M transformer pretraining. internal_validity=2: results are figures with no tables, no seeds, no error bars, and AdaGO gets an extra tuned hyperparameter (epsilon) that the baselines do not. The mechanism is genuinely trivial to implement (one extra scalar) if the campaign ever wants a cheap probe, but it is not evidence at our operating point.
statement: AdaGO, which scales Muon's orthogonalized update by a single AdaGrad-Norm-style scalar min(||G_t||,gamma)/v_t (with v_t the accumulated clamped squared gradient norms) and therefore preserves exact orthogonality of the direction, reaches lower final training loss and higher test accuracy than both Muon and Adam.

comparator: plain Muon, whose step length is set entirely by the learning-rate schedule
effect: structural property, no measured effect; convergence rates O(T^(-1/4)) stochastic and O(T^(-1/2)) deterministic, matching known lower bounds
locator: section 2, discussion following algorithm 2 ('null gradient consistency')
notes: transfer=1: the property is real and applies to our Muon group, but nothing in the paper connects it to loss at LM scale, and at ~1000 steps we are nowhere near a stationary point so 'null gradient consistency' is not a property our run would ever exercise. Registered because it names the actual degree of freedom - Muon's step magnitude is schedule-only - that several papers in this batch (Hyperball, AdaGO, AdaMuon) attack differently.
statement: Because Muon's orthogonalized update has unit magnitude by construction, its step length carries no gradient-magnitude information; AdaGO restores this by scaling the update by the clamped current gradient norm so the step decays to zero at a stationary point.

comparator: unspecified - stated as a general empirical observation motivating adaptive stepsizes, not tied to either reported experiment
effect: qualitative only; no curves, tables or run details are attached to this statement
locator: section 1, paragraph beginning 'In general, empirical observations show'
notes: transfer=2 despite internal_validity=1: if true it is directly consequential for us, because a 300-second budget wants exactly the 'rapid initial decrease' half of the tradeoff and never reaches the horizon where the small-LR arm overtakes - the same early-vs-late crossover structure as the Hyperball claim. But it is an unsupported assertion in an introduction, so it must be treated as a hypothesis to test at our own operating point, not as evidence. Do not let this alone justify a learning-rate change.
statement: With Muon, a large learning rate produces a rapid initial decrease in training loss that soon plateaus and oscillates, while a smaller constant learning rate converges more slowly but reaches a lower final loss.

comparator: fixed-threshold clipping at c=1.0, 1B LLaMA (16 layers), SmolLM corpus 50B tokens, fused AdamW (0.9,0.999), 2B warmup tokens then cosine decay, global batch 2048 x seq 2048
effect: >35% fewer training steps to the baseline's best validation loss; 18.6B fewer tokens out of a 50B budget; at lr=3e-3 train loss 2.14 (ZClip) vs 5.14 (fixed threshold, which did not converge)
locator: section 4.1, table 2 and figure 4
notes: transfer=2: the mechanism is a small self-contained train.py edit that generalizes our existing `clip` knob, and the payoff mode - stability at a higher learning rate buying steps-to-target - is exactly the currency of a 300s budget. Scored 2 not 3 because the study is AdamW-only (our Muon group is not covered, and orthogonalized updates already bound their own step magnitude), 1B params, and ~12K steps with a 2B-token warmup that alone exceeds our whole budget. Single run per cell, no seeds; the 35% figure compares runs at DIFFERENT learning rates, so it is a joint clip+lr effect, not a clip effect.
statement: Replacing fixed-threshold gradient clipping with ZClip (clip the gradient norm to mu_t + (z_thresh^2/z_t)*sigma_t whenever its EMA z-score exceeds z_thresh) let a 1B LLaMA train stably at learning rate 3e-3 and reach the best fixed-clip baseline validation loss more than 35% earlier in steps than that baseline at its own best learning rate of 5e-4.

comparator: fixed-threshold clipping c=1.0, same 1B LLaMA / 50B token setup
effect: train loss ZClip vs fixed threshold: 2.24 vs 2.27 at 5e-4, 2.33 vs 2.34 at 3e-4, 2.46 vs 2.46 at 1e-4 - versus 2.14 vs 5.14 at 3e-3
locator: section 4.2, table 2 (rows for lr 5e-4, 3e-4, 1e-4)
notes: transfer=3: this is the decision rule for us. Adaptive clipping is not a free win, it is a lever that only pays if we are ALSO pushing the learning rate into a spike-prone regime; adopting ZClip at our current stable learning rate should be predicted to move val_bpb by nothing. Any ZClip experiment must therefore be run jointly with a learning-rate increase or it is a guaranteed null. Same single-run caveat as the supporting claim.
statement: In already-stable learning-rate regimes, ZClip's advantage over fixed-threshold clipping shrinks to nothing.

comparator: 1B LLaMA, SmolLM 50B tokens, lr 1e-3, AdamW
effect: test loss 2.90 (none) -> 2.33 (fixed c=1.0) -> 2.20 (AutoClip) -> 2.18 (ZClip); spike counts 12 -> 6 -> 0 -> 0
locator: section 4.2, table 3
notes: transfer=2: prices the existing `clip` knob's ON state - the gap from no-clipping to any-clipping (0.57 loss) dwarfs the gap between clipping schemes (0.15), which says our clip knob's value is mostly binary and that sweeping clip thresholds is low-yield. Scored 2 because it is 1B/50B tokens with AdamW on all parameters, and because at 1000 steps we may simply not encounter the spike population that drives the no-clipping arm's failure. Single run per method.
statement: At a spike-prone learning rate, removing gradient clipping entirely is far worse than any clipping scheme: no clipping gives 12 loss spikes and 2.90 test loss, fixed clipping at 1.0 gives 6 spikes and 2.33, AutoClip 0 spikes and 2.20, and ZClip 0 spikes and 2.18.

comparator: gradient norms collected from the 1B LLaMA run at lr=1e-3, fitted against a Gaussian over 135-step sliding windows
effect: normality rejected in the 500-635 step window, marginally accepted (p=0.0508) in the 3050-3185 step window; z_thresh 2.0-3.0 and alpha=0.97 are the tuned settings
locator: appendix 6.4.1-6.4.2 (figure 9, Shapiro-Wilk results); section 2.3.3 (warm-up with N_w=25)
notes: transfer=3: decisive caveat for our regime - our ENTIRE run is ~1000 steps, i.e. almost entirely inside the window where the paper's own normality assumption is rejected, and the tuned alpha=0.97 EMA has a ~33-step memory calibrated on a 12K-step run. Any ZClip port must retune alpha and z_thresh for a 1000-step horizon, and the 25-step warmup eats 2.5% of our steps. This is the concrete blocker on the otherwise attractive ZClip mechanism.
statement: ZClip's z-score machinery rests on gradient norms being approximately normal over short windows, but the paper's own test finds this fails early in training - a Shapiro-Wilk test over steps 500-635 did not support normality (heavier tails, right skew), while by steps 3050-3185 it passed at statistic 0.9792, p=0.0508; the method additionally needs a 25-step statistics warmup.

comparator: gradient descent on the same problems, and Adam runs at different beta_2, on f(theta)=theta^2/2, a 2-layer FCN, a CNN, and a small transformer on a synthetic compositional-rule dataset
effect: on an 8-layer 10M transformer, seven observed spikes each preceded by ||v_hat|| decaying at ~0.999003 (approximately beta_2); a 'sustained' predictor min over three consecutive steps of lambda_grad shows perfect correspondence with spike occurrence, whereas lambda_max alone over-predicts (10 crossings, 7 spikes)
locator: sections 4.2-4.4 (figure 3, eq. 8); section 5.3 and figure 7 (8-layer, 10M-param transformer)
notes: transfer=2: mechanism only, verified at 3K-10M parameters on synthetic tasks, never at LM pretraining scale, and the authors state the Hessian-eigenvalue diagnostics are computationally prohibitive at scale. Relevant to us only through the AdamW group (embeddings/lm_head/scalars), and it predicts spikes in layers whose gradients have gone SMALL - the opposite of the high-variance lm_head picture from 2506.16659. The predictor is not measurable in our run without extra Hessian-vector work we cannot afford in 300s.
statement: Adam loss spikes can be caused by the adaptive preconditioner rather than by landscape sharpness: when the squared gradient falls far below the second-moment estimate, v_t enters a beta_2-exponential decay, pushing the maximum eigenvalue of the preconditioned Hessian past 2/eta, and a spike occurs precisely when the gradient-directional curvature also exceeds 2/eta for a sustained period.

comparator: Adam with beta_1=0.9 on the 1-D quadratic f(theta)=theta^2/2, varying beta_2 only
effect: at beta_2=0.99 a spike appears at epoch 782 and resolves at 845; at beta_2=0.9 the observed v decay rate is 0.93 (larger than beta_2) and no large spike forms, only a minor rise and oscillations
locator: section 4.2, figure 3(c)-(d) (beta_2=0.9 vs 0.99); section 6 'Conclusion and Discussion' mitigation paragraph
notes: transfer=2: beta_2 (and epsilon) on our AdamW group is a self-contained train.py edit needing no new knob, and the direction is concrete. But internal_validity=2 because the beta_2 comparison is demonstrated on a ONE-DIMENSIONAL QUADRATIC, not on the transformer, and the paper itself notes beta_2=0.9 is avoided in practice for weaker convergence guarantees. Contradicts nothing we have registered, but the expected effect size at 1000 steps with gradient clipping already on is unknown and plausibly zero.
statement: Reducing beta_2 makes the second moment responsive to current gradients and prevents the persistent above-threshold excursions that produce large spikes, converting a spike into a minor rise plus oscillation; increasing epsilon or beta_1 is listed as an alternative mitigation.

comparator: full-batch Adam on a Transformer trained to identify anchors in sequences, 1800 train / 200 test examples
effect: four qualitatively distinct train/test outcomes after spikes, all with the same curvature signature; no frequency or magnitude statistics given
locator: appendix C 'The Pros and Cons of Loss Spikes', figure D1(a)-(h)
notes: transfer=1: the experiment is a 2000-sample synthetic anchor task with full-batch Adam, and 'beneficial' is defined via a train/test generalization gap that does not exist in our single-epoch pretraining setting where train and val loss track each other. Registered because it directly opposes ZClip's premise that suppressing all spikes is good - the campaign should see that contradiction rather than have it resolved away. Not actionable on its own; the authors state that distinguishing the spike types remains unsolved.
statement: Loss spikes come in at least four kinds - neutral, beneficial (test loss drops after the spike), malignant (test loss plateaus after) and catastrophic (neither loss recovers) - all of which show the same lambda_grad > 2/eta signature, so spike suppression is not unconditionally desirable.

comparator: PreNorm baseline, identical Megatron 'Scale Init', AdamW lr 2e-4, 512K-token batch, SlimPajama 30B tokens, 24-layer 740M dense
effect: Wikitext ppl 22.5 -> 20.6 at 740M/30B tokens (24 layers); LM-harness avg 49.8 -> 50.8
locator: section 5 / Table 1, row 'SpanNorm 740M 30B'
notes: Transfer 2: smallest data point is 740M / 24 layers / 30B tokens; our model is 124M / 8 layers / ~0.5B tokens. The mechanism is a topology change to the residual, implementable in train.py, and Appendix E reports zero throughput cost, so it is not blocked by the 300s budget. But the paper's own scaling (claim r20_spannorm_gain_is_depth_driven) says the gain comes from deep-network pathologies absent at depth 8. Single run per cell, no seeds reported for Table 1.
statement: Replacing PreNorm with SpanNorm (PostNorm blocks whose FFN residual adds the block input X'_l rather than the post-attention Y_l) lowered Wikitext perplexity at the smallest scale tested.

comparator: PreNorm at matched params/tokens; 128-layer runs all use lr 1.2e-4 tuned on PreNorm
effect: LM-harness average improvement 1.0-2.5 points across 740M-5B dense (24-64 layers), rising to 'up to 4.0' at 128 layers (6.5B, 400B tokens: 64.4 -> 68.4)
locator: section 5 'Results on LM Evaluation Harness' and 'Scalability on Ultra-Deep Networks'; Table 1 vs Table 3
notes: Transfer 3 as a NEGATIVE boundary: it directly predicts a near-null result at depth 8. Registered so the controller does not read the headline number as depth-agnostic. The measured resolution here is 0.000174 bpb; a depth-8 extrapolation of a depth-driven effect is plausibly below that.
statement: The SpanNorm advantage over PreNorm grows with depth rather than being depth-independent.

comparator: PreNorm under both inits (PreNorm is robust to the init choice); 24-layer model, first 5000 steps, 3 random seeds
effect: With Global Init, SpanNorm gradient norms drop below 10^-12; with Scale Init they hold at approximately 10^-1, matching the PreNorm baseline
locator: section 4 Theorem 4.1 / 'Practical Initialization Strategy'; Appendix F, Figure 14
notes: Transfer 3 because it is a hard prerequisite: any attempt to try SpanNorm here that keeps our current init will fail for reasons unrelated to the mechanism. Note PreNorm itself is reported insensitive to this init, so the 1/sqrt(L) rescale is NOT independently motivated as a lever for our current PreNorm-style stack.
statement: SpanNorm collapses under standard global initialization and requires O(1/sqrt(L)) scaling of the FFN output matrix W2 and the attention output matrix W_O.

comparator: PreNorm baseline, 5B model, same cluster
effect: Identical tokens/s before and after a data-parallel scale-up at 21.5B tokens; reported as 'no computational overhead'
locator: Appendix E 'Computational Efficiency Analysis', Figure 13
notes: Transfer 3 because throughput-neutrality is the decisive question for a 300s budget where step count dominates. Internal validity 2: this is a qualitative reading of a throughput plot at 5B with data parallelism, no numbers given, and it says nothing about a 124M single-GPU regime where per-layer kernel launch overhead is a larger relative share.
statement: SpanNorm's altered normalization placement produced training throughput indistinguishable from the PreNorm baseline.

comparator: PreNorm at the same lr 2e-4, 5B dense, 200B SlimPajama tokens
effect: Wikitext ppl 13.6 vs PreNorm 12.5; LMBADA ppl 14.9 vs 6.9; LM-harness avg 60.2 vs 64.1 (5B, 200B tokens, 64 layers)
locator: section 5 'Comparisons with Other Variants', Table 2
notes: Transfer 2: registers depth-dependent LN rescaling as a measured LOSS, not a win, so the controller should not treat 'scale the norms by depth' as free. Authors attribute the failure to over-shrinking shallow-layer gradients at depth 64, which is a mechanism that would be weaker at depth 8, so the harm may also not transfer. Reimplemented by the SpanNorm authors, not the original authors.
statement: LayerNorm Scaling, a depth-dependent normalization rescaling, performed worse than the plain PreNorm baseline at matched hyperparameters.

comparator: GPT-2 124M (nanoGPT implementation), OpenWebText, 100k iterations, hyperparameters tuned for Pre-LN, H200 GPUs
effect: Peri-LN val loss 3.12 (dt=1) -> 3.10 (dt=0.1); perplexity 24.17 -> 23.63
locator: section 6 'Benefits of Scaled Residual Steps', Table 2, 124M rows
notes: Transfer 3: exactly our parameter count, a one-line change, and stated to cost nothing in compute or memory. Downgraded from 4 because the run is 100k iterations vs our ~1000, and a 10x shrink of every residual update plausibly trades early-training speed for late-training stability, which is the wrong side of the trade at 1000 steps. Effect size 0.02 nats at 124M; single run per cell, no seeds.
statement: Scaling every residual branch by a constant dt < 1 (forward-Euler step size on the residual stream) improved validation loss at 124M scale when combined with Peri-LN.

comparator: Same architecture and hyperparameters, only dt changed; 100k iters at 124M, 60k at 774M/1.5B
effect: 124M Pre-LN val loss 5.43 (dt=1) -> 3.13 (dt=0.1); at 774M the same change gives 2.90 -> 2.91 and at 1.5B it gives 2.88 -> 2.88
locator: section 6, Table 2: 124M Pre-LN rows vs 774M and 1.5B Pre-LN rows
notes: Transfer 3 as a boundary: it tells the controller the headline 124M number is an instability artifact. Where training is already stable, the measured effect is 0.00-0.01 nats, i.e. plausibly under our 0.000174 bpb resolution. Our run uses QK-norm and 1000 steps and shows no divergence, so we are in the 774M/1.5B-like stable regime, not the unstable one.
statement: The large gain from dt=0.1 under Pre-LN was a rescue of a run that was otherwise unstable, not a general improvement.

comparator: Pre-LN with hyperparameters tuned for Pre-LN; Peri-LN untuned, same budget
effect: 774M: Pre-LN 2.90 vs Peri-LN 2.91 val loss; 1.5B: 2.88 vs 2.89. Authors state Peri-LN 'does not consistently improve performance'
locator: section 6 'Training Stability Test' and Table 2 (774M rows: Pre-LN dt=1 2.90 vs Peri-LN dt=1 2.91)
notes: Transfer 3: directly opposes 'move the LayerNorms' as a val_bpb lever at our operating point, and contradicts the SpanNorm paper's Table 2 where Peri-LN beat PreNorm (12.3 vs 12.5 Wikitext ppl at 5B). Hyperparameters favored Pre-LN here, so the comparison is conservative toward Peri-LN, which strengthens the null.
statement: Peri-LN did not consistently improve loss over Pre-LN; its reported benefit was stability, not performance.

comparator: GPT-2 base, 20k iterations, hyperparameters tuned for Pre-LN
effect: Diverged runs out of 5: Pre-LN 1/5 (weight decay on), 3/5 (off); Peri-LN 0/5 and 0/5; LN off 5/5
locator: section 6 'Training Stability Test', Table 1
notes: Transfer 2: 5 trials is real replication, but our 1000-step runs are not observed to diverge, so the failure mode being fixed does not occur here. Useful only as a prior if a future high-LR lever pushes us into an unstable regime. Note the 5/5 'LN off' row makes normalization itself non-optional.
statement: Peri-LN eliminated training divergence across repeated trials where Pre-LN diverged, with or without weight decay.

comparator: unmodified transformer blocks (dt=1)
effect: stated as 'at no additional computational or memory cost'; no measured throughput numbers given
locator: section 5 'Overall Stabilization' and section 6 final paragraph
notes: Transfer 3 because a zero-throughput-cost knob is the only kind worth spending a 300s budget on. Internal validity 2: asserted, not benchmarked. Under torch.compile a constant scalar multiply on the residual should fuse, so the assertion is credible here.
statement: Residual step scaling by dt requires only a code change and adds no computational or memory cost.

comparator: Same Llama-3-style recipe, AdamW, ctx 1024, d=2048, 32 heads, batch 1024, 2000-step linear warmup, only depth varied
effect: At peak lr 8e-3 on FineWeb: 8 layers (640M) converges with low, stable lambda_max(H) and lambda_max(G_t); 16 layers (1B) and 32 layers (3B) spike during LR warmup, cross the stability boundary, and diverge
locator: section 4.3 'Depth, Effective Curvature, and Stability', Figure 3
notes: Transfer 3 and registered as OPPOSING the whole depth-stability family: our model is exactly 8 layers, and this paper's own control says depth 8 is the stable case. It predicts near-zero headroom here for architecture warm-up, QK-Clip, Softcap and similar stabilizers, whose measured wins all came from rescuing 16-layer divergence. Curvature values are normalized in the figure, so no absolute number is quotable.
statement: An 8-layer transformer maintained low curvature and converged stably at a peak learning rate that made 16- and 32-layer models diverge.

comparator: 16-layer 1B Llama-3-style models, peak lr 8e-3 chosen intentionally to shrink the stability threshold
effect: FineWeb perplexity 25.02 +/- 0.001 (Arch-Warmup) vs 49.88 +/- 0.003 (QK-Norm), with baseline and QK-Clip diverged; DCLM 22.64 vs 61.57; OLMo-Mix 18.54 with all four comparators diverged
locator: section 4.5, Table 1
notes: Transfer 2 only: the comparators mostly diverged, so this measures rescue of a deliberately broken configuration rather than a loss lever in a healthy run. At 8 layers (see r20_depth8_is_already_curvature_stable) nothing diverges, so the mechanism has no pathology to fix. Error bars are tight but come from a regime where the baseline is NaN.
statement: Architecture warm-up (train at half depth during LR warmup, then unlock remaining layers zero-initialized and excluded from the optimizer while locked) outperformed QK-Norm, QK-Clip, Softcap and an unmodified baseline under a deliberately high peak learning rate.

comparator: QK-Norm, the strongest baseline from the short runs, same 1B 16-layer model and 25B-token budget
effect: FineWeb val PPL 18.35 (Arch-Warmup) vs 20.28 (QK-Norm) vs 32.44 (Softcap), 1B / 16 layers / 25B tokens
locator: Appendix 10 'Validation at compute optimal', Table 2
notes: Transfer 2: 1B/16-layer/25B tokens is far outside 124M/8-layer/~0.5B tokens, and the peak LR for this table is not restated so the high-LR confound may persist. Registered because it is the only evidence the gain is not purely a divergence rescue. No seed replication for Table 2.
statement: Architecture warm-up retained an advantage over QK-Norm at a Chinchilla compute-optimal budget, not only in short high-LR runs.

comparator: Same 16-layer 1B FineWeb run with the standard 2000-step LR warmup
effect: Warm-up steps set from 2000 to 0 at peak lr 4e-4 with cosine decay and all optimizer hyperparameters fixed; reported as 'on-par convergence while exceeding the stability of LR warmup'
locator: section 4.6 'Can learning-rate warmup be replaced by architecture warm-up?', Figure 6
notes: Transfer 3 because warmup steps are a large fraction of a ~1000-step budget, so anything that makes warmup unnecessary is directly worth testing here even though the demonstration is at 1B/16L. Internal validity 2: the claim is read off a figure with no perplexity number and no seeds, and 'on-par' is not quantified.
statement: Removing learning-rate warmup entirely and using architecture warm-up instead achieved on-par convergence with a well-tuned warmup schedule.

comparator: Default architecture warm-up schedule on the same model
effect: Zero spacing (all layers unlocked simultaneously at peak LR) gave results 'similar' to the default half-depth-then-four-groups-spaced-by-500-iterations schedule
locator: Appendix 11 'Sensitivity to the warm up schedule', Figure 9
notes: Transfer 2: reduces the tuning surface if this family is tried here, which matters because our resolution (0.000174 bpb) cannot support a multi-point schedule sweep. Internal validity 2: qualitative figure reading, no numbers, and the sweep is at 1B/16 layers.
statement: Architecture warm-up results were insensitive to the unlock schedule, including unlocking all remaining layers at once at peak learning rate.

comparator: Naive zero-projection-only locking
effect: No number reported; mechanism is that with only W_p1, W_p2 zeroed the Jacobian terms ||J X_concat|| and ||J X_hidden|| are already large at unlock, so tiny projection updates abruptly raise the block Jacobian
locator: section 3.2.2 'Progressive Depth via constraining Block Weights to zero' incl. footnote 2, equation 16
notes: Transfer 3 as an implementation prerequisite: the obvious cheap implementation (zero the out-projections) is explicitly called out as the broken one, and RMSNorm weights 'show inferior convergence from zero initialization'. Internal validity 2: the failure of the naive variant is argued from a first-order bound, not shown with an ablation curve.
statement: Progressive-depth unlocking requires zeroing ALL block weights and removing them from the optimizer while locked; zeroing only the output projections still causes a curvature jump, and RMSNorm weights must be excluded from the zeroing.

comparator: QK-Norm, Softcap and unmodified baseline on the same 16-layer 1B models
effect: QK-Clip diverged on all three datasets (FineWeb, DCLM, OLMo-Mix) at peak lr 8e-3; authors note it 'often diverging to NaN values mid training'
locator: section 4.5, Table 1 (asterisked diverged runs on FineWeb, DCLM and OLMo-Mix)
notes: Transfer 2: rules out QK-Clip as a substitute for our existing QK-norm. Corroborated independently by 2606.16310 (QK-Clip NaN at step 884 under lr 2e-2). The high-LR setting is adversarial by construction, so this is evidence about the tail, not about typical behaviour.
statement: QK-Clip was the least stable of the tested attention stabilizers, diverging to NaN mid-training.

comparator: Adam on all parameters, with a two-stage tuning protocol (Adam tuned first over 6 LRs x 4 WDs, then the Muon group tuned over 7 LRs x 6 WDs)
effect: Average 32.4% reduction in training steps across all tested scenarios; TIGER converged in 1200 vs 3600 steps on Industrial (3x)
locator: section 2.4 'MuonRec' and section 3.2 'Training Efficiency and Effectiveness', Table 1
notes: Transfer 1: this is exactly the partition our train.py already uses, so it is confirmatory rather than a lever, and the domain is sequential recommendation on 13.5k-interaction Amazon datasets with NDCG/Recall metrics, not val_bpb. 'Steps to converge under early stopping' is not the same objective as loss at a fixed 300s wall clock.
statement: Applying Muon to 2D weight matrices in transformer blocks while leaving embeddings, output heads and 1D parameters on Adam reduced steps-to-convergence versus all-Adam.

comparator: Adam, whose optimal Muon-group LR is stated to be lower; MiniOneRec at 0.5B/1.5B/3.0B on the Office dataset
effect: Bell-shaped NDCG@10 curve peaking at lr ~= 1e-2, lowest training loss at the same point; recommended range [5e-3, 5e-2]; sharp divergence at lr >= 1e-1
locator: section 3.3.2 'Hyperparameter Study', Figure 2
notes: Transfer 2: LR-scale-invariance for Muon is architecture-general enough to be worth registering, and the recommended band is a concrete testable range. But this is SFT+RL of a pretrained Qwen2.5 backbone, not from-scratch pretraining, so the loss landscape is not ours; and MuonRec reports 2 datasets, 1 seed.
statement: Muon's optimal learning rate sat near 1e-2 and did not move with model scale across 0.5B, 1.5B and 3.0B backbones, with divergence above 1e-1.

comparator: (i) constant batch + decaying LR, (ii) growing batch + decaying LR, (iii) growing batch + growing LR; all NSHB on CIFAR-100 / ResNet-18, 300 epochs, momentum 0.9
effect: Configuration (iv) (batch doubling every 30 epochs, LR warmed up over the first 30 epochs to 0.2/0.5/1.0 then constant or cosine) beat (i)-(iii); mean over 3 runs
locator: section 'Experiments', configuration (iv) and 'Summary', Figures 8 and 9
notes: Transfer 1: CIFAR-100 image classification with normalized stochastic heavy ball, no transformer, no language model, no Adam/Muon. Our tokens-per-step is fixed at 524288 and prepare.py packing is frozen, so a growing-batch schedule is largely out of scope. Registered at transfer 1 only so the schedule family has this evidence attached; 3 runs per config is the one methodological strength.
statement: Combining a learning-rate warmup with a progressively increasing batch size gave the fastest gradient-norm convergence and best accuracy among four schedule families.

comparator: beta = 0.9 used in all other configurations
effect: To reach eta_max = 1.0 with an LR growth rate gamma ~= 1.292, momentum was set to beta = 0.87 instead of the default 0.9
locator: section 'Experiments', configuration (iii)
notes: Transfer 1: derived for SHB/NSHB on CIFAR-100, and the authors themselves note configuration (iv) violates the assumptions of their theory because LR and batch size are updated on different intervals. Only registered as a coupling warning if a rising-LR schedule is ever tried with Muon's momentum.
statement: Increasing the learning rate over training required reducing the momentum coefficient to satisfy the paper's stability condition.

comparator: 10 seeds each at 14M, 31M, 70M, 160M and 410M, identical hyperparameters, codebase and data, 143k steps on the Pile
effect: 2 of 50 model-seed combinations (410M seeds 3 and 4) fell outside 2 standard deviations of the per-size mean on ARC-Easy/LAMBADA/PIQA/SciQ; only these two show loss spikes
locator: section 3 'Finding outlier seeds based on Accuracy and Validation Loss'; Appendix A, Figure 5
notes: Transfer 2: sizes bracket our 124M and the seed-only manipulation is exactly our noise question, but the outlier criterion is downstream multiple-choice accuracy, not val_bpb, and 143k steps is 140x our budget. The authors note a formal ANOVA was infeasible with their sample size, so '2 of 50' is a heuristic, not a test. Does NOT license reading our own 0.000174 bpb resolution as small.
statement: Across 50 language-model pre-training runs differing only in initialization and batch-composition seed, only two runs were outliers, and those were the only ones showing loss spikes.

comparator: Pythia recipe, batch slightly over 2M tokens, 14M-410M params, cosine LR with warmup
effect: Inter-seed agreement peaks at kappa ~= 0.7 around step 10^3 then settles to kappa ~= 0.5 by step 10^4; models 'begin generating non-random answers' at step 10^3, aligning with the 2.5B-token induction-head formation point
locator: section 6 'Linguistic information is encoded in the initial learning phase' and section 3 'What is special about step 10^3?'
notes: Transfer 3 as a scoping boundary: our whole run is ~1000 steps x 524288 tokens ~= 0.5B tokens, i.e. BELOW the 2B-token point where these authors first see non-random behaviour. Any paper claim whose mechanism is about induction heads, in-context learning or downstream circuits is therefore probably out of regime for us, and val_bpb here is being driven by earlier-phase statistics. This claim exists to discount a whole class of otherwise attractive mechanisms.
statement: Metrics of learned linguistic ability stayed at the random baseline until roughly step 10^3 (about 2B tokens) and only converged around step 10^4 (about 20B tokens).

comparator: 410M, which does not saturate, over the same 143k-step Pile run
effect: Accuracy 'drops between step 10^4 and 10^5 for all but 410M, especially for the smallest models' (14M-160M)
locator: section 3 'Downstream Performance'; section 6 'Language modelling is largely stable'
notes: Transfer 2: our n_embd is 512 with a full vocab head, which is precisely the narrow-representation-vs-high-rank-head geometry described, and it argues that pushing token exposure indefinitely at small width eventually reverses. But the onset is at 10^4 steps, 10x past our budget, and the metric is downstream accuracy not loss, so it is a warning for capacity/width levers rather than an actionable effect.
statement: Smaller models' downstream accuracy dropped between step 10^4 and step 10^5, attributed to a mismatch between representation dimension and the rank of the output embedding matrix.

comparator: Chinchilla scaling-law prediction for the same parameter counts
effect: All benchmarks still improve past the predicted optimum of 8.2B tokens (around 4k-5k steps), out to 143k steps
locator: section 6 'Most improvements happen in the critical learning phase', final sentence
notes: Transfer 2: supports spending the budget on tokens/steps rather than parameters, which matches a 300s wall-clock objective where step count dominates. But the observation is at 4k-143k steps and our budget ends near 1000, and the measurement is downstream accuracy. Qualitative, no numbers per checkpoint.
statement: Benchmark performance continued to improve past the Chinchilla-optimal token count for these model sizes.

comparator: the TabICLv2 default normalization placement
effect: 'We did not see improvements from different placements of normalization layers (though the experiments used more shallow nets)'; no numbers reported
locator: Appendix D 'Other things we tried', subsection 'Architecture: normalizations'
notes: Transfer 2 and registered as OPPOSING the SpanNorm/Peri-LN/HybridNorm family, which is why it is worth keeping despite internal_validity 1. The authors explicitly caveat that pretraining runs are 'somewhat noisy', that these were smaller-scale runs 'without careful analysis', and that the nets were shallow. Shallow is our case, which is exactly why the null is relevant here. Domain is tabular ICL, not LM.
statement: Varying the placement of normalization layers produced no observed improvement in this team's pretraining experiments.

comparator: full LayerNorm with learned scale and bias
effect: 'seemed to perform similar to full layernorms while being faster'; authors add 'we were not very confident in whether these measurements are good enough'
locator: Appendix D 'Other things we tried', subsection 'Architecture: normalizations'
notes: Transfer 2 because a same-quality-but-faster norm converts directly into extra steps in a 300s budget, and it is a small edit to train.py. Internal validity 1: explicitly self-flagged as low-confidence anecdote with no numbers and no seeds. Would need our own counterbalanced A/B to resolve against the 0.000174 bpb floor.
statement: Bias-free or fully parameter-free LayerNorms performed similarly to full LayerNorms while being faster.

comparator: the default AdamW beta2 in their recipe
effect: 'For AdamW, decreasing beta_2 showed improvements at least for shorter runs'; no value or magnitude reported
locator: Appendix D 'Other things we tried', subsection 'Pretraining'
notes: Transfer 2: our AdamW group (embeddings, 1D params, head) runs for only ~1000 steps, which is squarely the 'shorter runs' condition where a long second-moment horizon never warms up, and beta2 is a free scalar knob costing zero throughput. Internal validity 1: anecdotal, no number, no seeds, tabular domain. Worth an A/B precisely because it is free.
statement: Decreasing AdamW's beta2 improved results, at least for shorter training runs.

comparator: AdamW with cosine LR schedule
effect: 'we did not see a benefit from using schedule-free AdamW over regular AdamW with a cosine schedule'; explicitly contradicts a cited prior result (Ma et al. 2025a)
locator: Appendix D 'Other things we tried', subsection 'Pretraining'
notes: Transfer 2: schedule-free methods are attractive at a fixed 300s budget because the horizon is uncertain, so a registered null is useful. Internal validity 1: anecdotal, no numbers, and the authors flag that it contradicts published work, so this is exactly the kind of contradiction the campaign wants left visible rather than resolved.
statement: Schedule-free AdamW gave no benefit over regular AdamW with a cosine schedule in these experiments.

comparator: AdamW and Muon on the same tabular pretraining setup
effect: 'some benefit from AdEMAMix in small-scale runs compared to AdamW, but it performed worse than Muon, and a combination of both did not seem to help'
locator: Appendix D 'Other things we tried', subsection 'Pretraining'
notes: Transfer 2: we already run Muon on 2D matrices, so this argues against spending budget on AdEMAMix as a replacement or addition. Internal validity 1: anecdotal, no numbers, tabular ICL rather than LM, small-scale runs the authors call noisy.
statement: AdEMAMix improved over AdamW in small-scale runs but was worse than Muon, and combining the two did not help.

comparator: AdamW with regular weight decay at lr 1e-4 following TabICL, same architecture, 280k-step ablation runs
effect: Max lr 8e-4 for Muon vs 1e-4 for AdamW in stage 1; Muon-instead-of-AdamW is one of three components each worth about 100 Elo / 64% win rate on 60 validation datasets
locator: section 4.1 'Optimizer'; section 7 'Ablation study', Figure 10
notes: Transfer 2: the 0.2*sqrt(max(n,m)) shape-dependent LR multiplier is a concrete, cheap, implementable rule for our Muon group and the 'Muon prefers higher LR' finding is architecture-general. Downgraded from 3 because the objective is tabular in-context classification log-loss over 500k steps, not next-token bpb over 1000, and the ablation confounds the optimizer swap with a weight-decay change (cautious vs regular).
statement: Muon with the Moonlight per-parameter LR multiplier 0.2*sqrt(max(n,m)) supported an 8x higher peak learning rate than AdamW and was one of the three largest single-component gains in the ablation.

comparator: regular decoupled weight decay and no weight decay
effect: 'The comparisons between cautious weight decay, weight decay, and no weight decay were not very clear; we went with cautious weight decay due to its inclusion in the NanoGPT speedrun'
locator: Appendix D 'Other things we tried', subsection 'Pretraining'; section 4.1 'Optimizer'
notes: Transfer 2 because cautious weight decay is a live candidate in speedrun-derived recipes like ours and this is a direct report that its measured benefit is not resolvable. Internal validity 1: no numbers. Important as a contradiction: the technique's presence in the NanoGPT speedrun is cited here as the reason for adoption, not evidence for it.
statement: The comparison between cautious weight decay, ordinary weight decay and no weight decay was not clear; cautious weight decay was chosen for provenance reasons rather than measured superiority.

comparator: standard SFT, plus LoRA (58.43 min), gradient checkpointing (86.49 min) and GaLore (109.56 min); LLaMA3-3B on GSM8K
effect: Linear-activation memory 14.676 GB -> 2.834 GB and optimizer 11.960 GB -> 1.553 GB at batch 32; training time 56.75 min (SFT) -> 47.76 min (Ours+), while the non-compressing variant 'Ours' is slower at 62.88 min
locator: section 5.2, Table 3 and Table 4
notes: Transfer 1: our binding constraint is 300 charged seconds on a 124M model where VRAM is not scarce and roughly 94% of charged time is the frozen CPU packing loop, so trading compute for activation memory buys nothing. The wall-time win is measured on 3B-parameter fine-tuning, and the sibling variant 'Ours' is actually SLOWER than the baseline. Scored 1, not 0, only because it is a training-loop change rather than an inference technique.
statement: Low-rank activation-gradient co-compression reduced GPU memory substantially while changing fine-tuning wall time only modestly.

comparator: uncompressed fine-tuning baseline, per-component compression of SiLU, RMSNorm, Softmax and All_Linear
effect: For a linear operator the input gradient is exact (G_X = G_X_hat = dL/dZ * W), so compression introduces no error; for nonlinear operators the estimator is biased at second order and Softmax compression 'causes training to collapse'. Qwen3-4B / GSM8K, rank 32, batch 8
locator: section 5.1 'Empirical Verification of the Theory', Table 1 and Figure 3; Theorem 3.2, Theorem 3.3
notes: Transfer 1: internally clean (theorem plus matching per-component ablation) but the setting is supervised fine-tuning of a 4B model for memory reduction. The only generalizable takeaway for us is a negative one: any low-precision or low-rank approximation applied across a nonlinearity injects a biased gradient, which is a caution for aggressive numeric tricks, not a val_bpb lever.
statement: Compressing activations of linear operators left training essentially unaffected, while compressing activations of nonlinear operators degraded training and, for Softmax, collapsed it.

comparator: identical model, data, initialization (seed 42), 1500-step warmup, cosine schedule with 10% floor, gradient clipping 1.0; only the optimizer differs
effect: Final val loss at 4000 steps: AdamW 1.59, SGD+momentum 5.10, SGD without momentum 8.12 (failed to train). Trajectory PCA: AdamW PC1 61.5% with k_95 = 9, all SGD variants PC1 100.0% with k_95 = 1
locator: section 5.1 'SGD-Family Control Experiment', Tables 8 and 9
notes: Transfer 3: 8 layers, d_model 512, 16 heads, d_ff 2048 is nearly our exact architecture, and 4000 steps is the closest horizon in this batch to our ~1000. Registered as OPPOSES because Muon is a momentum-SGD-style update with orthogonalization and no per-parameter adaptive scaling; this result is the strongest evidence in the batch that our AdamW group should not be narrowed. Caveats: TinyStories with a 10%-probability synthetic probe objective and lambda-weighted composite loss, LRs not separately tuned per optimizer (SGD runs use 1e-2 vs AdamW 1e-3), 2 seeds.
statement: At an 8-layer, d_model=512 GPT-2-family model, replacing AdamW with SGD-family optimizers while holding everything else fixed collapsed performance, and the authors attribute the difference to per-parameter adaptive scaling rather than momentum.

comparator: standard momentum-SGD at the same LR 1e-2 and momentum 0.9, same 51M 8-layer model
effect: At step 2000, run C-prime (SGDW + Nesterov, decoupled WD 0.5) differed from run C (SGD+momentum, L2 WD 0.05) by less than 0.03 in val loss and about 0.001 in probe accuracy; final val 5.25 vs 5.10
locator: section 5.1, Table 9 rows C and C-prime and the dagger footnote
notes: Transfer 3: Nesterov and weight-decay coupling are exactly the kind of cheap optimizer knobs a saturated campaign reaches for, and this is a clean isolation showing a <0.03 nat effect at 2000 steps in an 8-layer d=512 model. Our resolution is 0.000174 bpb, so a knob this small is only resolvable if it happens to be much larger for Muon; the WD values differ between C and C-prime (0.05 vs 0.5), which weakens the isolation.
statement: Switching momentum-SGD to Nesterov momentum with decoupled weight decay produced negligible improvement at a matched step count.

comparator: per-block decomposition of the same combined-loss gradient within one 8-layer model; replicated on seed 271
effect: Mean signed gradient projection onto the block backbone at step 2000: Block 0 = 0.029 vs Block 1 = 0.001, Blocks 2-5 = 0.001, Block 6 = 0.005, Block 7 = 0.005 (Block 0 larger by 3-10x); cumulative bias B_0 ~= 0.12 vs ~0.01 for blocks 1-7
locator: section 4.4 'Block Localization', Table 5
notes: Transfer 3: an 8-block model with the same width, and the finding suggests a concrete cheap lever (per-block LR or per-block residual scale favoring block 0, or extra capacity there) that costs no throughput. Two seeds is thin but the pattern is stated to hold in both. This is a diagnostic, not a demonstrated loss improvement, so it proposes an experiment rather than predicting an effect size.
statement: The dominant direction of parameter drift is concentrated in the first transformer block, with middle blocks contributing near zero.

comparator: uncentered PCA of the drift matrix with an anchor checkpoint; SGD+momentum over its plateau
effect: Over window [600,2000], AdamW PC1 = 61.5%, k_95 = 9, k_99 = 19, drift 113.7; at matched loss regime (val ~5.2) AdamW is 77.4-81.9% PC1 with k_95 = 2 while SGD+momentum is 97.7-98.1% with k_95 = 1
locator: section 3.1 'Trajectory PCA: One Direction Dominates'; section 5.2, Table 10
notes: Transfer 2: a geometric diagnostic rather than a lever, and the matched-loss comparison is imperfect because AdamW has no checkpoint at val ~5.2 (it passes through between steps 1 and 200 with no intermediate checkpoints), so the authors substitute early windows spanning val 10.8-3.0. Useful for designing a probe, not for predicting bpb.
statement: Under AdamW the parameter trajectory is dominated by a single slow direction that explains most of the drift, but is not degenerate as it is under SGD.

comparator: the same run's own trajectory; three reheating LRs 1e-3, 6e-4, 3e-4, of which 3e-4 fails to re-enter
effect: Probe OOD accuracy oscillates 0.40-0.78 (seed 42) then settles below 0.20 while LM val loss falls monotonically from ~10 to ~1.2 over 10,000 steps; reheating from step 10,000 with a fresh AdamW at lr 6e-4 recovers a peak of 0.782 by step 1000 before decaying back to 0.279
locator: section 2.3 'Oscillation Phenomenology'; section 6.2 'Results', Table 11
notes: Transfer 2: relevant if the campaign considers auxiliary losses to shape val_bpb, since it says an auxiliary objective's influence decays as the dominant direction stiffens even at constant loss weight. But the probe is a synthetic codeword-retrieval task with lambda=2.0 then 4.0, not a natural auxiliary loss, and the phenomenon is observed over 10,000 steps, ten times our horizon. Two seeds.
statement: Under a composite objective, an auxiliary capability oscillated and was ultimately suppressed while the language-modelling validation loss decreased monotonically, and the auxiliary basin remained reachable only by re-raising the learning rate.

comparator: QK-Clip with threshold 100 and alpha_clip 0.5, same 400M 12-layer MLA architecture, Muon at lr 2e-3, WSD minus-sqrt decay, same data mixture and attention backend
effect: 3-shot downstream average 44.75 -> 46.33 and LAMBADA perplexity 16.28 -> 14.18; training loss lower throughout the full 100B-token run
locator: section 5.1 'Training Loss', Figure 1; section 5.2, Table 1
notes: Transfer 2: we already use QK-norm, so this is confirmatory for keeping it rather than a new lever, and the architecture is Multi-head Latent Attention with content plus RoPE component splits, which we do not use (we run SSSL sliding-window attention). 100B tokens is 200x our budget. Single run per arm, no seeds.
statement: QK RMS normalization gave persistently lower training loss than post-hoc QK clipping over a long token horizon at 400M scale.

comparator: QK-Normed MLA on the same 400M MLA model and data
effect: At lr 2e-2, QK-Clip diverges with gradient NaNs at step 884, with max attention logit growing rapidly and loss failing to fall past the initial transient; QK-Normed MLA continues reducing loss
locator: section 5.4 'High-Learning-Rate Stress Test', Figure 2
notes: Transfer 2: independently corroborates 2606.16768 Table 1 that QK-Clip is the least stable of the attention stabilizers, from a different group with a different architecture. Internal validity 2 because the authors themselves label lr 2e-2 a stress test 'not intended as a recommended training recipe', so it characterizes the tail only. Single run.
statement: QK-Clip diverged with gradient NaNs under a high learning rate while QK RMS normalization remained stable over the same run.

comparator: n/a - self-reported scope statement
effect: 'The empirical comparison uses 400M-parameter models trained for up to 100B tokens ... not to establish frontier-scale behavior'; also notes practical speed depends on fusing the per-query and per-key scalar factors into the attention kernel
locator: section 7 'Limitations'
notes: Transfer 2: the fusion caveat is the operative part for us. Any QK-scale intervention that is not fused into the attention kernel adds memory traffic, which at 300 charged seconds costs steps. Registered so the controller prices kernel integration into any attention-detail proposal.
statement: The authors state their evidence does not establish that the QK-normalization training-loss advantage persists at billion-parameter scale.

comparator: DeltaNet at identical 8B-token budget, AdamW peak lr 3e-4, cosine schedule, 1B-token warmup, 1M-token global batch, head dim 128, seed 42
effect: Wikitext ppl 38.09 -> 37.01, LAMBADA ppl 96.26 -> 81.28, zero-shot average 40.9 -> 42.6 at 340M / 8B tokens
locator: section 5.2 'Main Results', Table 1, 340M rows
notes: Transfer 2: it is a genuine LM result at a smallish scale and the change itself is a scalar substitution. But it presupposes a DeltaNet-family linear-attention layer, which our SSSL sliding-window softmax stack does not have, so adopting it means swapping the attention mechanism wholesale plus a chunkwise Triton kernel. One seed, one run per arm, and the 1.3B rows are explicitly preliminary and unconverged.
statement: Replacing DeltaNet's Euler update coefficient beta_t with the exact continuous-time gate (1 - exp(-beta_t*lambda_t))/lambda_t improved language-modelling perplexity at 340M parameters.

comparator: naive matrix-exponential evaluation at O(d^3), and DeltaNet's Euler update
effect: The rank-1 property A_t^n = lambda_t^(n-1) * A_t collapses the matrix exponential to a closed form, avoiding the O(d^3) cost; the update becomes S_t = (I - alpha_t k k^T) S_{t-1} + alpha_t k v^T with alpha_t = (1 - exp(-beta_t*lambda_t))/lambda_t, identical in shape to DeltaNet
locator: section 3.2 'The Aha! Moment', equation 20; section 4 'Chunkwise Parallelism Form', equations 21-31
notes: Transfer 2: the derivation is airtight and means the mechanism costs no extra asymptotic compute, which matters for a 300s budget. But it only removes a cost that would arise if you already had the layer; the prerequisite kernel work is the actual blocker at our operating point. No wall-clock benchmark is reported anywhere in the paper.
statement: The exact gate preserves DeltaNet's algebraic structure, so its chunkwise-parallel formulation and O(L*d^2) complexity carry over unchanged.

comparator: DeltaNet's linear Euler response; lr sweep 1e-4 to 3e-3 on sequential MNIST under OOD scaling, additive noise and dropout
effect: Effective update magnitude is strictly sub-linear in key energy since (1-exp(-x))/x < 1 for x > 0; on sMNIST, lr 1e-4 'fails to learn robust features' while raising lr to 3e-3 substantially mitigates degradation
locator: Appendix B 'Discussion: Saturation Effects and Learning Rate Scaling', Figure 2
notes: Transfer 2 and worth flagging positively: 'superior semantic capture in the early training stages' is precisely the regime a ~1000-step budget lives in, so the mechanism's weakness (slow asymptotics) is not our weakness. Internal validity 1: the LR evidence is sMNIST robustness accuracy, not language modelling, and the early-vs-late characterization is asserted without a loss-curve crossover figure for the LM runs.
statement: The exact gate converges faster early but slower asymptotically because of saturation, and therefore requires a larger global learning rate.

comparator: matched MoE transformers with 150M forward-pass and 900M total parameters, 50B Zyda2 tokens, Muon, ~3M-token batch, cosine LR 7.5e-4 -> 5e-5, seq len 2048, CCGQA attention
effect: At ratio 60 (22 layers), no-MoD NAG loss 2.33661 vs BASELINE 2.35539; NAG beats baseline on HellaSwag at every evaluated depth (e.g. 0.512547 -> 0.525991 at ratio 60)
locator: section IV-A 'NAG Loss and Evaluations', Figure 2 and Table II; baseline/NAG ratio-60 losses given in Figure 9 caption
notes: Transfer 2: MoE with 8 experts per layer and 18-40 layers at 50B tokens is well outside our dense 8-layer 124M / ~0.5B-token point, and the paper states the gain 'grows substantially with depth', so a depth-8 extrapolation is small. Also note our value-embedding path writes to the residual stream, which NAG's orthogonalization would alter. One run per cell; the loss differences are ~0.02 nats.
statement: Decoupling residual-stream magnitude from direction, with each layer contributing an orthogonalized, renormalized, gated rotation, lowered training loss at every width-to-depth ratio tested.

comparator: the naive scaled-residual variant of equation 7 within the same codebase
effect: Layer outputs correlated with their inputs make the update act as a multiplicative gain g_l > 1 early in training, compounding across depth; the authors report gradients in later layers becoming 'many orders of magnitude larger than those in earlier layers'. Fix requires orthogonalizing f_l against the residual direction AND subtracting the feature-wise mean of the branch output
locator: section III-A, equations 7-11
notes: Transfer 3 as an implementation prerequisite: the cheap-looking half of this mechanism is the one reported to blow up, and the mean-centering (including centering the embedding table rows) is stated as necessary for numerical stability. No quantitative curve is shown for the failure, hence internal validity 2.
statement: The naive norm-agnostic update, scaling the layer output by the current residual norm without orthogonalization, was highly unstable and caused exponential residual-norm growth.

comparator: uniform alpha_l = 1 for all layers, and other exponents in alpha_l = 1/l^p
effect: p = 0.5 chosen over p = 0.25 (more uniform initial contributions) and p = 0.75 (deeper layers contribute less); derived to match the sqrt(1+l) additive orthogonal-growth of a standard residual stream
locator: section III-B 'Depth-Scaled Initialization', equations 19-24
notes: Transfer 2: a per-layer residual scale initialized as 1/sqrt(layer index) is a small, throughput-free edit that could be tried WITHOUT the rest of NAG, and it echoes the independent 1/sqrt(L) output-init prescription in 2601.22580 section 4. Internal validity 2: 'we find empirically that the best initial values are obtained with p=0.5' is stated without a table of losses per p.
statement: Initializing the per-layer residual-contribution scalar as alpha_l = l^(-0.5) was empirically the best exponent among the family alpha_l = l^(-p).

comparator: 0% MoD NAG model at 50B tokens / 16000 iterations, constant LR 7.5e-4 substituted for cosine so the differing token counts are comparable
effect: At 20% MoD: loss 2.38838 vs 2.38783 at 0% (difference +0.00055) while training tokens rise 50B -> 60.90B (16000 -> 19486 iterations) and active forward-pass parameters fall 156.00M -> 130.78M. At 40%: +0.01854 loss for 105.54M active params and 77.86B tokens
locator: section VI-B 'ISO-FLOP Ablations', Table V
notes: Transfer 2, and it is the most budget-relevant finding in this paper: our objective is loss at fixed wall clock, so 'cut per-step FLOPs, buy more steps' is the same trade. The authors themselves caution that differences of a few thousandths 'are close to the noise level of these runs', and our resolution is 0.000174 bpb. The mechanism requires the full NAG norm modulator, and our regime is input-pipeline bound rather than FLOP bound, which weakens the payoff of cutting GPU FLOPs specifically.
statement: Under a fixed total training-compute budget, skipping about 20% of per-token block computation and reinvesting the savings into more tokens matched the no-skip baseline loss.

comparator: a learned linear router g = sigmoid(R_bar . w + b) with matched local/global thresholds, same architecture and skip rates
effect: At 40% skipping, NAG-MoD raises loss by 0.03937 while the router baseline raises it by 0.10647, a difference of 0.06710; realized compute savings 35.79% at 40% skip
locator: section VI-A 'NAG Loss under MoD', Figure 9 and equation 40
notes: Transfer 2: relevant only if adaptive-depth is pursued here, and the whole comparison sits inside the NAG architecture at 22 layers / 50B tokens / MoE. At depth 8 there is very little depth to skip, and realized savings fall short of theoretical savings because KV elements are still computed for skipped tokens. Single run per skip rate.
statement: Tying layer-skipping decisions to residual-stream geometry via the norm modulator degraded loss much less than a separate learned linear router at the same skip rate.

comparator: Pythia-160M architecture (12 layers, d=768, head_dim 64), 50k steps, lr 2e-4, AdamW, WikiText-103 test PPL
effect: Transformer 18.5 PPL vs LA-ReLU 28.5, LA-ELU 31.3, HedgeHog 22.4, Fast-Decay GLA 20.8, best pure linear variant ReGLA 19.0
locator: section 4.1, Table 4 (w/o Pretrain rows)
notes: Transfer 2: same parameter class as our 124M but 50k steps and a different (non-SSSL) attention baseline; the comparator is FULL softmax attention, not sliding-window, so it does not directly price a swap out of SSSL.
