Registered as opposing evidence against replacing our attention with a linear/gated-linear recurrence. Single run per cell, no seeds reported.
statement: Trained from scratch at 160M on WikiText-103, every pure linear-attention variant tested reached higher perplexity than the softmax-attention Transformer baseline.

comparator: 160M Pythia-style, 50k steps, WikiText-103, layer-wise 50% replacement, both branches randomly initialized
effect: Hybrid ReGLA 17.8 PPL vs Transformer 18.5 (-0.7 PPL); pure ReGLA 19.0
locator: section 4.1, Table 4 (Hybrid ReGLA, w/o Pretrain)
notes: Transfer 2: mechanism is implementable (interleave GLA layers among SSSL layers) but demonstrated at 50k steps on WikiText-103, and a GLA layer needs a chunkwise Triton kernel whose throughput at our 8-layer/512-dim shape is unknown -- in a 300s step-bound regime an unfused recurrence would likely cost more steps than the 0.7 PPL is worth. Single seed, no ablation of WHICH layers are replaced.
statement: A hybrid stack that replaces 6 of 12 softmax attention layers with ReGLA gated-linear-attention layers reached lower from-scratch perplexity than the all-softmax Transformer.

comparator: GLA, 8M-token budget, with and without an extra normalization layer on the hidden representation
effect: GLA on WikiText, 8M tokens: 33.9 PPL with norm vs 40.6 without; on SlimPajama with pretrained init: 36.9 vs 73.0
locator: section 3.2, Table 2
notes: Transfer 2: the 8M-token budget is far SHORTER than our ~530M tokens, so it is a genuinely short-horizon measurement, but the mechanism is specific to linear-attention hidden states and our SSSL attention already normalizes via softmax + QK-norm. Useful mainly as a caution that boundedness of the pre-normalizer does not remove the need for an output normalizer. Single run per cell.
statement: Removing the stable normalization layer from gated linear attention degraded language-model perplexity even when the feature map already guarantees a bounded inner product.

comparator: ReGLA 160M, WikiText-103, feature dim 64, all else held fixed
effect: exp feature map with 1/sqrt(d): 20.7 PPL; with 1/(e*sqrt(d(e^2-1))): 19.0 PPL
locator: section 5.3, Table 6 (feature mapping ablation)
notes: Transfer 2: the exact constant is derived for exp() feature maps and does not apply to softmax attention, but the general lever -- the correct logit scale depends on the feature map's second moment, not only on head_dim -- is testable cheaply at our operating point (we use head_dim 128 with QK-norm, which already fixes the query/key norm, so the expected gain is probably small). No seeds.
statement: Replacing the conventional 1/sqrt(d) scaling on the attention inner product with a feature-map-matched variance-reduction factor lowered perplexity in gated linear attention.

comparator: Moonlight/Muon with coefficients equal to 1 in the same two places
effect: U_t = beta*U_{t-1} + ((1-gamma_t)(1-beta)/beta)*grad; M_t = beta*U_t + gamma_t*grad, then NewtonSchulz(M_t); gamma in {0.01, 0.025}
locator: section 4.2, equations 4.2-4.5
notes: Transfer 3: this is a ~5-line change to our existing Muon path with one extra state tensor per 2D matrix and NO extra forward/backward, so it is implementable and essentially throughput-neutral in our step-bound regime. Scored 3 not 4 because the supporting loss evidence is at 125M-1.5B over 100,000 steps, two orders of magnitude longer than our ~1010 steps.
statement: The practical (approximate) MARS-M update is algebraically equivalent to Muon/Moonlight with two rescaled momentum coefficients, requiring no second gradient evaluation.

comparator: Moonlight (Muon) with grid-searched lr, FineWeb-Edu 100B, 100,000 steps, batch 480x1024
locator: section 5.2, Tables 1-3
notes: Transfer 1: the endpoint is lm-eval-harness accuracy after 100k steps, not val bpb at ~1000 steps, and downstream accuracy deltas of 0.2-0.6 points are not convertible to our 0.000174 bpb resolution. Learning rate was tuned for Moonlight and REUSED for MARS-M, which biases against MARS-M but also means the comparison is not lr-matched-optimal for both.
statement: MARS-M improved average downstream 2-shot accuracy over the Muon/Moonlight baseline at 355M, 770M and 1.5B when both used the same grid-searched learning rate.

comparator: 125M small model on OpenWebText, same lr and beta=0.95
effect: gamma in [0.005, 0.025] gives very close train/val loss; gamma near 1 degrades
locator: section 5.4, Figure 6
notes: Transfer 2: the ablation is at 125M which matches our capacity, but at 100k steps. Practical value is that it removes a hyperparameter sweep -- pick gamma=0.025 and test once. Read from a figure, no table of numbers, so effect is qualitative.
statement: MARS-M training and validation losses were nearly indistinguishable for gradient-correction scale gamma in [0.005, 0.025], and gamma must be much smaller than 1.

comparator: same 100,000-step cosine schedule for all optimizers
effect: AdamW lower in mid-training (attributed to smaller max lr); MARS-M lower only in the final phase of the 100,000-step run
locator: section 5.2 (text accompanying Figures 1-4)
notes: Transfer 2 and registered as a BOUNDARY: our entire run is ~1% of their step budget, i.e. we live permanently in the phase where the authors report the variance-reduction advantage has NOT yet separated. This is the single strongest reason to expect MARS-M to measure as null here. Claim is read off zoomed-in loss curves, not tabulated.
statement: The authors report AdamW attaining lower loss than MARS-M in the MIDDLE of training and MARS-M only overtaking it in the final phase.

comparator: approximate MARS-M using the previous step's gradient on its own minibatch
effect: exact version evaluates grad f(X_t, xi_t) and grad f(X_{t-1}, xi_t); exact beat approximate only on CIFAR-10 (Figure 5), not tested on LLMs
locator: section 4.2 and section 5.1 footnote 2
notes: Transfer 3 as a cost constraint: doubling the backward pass roughly halves our step count at fixed 300s, which by any token-count law costs far more than the variance-reduction gain. Only the approximate form is admissible here. The only evidence exact > approximate is a ResNet-18/CIFAR-10 figure.
statement: Exact MARS-M requires computing stochastic gradients twice per step, which the authors call significantly more expensive, so all their LLM experiments used the approximate variant.

comparator: 2-block decoder-only transformer on a WikiText-103 subset and a 4-hidden-layer ResMLP on CIFAR-10, Adam with constant lr, EMA beta=0.9, measured every 100 iterations, 8 seeds for base recording
effect: monotone decay of ||Delta_l f||_RMS for hidden/QK/VO/readout; input embedding FSLR increases over time
locator: section 4.1, Figure 1 (and Figure 6, Appendix C.1)
notes: Transfer 2: measured on a 2-block toy transformer with Adam, not on our 8-layer Muon+AdamW hybrid, and no loss improvement is attached to the observation. Its value here is diagnostic -- it says a flat parameter-space lr already implies a decaying function-space schedule, so our explicit lr decay is compounding an implicit one, and that the EMBEDDING is the group whose function-space rate moves the wrong way.
statement: Under a constant parameter-space learning rate with Adam, the measured layerwise function-space learning rate falls monotonically over training for every parameter group except the input embedding, which rises in the transformer.

comparator: same 2-block transformer, three LayerNorm placements, Adam constant lr
effect: second FFN matrices ~1 order of magnitude larger ||Delta_l f||_RMS than the readout layer
locator: section 4.1, Figure 1
notes: Transfer 2: it identifies WHERE per-group learning-rate surgery would actually move the function (FFN down-projection, not the readout), which is a cheap thing to test at our scale. But the measurement is at depth 2 with Adam; our depth-8 Muon-on-2D setup already normalizes update spectra, which plausibly changes the ordering. No loss number attached.
statement: In the measured transformer the second feedforward weight matrices had function-space learning rates an order of magnitude larger than the readout layer.

comparator: PreNormPostMod transformer with QK-norm, Adam, sweeping init scale and lr
effect: loss vs lr curves vary wildly with init scale in the standard setting; they collapse onto each other under FLeRM
locator: section 4.2.3, Figure 4
notes: Transfer 3: we DO use QK-norm, so the same theoretical scale-invariance is broken the same way in our model -- init scale of QK-normed matrices is a live, cheap, single-knob experiment at our operating point. Scored 3 not 4 because the demonstration is on a 2-block model with Adam, and the fix they propose (FLeRM) needs a recorded base-model run we would have to pay for. Effect is read from a figure; no decimal reported.
statement: Transformers using QK-normalization and post-module normalization, which should be mathematically invariant to the magnitude of those weight matrices, nevertheless showed loss and optimal learning rate varying substantially with parameter initialization scale under standard training.

comparator: FLeRM with base FSLRs recorded from a small base model, same widths/depths/init scales
effect: uniform base FSLRs: transfer retained, training loss slightly worse than matched-profile FLeRM
locator: section 4.2.5, Figures 10-12 (Appendix C.3)
notes: Transfer 2: implies the per-layer relative learning-rate profile that Adam naturally induces is itself worth something beyond mere transfer, i.e. hand-set uniform per-layer rates are a slightly worse default. Boundary because the degradation is described only as 'slightly worse' with no number, and the setting is Adam-only at depth 2-ish. Cannot be resolved against our 0.000174 bpb floor from this evidence.
statement: Replacing the recorded base-model function-space learning rates with a uniform vector summing to one preserved hyperparameter transfer but gave slightly worse training loss.

comparator: decoder LM on FineWeb, GPT-2 tokenizer V=50304, 13.1B tokens / 100,000 steps, best over 7 learning rates {3e-4 ... 3e-1}
effect: 109M: baseline 3.20, z-loss 3.20, mu-loss 3.20, mu-centering 3.20; 221M: 3.05 for all four
locator: section 4, Table 2 subtable (i)
notes: Transfer 3: 109M is essentially our capacity and the data is FineWeb, but the budget is 100k steps. Registered as OPPOSING evidence: adding an output-logit regularizer at the conventional strength is a null at the tuned learning rate, so it should not be proposed as a bpb lever on stability grounds alone. Losses reported to 2 decimals only, which itself bounds resolution at 0.005 nats.
statement: At the default regularization strength lambda=1e-4, z-loss, mu-loss and mu-centering all gave virtually the same optimal loss as the unregularized baseline at every model size tested.

comparator: same model/data/lr-sweep, z-loss lambda varied over {1e-7, 1e-4, 1e-1, 1e2}
locator: section 5, Table 3 (z-loss, subtable (i))
notes: Transfer 3: -0.02 nats/token is roughly 0.007 bpb at ~4.4 bytes/token, i.e. ~40x our 0.000174 resolution, and the 109M cell is our capacity on FineWeb. Scored 3 not 4 because the horizon is 100k steps, the reported precision is only 2 decimals (so -0.02 sits right at the reporting granularity), and there is one run per cell with no seeds. Cost side: z-loss added 1.5% training time at 109M.
statement: z-loss with lambda=1e-1 gave a lower optimal loss than the baseline at the three largest model sizes tested, and the authors report 1e-1 rather than the conventional 1e-4 as the optimal z-loss strength.

comparator: same sweep, lambda in {1e-7, 1e-4, 1e-1, 1e2}
effect: z-loss lambda=1e2 at 109M: 3.64 vs 3.20 baseline; LRS blows up to 2.150. mu-loss lambda=1e2 at 109M: 3.20, LRS 0.034
locator: section 5, Table 3 (z-loss vs mu-loss, subtable (i) and (ii))
notes: Transfer 3: defines the usable band for any logit regularizer we add -- the improvement window for z-loss is narrow (1e-1 good, 1e2 catastrophic, 1e-4 null), so a lambda sweep is mandatory and a single bad pick costs 0.44 nats. mu-loss is by contrast flat in lambda for lambda >= 1e-4, which makes it the safer of the two to try first.
statement: z-loss with lambda=1e2 severely degraded optimal loss at every model size, while mu-loss at the same lambda did not.

comparator: identical architecture and schedule on 4 A100 with data parallelism
effect: 109M: mu-centering +0.4%, mu-loss +0.4%, z-loss +1.5% training time vs baseline; 16M: 0.6% / 0.4% / 6.4%
locator: section 4, Table 2 subtable (iii)
notes: Transfer 3: in a 300s step-bound regime a 1.5% throughput cost is ~15 lost steps, which is a real charge against the -0.02 nats z-loss gain; mu-centering at 0.4% is nearly free but was NOT the variant that improved optimal loss. Their timing is on 4 A100 with DP; our single-H200 fp8/compile step has a different vocab-projection share, so the percentage should be re-measured, not assumed.
statement: mu-centering (subtracting the mean output embedding after each optimizer step) and mu-loss each added under 1% training time, while z-loss added more, with the relative cost shrinking as model size grows.

comparator: LRS = E_eta[min(L(eta), L_0) - min_eta L] over 7 learning rates, 100k steps, FineWeb
effect: 109M LRS: baseline 0.344 -> z-loss 0.118 -> mu-loss 0.046 -> mu-centering 0.051, with optimal loss unchanged at 3.20
locator: section 4, Table 2 subtables (i) and (ii)
notes: Transfer 3: the actionable reading is that these methods let you push the learning rate HIGHER without divergence, and at ~1000 steps a higher usable peak lr is itself a plausible bpb lever -- that is the route by which this could pay here, not the regularization per se. Requires our own lr sweep to exploit; on their evidence the direct loss effect is zero.
statement: The measured benefit of z-loss, mu-loss and mu-centering was a large reduction in learning-rate sensitivity rather than a lower optimal loss.

comparator: 7 learning rates up to 3e-1, five model sizes 16M-221M
effect: z-loss diverges at large lr; mean embedding norm grows for both baseline and z-loss, showing z-loss fails to prevent anisotropic embeddings (Figure 3, bottom left)
locator: section 4, Training Stability paragraph and Figure 2
notes: Transfer 2: registered as opposing evidence against z-loss being the stability tool of choice -- if we adopt z-loss for lr headroom we may still blow up. Our runs use a much smaller max lr than 3e-1 and only ~1000 steps, so divergence is a less likely failure mode here; that is why this is 2 not 3.
statement: Models trained with z-loss still exhibited occasional divergence at large learning rates, whereas mu-loss and mu-centering did not diverge to any significant extent.

comparator: 6B decoder, 32 layers, 4096 hidden, GQA, 6e5 steps at 4.2M tokens/step, AdamW WSD, token-count-matched checkpoints
effect: shuffle leads on OLMES for ~half of the 2.5T-token run; sequential closes the gap only in the final third
locator: section 5.1, Figure 3 (and Figure 8, Appendix A.1)
notes: Transfer 1: our prepare.py is frozen so data ordering is not an available lever at all, and the study is at 6B/2.5T with a confounded temporal window (shuffled corpus 2020-2024 vs sequential 2018-2025, acknowledged by the authors). Recorded only as opposing evidence should anyone propose a non-stationary data order: the early-training penalty is exactly the regime we live in.
statement: A chronologically ordered pretraining corpus lagged a globally shuffled baseline on general language understanding through roughly the first half of training, converging to parity only in the final third.

comparator: Modded-NanoGPT 124M on FineWeb, batch 512 x seq 1024 = 524,288 tokens/step, 6,200 iterations, WSD schedule, Muon lr 3.6e-4, beta1 grid {0.9,0.95}, NorMuon beta2=0.95
effect: Muon needs 6% more iterations than NorMuon to reach the same val loss at 124M; 15% more at 350M
locator: section 4.2, Figure 5(a) (Muon-rescale comparison)
notes: Transfer 4: this is the closest match in the whole batch -- 124M, FineWeb, and EXACTLY our 524,288 tokens/step, with a Muon baseline that was already hyperparameter-tuned by the Modded-NanoGPT authors. The only extrapolation is 6,200 -> ~1010 steps. Caveat: they grid-searched beta1 for Muon AND NorMuon and report the best, and the 6% is read off a rescaled-schedule figure, single seed.
statement: Adding a per-neuron (row-wise) second-moment normalization after Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization let a 124M model reach the same validation loss in 6% fewer iterations than Muon.

comparator: AdamW baseline at 28.73s/step, 5.4B model on 16 A100 with FSDP2
effect: 5.4B training step time: Muon 29.56s (+2.8% vs AdamW), NorMuon 29.57s (+2.9%); optimizer state memory Muon 21.14GB vs NorMuon 21.19GB; state is m(n+1) vs Muon's mn
locator: section 3.3 and section 4.1.4, Table 2
notes: Transfer 3: the incremental cost over Muon is ~0.01s in 29.5s, i.e. under measurement noise, and the added ops (row mean of squares, broadcast divide) are elementwise and compile cleanly -- so at our ~297ms step this should be well under the 0.2% that Newton-Schulz iteration removal buys. Scored 3 not 4 because the timing is a multi-GPU FSDP2 measurement where their gain came partly from distributing orthogonalization, which is irrelevant on our single H200.
statement: The per-neuron second-moment statistic costs one extra vector of length m per matrix and did not measurably increase training step time over Muon.

comparator: 1.1B model, SlimPajama 50B tokens, batch 2M tokens, Depth-muP lr scaling, all variants same lr
effect: NorMuon (Front) > Muon but < NorMuon across the 1.1B training trajectory
locator: section 4.1.3, Figure 3 (NorMuon (Front) variant)
notes: Transfer 3: this is an ordering decision we must make when implementing, and getting it backwards costs part of the gain. Note the direct CONTRADICTION with MONA (2605.26842 section 4.1), which asserts the acceleration term must be applied BEFORE orthogonalization because applying it after would destroy the orthogonal structure -- NorMuon shows an after-orthogonalization row rescaling is fine and better. Effect read from a figure with no numbers, single seed.
statement: Applying the neuron-wise adaptive learning rate before orthogonalization instead of after improved on Muon but underperformed the after-orthogonalization placement.

comparator: 350M Modded-NanoGPT on FineWeb, 7,500 iterations, batch 512x1024
effect: Muon w/ normalization better than Muon in early stages, worse by the end of the 350M run
locator: Appendix A.2, Figure 7 (variant 'Muon w/ normalization')
notes: Transfer 3 and flagged as a BOUNDARY that matters here: the cheap global-rescale imitation of NorMuon looks like a WIN early and a loss late, and our runs terminate at ~1010 steps, i.e. in the early regime. So a short-horizon A/B could adopt the wrong variant for the wrong reason. Read from a figure, single seed.
statement: Rescaling Muon's update to have exactly Frobenius norm sqrt(mn) helped slightly early in training but was eventually surpassed by plain Muon, so the NorMuon gain is not attributable to global norm control.

comparator: 1.1B SlimPajama run and 350M Modded-NanoGPT run
effect: m>n-only variant underperforms full NorMuon; authors note m>n covers only the MLP up-projection, a small share of parameters
locator: section 3.1 and section 4.1.3, Figure 3 ('NorMuon (m>n only)'); Appendix A.2
notes: Transfer 3: tells us to apply the row normalization to ALL Muon-managed 2D matrices in our depth-8 model, not just the 4x MLP up-projection. The stated reason -- NS5 only approximates orthogonalization, so per-row norms are not actually 1 -- applies at our shape too. Figure-only evidence.
statement: Restricting the neuron-wise normalization to matrices with m>n greatly diminished the benefit, so the normalization must also be applied to matrices with m<=n despite the idealized-orthogonalization argument that it should be a no-op there.

comparator: 1.1B SlimPajama, same lr for all orthogonalization-based variants
effect: Muon+Adam underperforms NorMuon across the 1.1B trajectory; optimizer state 40.56GB vs 21.19GB at 5.4B
locator: section 4.1.3, Figure 3 ('Muon+Adam' baseline) and section 4.1.4, Table 2
notes: Transfer 3: rules out the more obvious 'just put Adam's v after Muon' variant, which we would otherwise be tempted to try first. Registered as opposing the coordinate-wise version specifically. Their Muon+Adam removes the sign-stabilization of the concurrent work it is adapted from, which is a deviation from that baseline's published form.
statement: Applying Adam's full coordinate-wise second-moment normalization after Muon's orthogonalization improved on Muon but underperformed the row-wise variant while doubling optimizer memory.

comparator: GPT-MHA-RoPE on FineWeb-Edu 50B, 100,000 steps, context 1024, global batch 480, tied embeddings + input-embed RMSNorm, identical seed
locator: section 5.1, Table 1 (baseline rows, R=1,3,5,7)
notes: Transfer 3 BECAUSE our v3 scope is input-pipeline bound -- the frozen Python packing loop dominates charged wall clock and GPU capacity is comparatively free, so spending 3x forward FLOPs to buy -0.055 nats is exactly the trade this operating point favors. Scored 3 not 4: single seed per cell (authors say multi-seed runs would be needed), 100k steps, and their own Appendix D shows wall clock scales roughly LINEARLY with R (9h -> 22h for R=3 at small scale), so if any of our step time is GPU-bound the step loss could eat the gain.
statement: Reusing the same physical transformer blocks for more rounds monotonically lowered final validation loss at fixed parameter count, at both GPT-2 small and medium scale.

comparator: identical looped backbone, embedding tying, optimizer, data pipeline and seed; only alpha and beta change
locator: section 5.1, Table 1 (Delta rows)
notes: Transfer 3: a one-line init/residual-scale change, but it is defined for a POST-normalized residual (x_{i+1} = Norm(alpha*x_i + f(x_i))) -- if our SSSL blocks are pre-norm, the DeepNorm/DeepLoop derivation does not apply unchanged, which is the main implementation blocker. Single seed per cell, 100k steps; -0.016 nats is ~0.005 bpb, well above our resolution.
statement: Setting the residual scaling exponent to p=1/2 (alpha=(2N)^{1/2}, beta=(8N)^{-1/2}) improved final validation loss over an unscaled looped baseline (alpha=beta=1) at every loop count R>=3, at both scales.

comparator: same backbone, R=1, single seed
effect: +0.0004 nats (GPT-2 small) and +0.0011 nats (medium) for DeepLoop vs baseline at R=1
locator: section 5.1, Table 1 (R=1 column)
notes: Transfer 3 and important as a BOUNDARY: it says the residual-scaling knob pays only in the weight-tied looped regime. If we adopt DeepLoop scaling without adopting looping, this evidence predicts a null (within their single-seed noise). Prevents a wasted A/B.
statement: At loop count R=1 the DeepLoop residual scaling was neutral versus the unscaled baseline at both model scales.

comparator: GPT-2 small, R=3, FineWeb-Edu 50BT, up to 5 seeds per p value, validation loss at the common step-2000 checkpoint
effect: no seed trains at p in {0.30,0.35,0.40}; at p=0.45 >=1/3 of seeds stay at the ~7.67-nat unigram floor; trained-seed mean val loss at step 2000: 3.70 (p=0.45), 3.73 (p=0.50), 3.76 (p=0.55), 3.80 (p=0.60)
locator: Appendix C, Figure 6 (p-sweep at R=3, GPT-2 small)
notes: Transfer 3 and the best-designed cell in this paper: it is MULTI-SEED and measured at step 2000, the only short-horizon multi-seed evidence in the batch. It shows residual scale trades aggressiveness against divergence probability monotonically, with ~0.03 nats per 0.05 of exponent among surviving seeds. Caveat: R=3 looped post-norm only; authors explicitly say the boundary may move at different normalization placements.
statement: In a seeded sweep of the residual scaling exponent at fixed loop count, every seed below p=0.45 failed to escape the unigram-frequency loss floor, while p>=0.50 trained reliably, and among trained seeds smaller p gave lower loss.

comparator: same 100,000-step budget at each R
effect: GPT-2 small wall clock: 9h (R=1), 22h (R=3), 35h (R=5), 50h (R=7) on 4xH200
locator: Appendix D, Per-cell cost table
notes: Transfer 3 and registered as OPPOSING the looping direction: at fixed 300 charged seconds, a ~2.4x step-time increase for R=3 would cut our ~1010 steps to ~420 unless the loop cost is genuinely hidden behind the frozen CPU packing loop. Whether it is hidden is the decisive measurement -- run one R=3 step-time probe BEFORE any loss A/B. Their timing is on 4xH200 with a 1024 context and no CPU-bound loader, so the ratio is an upper bound on what we would pay.
statement: Wall-clock time for the looped runs scaled roughly linearly with loop count.

comparator: 143M-param MobileLLM-style model, 30 layers, d=576, LLaMA-2 tokenizer, 2B-token FineWeb-Edu subset, AdamW lr 3e-4, single seed 42
effect: 124M zero-shot avg: BASELINE (2 epochs of HW) 34.28, INTERLEAVED 34.50, SIMP->HW 34.42, HW->SIMP 34.18
locator: section 4.1, Table 3 (124M rows) and section 4.2
notes: Transfer 1: our prepare.py is frozen so no data schedule is available, AND the paper reports no LM loss/perplexity at all -- only downstream accuracy, which cannot be mapped to val_bpb. Recorded only because our run is also a 2-epoch pass over a fixed dataset: at 124M their data-schedule interventions moved less than the spread between their own task columns, which is weak evidence that the 2-epoch repetition regime is not badly mis-specified at this capacity.
statement: At 124M, replacing the second epoch of repeated human-written text with LLM-simplified text or with a simple-to-complex ordering changed averaged downstream scores by well under one point.

comparator: Muon with identical lr, lr schedule and batch size; ScMoE + MLA architecture, seq len 8192
effect: MONA below Muon on code and general-English validation loss at 1B/400B tokens and 6B/1.2T tokens (curves only, no tabulated loss)
locator: section 6.1, Figures 2-5 (MoE-1B-A0.2B and MoE-6B-A0.5B validation curves)
notes: Transfer 2: the mechanism is cheap and implementable on our Muon path (one gradient-difference EMA buffer), but every LM experiment is a sparse MoE with MLA at 400B-1.2T tokens, which is far from a dense 124M/0.5B-token run, and the loss evidence is figures with no numbers and no seeds. Note the sign: alpha is NEGATIVE (see the alpha = -1/(2(1-beta_a)) rule), so this is not the same correction as MARS-M's positive gamma.
statement: Adding an EMA of consecutive gradient differences to the gradient before momentum accumulation and orthogonalization gave lower validation loss than Muon at every scale tested, under identical learning rate, schedule and batch size.

comparator: their own three MoE pretraining scales
locator: section 8 Limitations, Hyperparameter tuning paragraph
notes: Transfer 2: collapses two hyperparameters to one, which matters when a single A/B costs 300s and our resolution is 0.000174 bpb. But the rule is an observation over three runs, not an ablation, and the trend beta_a -> smaller with larger models gives no guidance for going DOWN to 124M. Their smallest is 1B.
statement: Across all their experiments the two extra hyperparameters satisfied a single relation, alpha = -1/(2(1-beta_a)), with beta_a between 0.975 and 0.99 and decreasing with model size.

comparator: none run
effect: asserted design constraint; no ablation of the alternative ordering is reported
locator: section 4.1, text preceding Algorithm 1
notes: Internal validity 1: this is an unablated assertion. Registered as a BOUNDARY because it directly contradicts NorMuon (2510.05491 section 4.1.3), which measures a row-wise rescaling applied AFTER orthogonalization and finds it BETTER than the same rescaling applied before. The two papers disagree about whether post-orthogonalization modification is admissible; the campaign should treat placement as an open empirical question, not a rule.
statement: The authors state the acceleration term must be applied before momentum accumulation because applying it after orthogonalization would destroy the orthogonal structure Muon relies on.

comparator: Muon on the same MoE-6B-A0.5B pretraining run
effect: ~1% higher optimizer inner step time; no practical difference in end-to-end iteration time; extra state = previous gradient + acceleration buffer (streaming removes the former, BF16 halves the latter, ~75% total reduction)
locator: Appendix C, Figures 13-14
notes: Transfer 3 as a cost estimate: elementwise buffer ops of this kind are the same class as NorMuon's row statistics and should land far below the ~0.2% that dropping two Newton-Schulz iterations buys on our box. Caveat: their iteration time is dominated by communication and data loading which HIDES the overhead; on our single H200 with a compiled step there is less to hide behind, so re-measure.
statement: The extra gradient-difference operations made the optimizer inner step about 1% slower than Muon, a difference the authors report as invisible in end-to-end iteration time.

comparator: four optimizers under identical settings, uniform (not layer-wise) learning rate for AdamW-Acc
effect: loss ordering MONA lowest, then Muon, then AdamW-Acc, then AdamW on MoE-1B-A0.2B
locator: Appendix D, Figures 15-16
notes: Transfer 2: relevant because our non-2D parameters run on AdamW, so if we adopt the acceleration term we could apply it on both legs. But it is a single 1B MoE run read from figures, and the AdamW-Acc baseline is a modified version of ALTO with its layer-wise lr regularization removed, so it is not the published method.
statement: The same gradient-difference acceleration term applied to AdamW also improved on plain AdamW, though the ordering MONA < Muon < AdamW-Acc < AdamW in loss means orthogonalization contributed more than acceleration.

comparator: exact polar decomposition UV^T
effect: ||O_tilde - UV^T||_F <= eps_NS * sqrt(r) with eps_NS decaying exponentially in T; T=5 stated negligible
locator: section 5.2, Remark 1
notes: Transfer 3 and CONSISTENT with our measured fact that cutting Newton-Schulz from 5 to 3 iterations costs +0.002645 bpb while saving only ~0.2% of a ~297ms step: exponential convergence means the error at T=3 is materially worse than at T=5 while the compute saved is a fraction of a percent. This is a theory remark, not a measurement, hence internal validity 2. Do NOT propose NS-count reduction; it is already measured here and this paper agrees T=5 is the right side of the tradeoff.
statement: Newton-Schulz iteration converges to the polar factor exponentially in the iteration count, and with standard coefficients T=5 leaves error the authors call negligible for practical purposes.

comparator: GPT-2 124M on OpenWebText, nanoGPT implementation, batch 512 x 1024 tokens, cosine decay with 2000 warmup, wd 0.1, grad clip 1.0, lr tuned per method; no-momentum blocks used 0.75x the lr of other blocks
effect: all blocks full momentum: 2.962 final loss; momentum off for Embedding and Attention-Output only: 2.964
locator: section 4.1, Table 1
notes: Transfer 3: 124M on 524,288 tokens/step matches our shape and the change is a per-parameter-group optimizer edit. The gain is not in loss (2.964 vs 2.962 is a slight regression) but in state and memory traffic. Note that 0.002 nats of regression is ~12x our resolution in the WRONG direction, so this is 'droppable, not free'. Their step budget is not stated; loss 2.962 implies a long OpenWebText run. Note also they had to drop the lr to 0.75x on the momentum-free groups, which is a confound.
statement: Disabling first-order momentum entirely on the embedding and attention-output-projection blocks of a GPT-2 124M model left final validation loss essentially unchanged.

comparator: GPT-2 124M on OpenWebText, same lr and schedule, differing only in which blocks get full/low-rank/no momentum
effect: V kept full (Q,K,MLP low-rank, Em/O none): 2.997; all of Q,K,V,MLP low-rank with Em/O none: 3.143
locator: section 4.1, Table 1 (V full vs V low-rank rows)
notes: Transfer 3: parameter groups are NOT interchangeable under optimizer surgery at 124M, and the value path is the sensitive one -- directly relevant given our architecture uses value embeddings, i.e. the value pathway already carries extra signal. A 0.146-nat spread between partition choices is enormous relative to our 0.000174 resolution, so per-group optimizer treatment is a real lever with a real downside.
statement: Value-projection blocks were the one group where momentum reduction was inadequate: low-ranking the value momentum noticeably slowed convergence relative to keeping it full.

comparator: vanilla SGD without momentum, constant stepsize, Gaussian covariates with Sigma_ii = i^{-a}
effect: SGD bound O~(T^{1/a-1} + T^{1/a-b/a}); accelerated SGD bound multiplies each term by powers of beta; when a<=b any beta<=1 increases excess risk
locator: section 3.1, Theorem 1 and the discussion following it
notes: Transfer 2: a quadratic-model theorem, not an LM measurement, and our optimizer is Muon+AdamW not plain SGD. Its value here is that it predicts a REGIME where momentum coefficients should be lowered rather than raised -- worth pairing with the fact that our short 1010-step run has high per-step gradient noise at 524,288 tokens/step. Cannot be used to predict a magnitude.
statement: In a high-dimensional linear-regression analysis, adding momentum reduces the optimization term of the excess risk but increases the variance term, so in the variance-dominated regime any momentum raises the final validation loss.

comparator: identical hyperparameters, only bias correction toggled, GPT-2 124M
effect: convergence about 1.96x slower without bias correction at r=50%; training loss plateaus higher throughout
locator: section 5.1.2, Figure 4(a)
notes: Transfer 2: only relevant if we adopt low-rank momentum at all, which memory pressure does not force on a single H200 at 124M. Recorded because a 1.96x convergence-speed penalty is the largest single-knob effect in this paper and shows compressed optimizer state is not a free lunch without the correction term.
statement: Omitting bias correction from the low-rank momentum estimator slowed convergence by about a factor of two even at 50% rank.

comparator: Pre-Norm 550M dense transformer, 16 layers, 4096 ctx, OLMoE Mix, 400B tokens, AdamW
effect: C4 PPL 20.00 for HybridNorm vs 20.30 for Pre-Norm; training loss 2.74 vs 2.75; HellaSwag 53.35 vs 51.97
locator: section 4.4, table 4 (normalization position ablation, 550M dense, 400B tokens)
notes: Transfer 2: correct family (dense decoder LM pretraining, implementable purely in train.py as a block-structure change with no data or evaluator change), but demonstrated at 550M/400B tokens = ~800x our token budget, and no seed replication is reported so the 0.30 PPL gap is a single-run difference. At 124M/~1010 steps the run never leaves early training, where Pre-Norm's stability advantage is largest and Post-Norm's regularization advantage has least time to pay off. Blocker: our stack already has QK-norm, so only the V-norm and the FFN Post-Norm are new.
statement: Replacing Pre-Norm with QKV-Norm in attention plus Post-Norm in the FFN (HybridNorm) lowered C4 validation perplexity at a fixed 400B-token budget.

comparator: same 550M dense / 400B token protocol, other normalization placements in the same table
effect: QK-Post: diverge; QKV-Post (HybridNorm): loss 2.74, C4 PPL 20.00; QKVC-Post: 2.74 / 20.05
locator: section 4.4, table 4 row 'QK-Post' (listed as 'diverge')
notes: Transfer 3 because it is a sharp, cheap-to-check failure boundary and our stack already runs QK-norm: if anyone moves the FFN norm to Post, doing it without also normalizing V is reported to diverge outright. Divergence is a large effect far above our 0.000174 resolution and would show up in the first tens of steps. Caveat: single run, no seeds, and 'diverge' is not quantified.
statement: Normalizing only Q and K (not V) in attention while using Post-Norm in the FFN diverged, whereas adding V normalization trained stably.

comparator: three init schemes (Normal 1/sqrt(2.5d), Depth-Scaled sqrt(2l), Megatron sqrt(2L)) crossed with two norm placements, same 550M/400B protocol
effect: Pre-Norm: Normal 20.29 vs Megatron 20.44 C4 PPL; HybridNorm: Megatron 20.00 vs Normal 20.44
locator: section 4.4, table 3 (initialization ablation, 550M dense, 400B tokens)
notes: Transfer 2: the interaction is architecture-generic and implementable, but the whole spread (20.00-20.49) is within a range no seed replication is offered for, and at 550M/400B tokens. The transferable content is the warning that an architecture change and an init change are not separable levers, which matters here because our 1010-step run is dominated by early dynamics where init still matters. Single seed.
statement: The best initialization scheme depended on the normalization structure: Pre-Norm was best with Normal init while HybridNorm was best with Megatron (1/sqrt(2L)) init.

comparator: HybridNorm without first-block special treatment, 550M dense, 400B tokens
effect: HybridNorm* C4 PPL 19.85 / loss 2.73 vs HybridNorm 20.00 / 2.74; EmbedNorm reported as the one first-block variant that did not help
locator: section 4.4 'Special Treatment of First Block', figure 4 and table 4 rows HybridNorm vs HybridNorm*
notes: Transfer 2: a one-line change to layer 0 only, so cost is nil, but the effect (0.15 PPL at 550M/400B) is not obviously above our noise once translated to bpb at 124M, and there are no seeds. The negative EmbedNorm result is the more usable half: it argues against adding a norm right after the embedding, which interacts with our value-embedding placement.
statement: Applying Pre-Norm (rather than Post-Norm) in the first transformer block on top of HybridNorm further lowered training loss and perplexity, while adding a normalization layer after the embedding (EmbedNorm) did not.

comparator: depth swap at matched ~550M parameters, same 400B-token protocol
effect: 16 layers: HybridNorm C4 20.00 vs Pre-Norm 20.30 (gap 0.30); 29 layers: 19.67 vs 19.88 (gap 0.21) but Pre-Norm 29L 19.88 beats Pre-Norm 16L 20.30; Post-Norm diverged at 29 layers
locator: section 4.7, table 5 (550M/16 layers vs 543M/29 layers, 400B tokens)
notes: Transfer 1: our model is depth 8, i.e. shallower than both arms, so the depth-scaling story is out of regime and the reported benefit shrinks rather than grows in absolute PPL from 16 to 29 layers. Registered mainly as a boundary marker: the normalization-placement lever is depth-coupled and its evidence lives at 16-29 layers, not at 8.
statement: The HybridNorm advantage over Pre-Norm was larger at 29 layers than at 16 layers at matched parameter count, and Post-Norm alone failed to converge at 29 layers.

comparator: pure AdamW baseline at the same 130M/1e9-token protocol, per-regime LR calibrated on a 2e8-token pilot and frozen before full runs
effect: final val loss 3.3019 (Muon on out-proj only) vs 3.3472 (Muon on all eligible) vs 3.4178 (pure AdamW); dL = -0.116 and -0.071 respectively
locator: section VI-B, table II (OpenWebText, 1e9 tokens, seeds 42 and 1337)
notes: Transfer 3 and stance 'opposes' because our stack applies Muon to ALL 2D matrices, which this study measures as strictly worse than a restricted assignment. Same 524288 tokens/step as us; 1e9 tokens = ~1900 steps, only ~2x our step count; 2 shared seeds with inter-regime gaps ~10x seed sd (+/-0.001-0.002 under Muon vs +/-0.010 under AdamW). Discount: the backbone is Mamba-2, not a transformer, so 'out_proj' vs 'in_proj' maps onto our qkv/mlp/o_proj split only by analogy. Also note per-group LR was re-tuned per regime, so part of the gap could be LR-fit rather than assignment.
statement: Assigning Muon only to the output projections beat assigning Muon to all eligible matrices, which in turn beat AdamW, in Mamba-2 130M language-model pretraining.

comparator: same four regimes across two corpora and two budgets, 2 seeds each
effect: baseline-to-best gap fell 0.116 -> 0.063 on OpenWebText and 0.083 -> 0.043 on FineWeb-Edu between 1e9 and 2.6e9 tokens; best regime matched AdamW's 1e9-token loss in ~5.8e8 tokens
locator: section VI-C, table III bottom row; section X discussion
notes: Transfer 3: this is the single most operating-point-relevant statement in the batch. Our 300s/~530M-token run sits at or below the smallest budget tested, i.e. exactly where the paper says optimizer-assignment gains are LARGEST. It also predicts that any Muon-assignment result we measure will look better here than the literature reports at Chinchilla scale, so we should not down-weight it for being 'a short-run effect'. Verified as durable to 5e10 tokens (2.8853 vs 2.9027) though shrunk to 0.017 there, single seed at that budget.
statement: The Muon-over-AdamW advantage shrank monotonically as the token budget grew, indicating a token-efficiency effect rather than a lower loss floor.

comparator: Muon on out-proj only, 2e8-token OWT pilot, best Muon LR swept per variant, 2 seeds

This is a strong negative on any 'constrain the embedding/unembedding geometry' proposal at our scale, which matters because our stack has value embeddings and a large vocab relative to n_embd=512. That decoupled variant is UNTESTED here. The FP32 triangular-solve requirement is a concrete hazard for our bf16-autocast + torch.compile graph. Runtimes are wall-clock on unspecified shared hardware, so the 'negligible' reading is weak evidence.

Also a warning that a learned gate over-mixes; at ~1010 steps a learned gate has little time to converge anyway (compare 2607.10593's stabilization-bottleneck finding).

The perplexity gaps (0.7 on WikiText) are also not error-barred and there is one run per architecture. Registered so the controller can see the mechanism exists without treating it as reachable at 300s.

comparator: the same ~1.5B / 100B-token models compared in table 2

comparator: the full RLA model with L2 QK normalization and residual clipping at c=1, same pretraining budget

We already run QK-norm, so the relevant read is the reverse: any mechanism we add that ACCUMULATES a state or a side-path sum should be assumed to need an explicit bound. Figures only, no numbers, no seeds; hence internal validity 2.

comparator: seven other attention implementations dropped into the same GPT-2 backbone, identical 6,400-step schedule on one RTX 4090
effect: total GPU energy 1.42 MJ for sliding-window attention vs 1.07 MJ (FlashAttention), 1.17 MJ (MLA) and 1.32 MJ (GQA); sliding-window also had the highest GPU memory usage of the eight variants

notes: Transfer 1 and stance 'opposes' our confirmed span-halving lever - but the contradiction is almost certainly an implementation artifact, not a mechanism result: the paper gives no kernel details, the sequence length is only 512 (where a window saves nothing), the workload is instruction fine-tuning rather than pretraining, and it reports no loss comparison at all beyond 'all curves converge'. This is the same failure pattern our campaign already recorded for document masking, where a dense-mask implementation made a winning mechanism look catastrophic. Registered so the contradiction is visible and correctly attributed to implementation. Single run, no seeds, no accuracy metric.
statement: In a unified GPT-2 benchmark on a single consumer GPU, sliding-window attention consumed the most GPU memory and more total training energy than the unmodified baseline attention.

comparator: baseline GPT-2 masked scaled-dot-product attention on the same hardware and schedule
effect: FlashAttention lowest total energy 1.07 MJ and lowest memory 16.4 GB at 0.955e12 FLOPS; MLA 1.17 MJ at 0.923e12 FLOPS; linear attention, despite linear asymptotics, landed in the same FLOPS range as baseline attention
locator: section V-A and V-B (figures 1, 2, 3, 6, 7), single RTX 4090
notes: Transfer 2: the direction (fused kernels beat asymptotically-cheaper but unfused mechanisms) is the operative constraint on this campaign, where the step is ~297ms and the profile is dominated by small GEMMs and tiny kernels rather than by attention. It is a reason to prefer mechanisms that map onto existing fused kernels over mechanisms that require new elementwise passes. Internal validity 1: consumer GPU, 512-token fine-tuning, no seeds, no quality metric, and the FLOPS numbers are measured throughput not analytic counts.
statement: Attention variants with fused, memory-aware kernel implementations achieved the lowest training energy and memory, and the ranking was driven by the implementation rather than by the asymptotic complexity of the mechanism.

comparator: GPT-2 small (12L, 12H, width 768) on OpenWebText, AdamW lr 1e-3, block 1024, micro-batch 20, grad-accum 16; one-factor dtype change with tiling held on
effect: bf16 O + bf16 stats: 6/6 runs collapsed at steps 700-1400; accumulator -> fp32: 0/2 collapsed through step 4900 (one long run healthy at 103400 logged steps)
locator: section 2, Table 1(a) 'Localizing the fault'
notes: Transfer 2 only as a NEGATIVE boundary: the collapse window 700-1400 steps sits squarely inside our ~1010-1022-step horizon, so if we ever hand-roll an attention kernel with a bf16 accumulator this failure mode would land inside the run, not after it. It does NOT apply to the current config, which uses vendor kernels with fp32 accumulation. Six seeds on the fault arm, only two on the fp32 arm (censored, so a sufficiency counterexample not a rate). Blocker for reuse: their assay depends on a hand-written kernel we do not have.
statement: In a custom PyTorch re-implementation of FlashAttention-2, keeping the streaming online-softmax carries (running output O and softmax stats) in bf16 caused GPT-2-small training to collapse in every seed tested, whereas promoting the accumulator to fp32 did not collapse.

comparator: same GPT-2-small/OpenWebText recipe as the collapsing bf16-accumulator arm
effect: SDPA bf16 operands 0/2 collapsed through 4900 steps; FlashAttention-2 forced 0/2 through 4900; full matrix no tiling 0/2 through 4900; GPT-2 medium SDPA 0/2 through 4900
locator: section 2, Table 1(a), 'Scope: is another factor sufficient?' rows
notes: Registered as 'opposes' against any proposal to spend budget hardening our bf16 attention path: on vendor kernels the paper's own scope rows show no collapse. Internal validity capped at 3 because each scope row is only 2 seeds and all are right-censored observation bounds, not endurance limits. Transfer 2: directly tells us this whole failure family is out of regime for our torch SDPA/flash setup, which is a usable 'do not pursue' signal.
statement: PyTorch's fused scaled-dot-product-attention path with bf16 operands, and forced FlashAttention-2, produced no collapse in the same configuration that collapsed 6/6 under the authors' bf16-accumulator re-implementation.

comparator: same GPT-2-class recipe; contrasted against post-reduction 4-bit weight-gradient quantization which drove the runaway
effect: 0/2 seeds collapsed through 11900 steps with 4-bit attention-GEMM operands + fp32 accumulation; registered seed's sigma(W^Q) no higher than 39, versus 205-292 under the 4-bit weight-gradient arms
locator: Appendix D, 'Where fp32 accumulation is the boundary'
notes: Transfer 2: supports treating aggressive low-precision attention GEMM operands (e.g. fp8 QK/PV on H200) as a stability-safe throughput lever provided accumulation stays fp32, which is what the vendor kernels do. Deliberately not scored higher: the quantizer is software-emulated so it measures NO speedup, the authors flag the operand arm as carrying a milder effective dose, and only 2 seeds. Also note the campaign's own cross-GPU contention confound previously made an fp8 'win' an artifact, so any speedup claim here must be re-measured, not inherited.
statement: Quantizing both operands of all three attention GEMMs to a four-bit grid while retaining fp32 accumulation left training healthy, indicating that low-precision arithmetic in attention is not itself the trigger; the trigger tracks where low-precision error enters accumulation.

comparator: plain GPT-2 under the bf16-accumulator fault, seed-matched pairs identical through the fire step

Transfer 2: cheap and directly relevant if we ever see instability in a 300s run, but our runs are short, stable and QK-normed, so its practical value is as a triage rule rather than a bpb lever. 2 seeds per arm; the authors state earlier restore points and larger cuts were not tested, so the LR arm is not exhaustively falsified.
statement: At an identical trigger and fire step, a matched learning-rate cut failed to rescue a diverging run while QK-local actions did, so the action locus rather than reactivity decided the outcome.

comparator: three seeds per method, same-configuration reference; three unguarded controls collapsed at 7200, 8600, 7400 steps
effect: always-on QK-norm ended at 3.13, 3.09, 3.09 validation loss over three seeds; QK-Guard at 3.13, 3.10, 3.09; final-loss gap in the plain rescue arms +0.02 nats with every endpoint within 0.10 nats

Transfer 2, not higher: the comparison is at 60k steps on GPT-2 small with a live low-precision fault, whereas our 1010-step run has neither. Their resolution is far coarser than our 0.000174 bpb, so 'no detectable cost' does not mean 'no cost' at our resolution.
statement: Over a 60k-step schedule, always-on parameter-free per-head QK normalization and a dormant trigger-activated version reached indistinguishable validation losses, and the authors state only that no cost is detectable at their resolution.

comparator: AdamW, SGD-M, Lion and SWATS at published hyperparameters, 200 epochs, batch 128, seed 42

statement: Signal-triggered switching among AdamW, Lion and SGD-M improved accuracy and convergence speed, but every reported benchmark is a small convolutional vision model on CIFAR-10/100 and no language-model or transformer result is reported.

comparator: CIFAR-100 / WRN-28-10, 200 epochs (~78200 steps), against the calibrated AOS-R configuration
effect: recommended D_min >= 0.025 x T; D_min=1000 (under-calibrated at T~78200) cost 1.0 pp top-1 and +21% steps versus D_min=4000; no dwell (D_min=0) 81.3 +/- 0.5 versus 82.2 +/- 0.2; bridge length fixed at 400 steps

The paper's own overhead accounting (S x D_min = 8000 of 78200 steps) is a ~10% tax that becomes a ~80% tax at our horizon. Transfer 1.

comparator: 0.5B LLaMA3.2-style model, 10B CulturaX tokens, batch 1081344 tokens (~9250 steps), randomly shuffled same-data baseline

(2) The objective mismatch is total: this campaign optimizes val_bpb, and the paper argues that metric is the wrong one and never measures it, so even the direction of the effect on loss is unknown. Registered as 'opposes' so the controller does not launder benchmark-accuracy step savings into a bpb claim. Robustness is only 2 independent repetitions (section 5.3) with no reported variance figures.
statement: The curriculum-learning gains are reported exclusively as averaged 0-shot benchmark accuracy, with the authors explicitly declining to report training or validation loss on the grounds that loss poorly captures generalization.

comparator: Mistral-160M on a 1B-token FineWeb-Edu set, batch 256 x seq 1024 (~3800 steps), random baseline averaged over 3 seeds (8, 10, 42)

Transfer is still 1: every one of the four guidances (segment ordering, folding, zig-zag, jittering) is a permutation of the training stream, and prepare.py packing and ordering are FROZEN. Note also that the fitted irreducible loss E is identical across orderings, i.e. the ordering effect is a coefficient shift, not a floor shift. The Random-vs-STR/SAW extrapolated loss gaps are small fractions of a nat at every scale in Table 7.

comparator: Mistral-160M trained on 1B FineWeb-Edu tokens; FO versus ZIG at matched partitions
effect: FO-3 (folding order, 3 cycles) shows a sharp gradient-norm spike at each cycle boundary; ZIG (same partition with odd cycles reversed) maintains stable gradient magnitude. No numeric spike magnitude is given; the evidence is the figure.
locator: section 5.2.3 'G3: Curriculum Continuity', Figure 5
notes: Transfer 1. Mechanistically relevant to us because our run makes TWO passes over a fixed dataset (final_epoch 2.0), so the epoch boundary is a repeat rather than a distribution shift and this failure mode should not fire. It is recorded mainly so that if the controller ever sees a gradient-norm anomaly at the epoch-1/epoch-2 seam it has a prior explanation. Internal validity 2: figure-only evidence, no seeds, no quantified spike.
statement: Reordering that produces an abrupt jump in sample-difficulty at cycle boundaries produced a sharp global gradient-norm spike, and reversing every odd cycle so adjacent cycles connect at similar scores removed the spike.

comparator: Llama-3.2-1B up-scaled with 8 inserted head-wise memory blocks, continually pretrained on a 1.5B-token FineWeb-Edu subset with the base blocks frozen

locator: Appendix F.1, Table 7 'Effect of total memory slots on performance'
notes: Registered as 'opposes' against the campaign's standing hypothesis that key-value / n-gram memory capacity is a val_bpb lever. It is direct evidence that memory-table size buys retrieval-flavoured downstream accuracy without moving the language-modelling objective, which is the ONLY objective here. This is consistent with the campaign's own finding that the n-gram memory acts as a memorizer whose sign flips with the operating point. Internal validity 2: continual pretraining with a frozen pretrained base, one run per cell, no seeds; perplexity is on WikiText, not our BPB accounting. Transfer 2 because the mechanism is implementable in train.py but the base-frozen CPT setup is not our from-scratch regime.
statement: Scaling a product-key memory table from tens of thousands to one million slots raised averaged zero-shot accuracy but left language-modelling perplexity essentially unchanged.

comparator: Llama-3.2-1B + MIDUS-HML, memory size and all other hyperparameters fixed, CPT on 1.5B FineWeb-Edu tokens
effect: Wiki-PPL 11.67 / 11.63 / 11.64 / 11.64 at k = 1 / 2 / 4 / 8 (0.04 total range); average zero-shot accuracy 53.03 / 53.22 / 53.50 / 53.37
locator: Appendix F.2, Table 8 'Effect of the number of Top-k'
notes: Second independent knob on the same mechanism showing the same dissociation: the retrieval knob moves downstream accuracy, not the LM objective. Combined with the capacity ablation this makes top-k a KNOB rather than a MECHANISM at our operating point, and one whose measured effect on the objective we care about is ~0. Transfer 2: implementable but the ablation predicts a null on val_bpb, so this claim should be used to DEPRIORITIZE top-k tuning, not to motivate it. One run per cell, no seeds.
statement: Varying the number of retrieved memory slots per token from 1 to 8, at fixed memory size, left perplexity essentially unchanged while averaged zero-shot accuracy improved up to k=4 and then saturated.

comparator: single NVIDIA RTX 6000 Blackwell, global batch 16 with 16 grad-accum steps, sequence length 2048, same backbone
effect: on Llama-3.2-1B: 10.79 s/iter for a Linear memory layer and 8.42 s/iter for plain PKM, versus 4.74 s/iter for the un-upscaled base and 4.56 s/iter for the optimized head-wise HML; i.e. naive memory lookup costs 1.8-2.3x the step time of the dense baseline
locator: Appendix G, Table 12 (Llama-3.2-1B efficiency); section 5.2 'Efficiency of MIDUS-HML'; Table 4 (Llama-3.1-8B)
notes: Highest-transfer claim from this paper and the one that matters most here. Our regime is throughput-bound and step count dominates val_bpb at fixed 300s, and the campaign's own nsys trace already identified small n-gram-VE GEMMs plus ~194k tiny fill kernels as the step-time bottleneck. This paper independently measures that a memory/top-k gather layer added to a transformer costs ~2x step time unless its kernels are hand-optimized, and the authors explicitly attribute the crossover to 'non-fully optimized low-level kernels'. Transfer 3: measured on one GPU at a comparable-ish backbone with a real wall-clock number, but at 1B params / seq 2048 rather than 124M, and the s/iter figures include a frozen-base backward that we do not have.
statement: Memory-layer variants with unoptimized lookup kernels more than doubled training step time relative to the dense baseline, while the kernel-optimized head-wise variant matched it.

comparator: none - the paper asserts the property analytically and uses it in all MIDUS runs; no A/B against random value init
effect: with values initialized to zero, Mem(a) = 0 and M(x) = x at initialization; no ablation isolating this choice against a nonzero-init control is reported
locator: section 4.1, 'Weight initialization and residual connection'
notes: Internal validity 1 because it is an unablated design choice, not a measured effect. Transfer 2 because it is a zero-cost, zero-throughput-risk init pattern that generalizes to ANY new residual branch we add in train.py (an extra memory path, a gated side-branch, a second value-embedding route): start it at exact identity so the first steps cannot be spent undoing the perturbation. In a ~1010-step run where every step is scarce, an init that wastes no steps recovering the baseline is worth more than at long horizons. Relevant to the campaign's mechanism-exploration phase.
statement: Initializing the retrieved value table to zero makes an inserted residual memory block an exact identity map at step 0, so the expanded model reproduces the base model's output at the start of training.

comparator: single attention layer on synthetic Gaussian single-location regression data, L = 2, 3 or Uniform{1,2,3}; Bayes risk as the reference
effect: under max-SLR at infinite signal, E_softmax = 0 while E_lin = 1 - O(log L / L) -> 1; under spiked-SLR at large signal, E_lin ~ (L/(L-1)) / nu (polynomial) versus E_softmax = exp(-c_L nu) (exponential)
locator: section 4.3, Corollary 4.2 (equations 12 and 13) and Corollary 4.3; section 4.4 and Figure 1
notes: Transfer 1. This is a toy model: one attention layer, a squared-error denoising-style objective, synthetic isotropic Gaussian tokens, sequence lengths of 2-3, and no language modelling anywhere. It supports the status quo (we already use softmax attention with SSSL sliding windows) and argues against swapping in a linear or kernelized attention for throughput, but the argument is qualitative at our scale. The finite-sample result (Result 5.1) rests on the non-rigorous replica method, which the authors state explicitly. Corollary 4.3's 'variance in L hurts linear attention' does not apply to us: our packing gives fixed-length sequences.
statement: On a single-location regression task, softmax attention attains the Bayes risk while linear attention's risk approaches that of the trivial null predictor as sequence length grows, with element-wise erf and normalized softplus falling strictly between the two.

comparator: no empirical comparator - the theorem is proved, not measured; the paper's experiments only instrument gradient norms and do not compare any intervention
effect: Theorem 1 requires 1 - theta = sqrt(L(f(x1)-f*)/(K sigma^2)), eta = sqrt((f(x1)-f*)/(4KdL)), theta <= beta <= (1+theta)^2/4 and epsilon = sigma^2/d; the authors state this 'differs from standard implementations where (theta, beta) = (0.9, 0.999) is typically used'
locator: section 2, Theorem 1; section 2.5 'Unpractical Settings of eta, theta, and beta'
notes: Transfer 0: the paper offers no intervention to run. Its parameter settings are not a recipe (the authors disclaim them), and its experiments measure diagnostics rather than compare arms. Recorded so the controller does not mistake a convergence-rate result for a schedule lever. Internal validity 3 for the theory itself (assumptions are standard: smoothness, unbiasedness, coordinate-wise bounded variance, and notably no bounded-gradient assumption).
statement: The paper's O(sqrt(d)/K^{1/4}) l1-norm convergence rate for AdamW is proved only under hyperparameter settings the authors themselves describe as unpractical, and they state that analysis under standard constant momentum remains open.

comparator: GPT-2 Small (~125M) under Megatron-LM, lr 3e-3, weight decay 0.05, betas (0.9, 0.95), global batch 640, 50000 steps, 8xA100; also ResNet-50 on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet
effect: for GPT-2 on OpenWebText with d = 1.24e8 and K = 50000, sqrt(d)/K^{3/4} ~ 3.33 (versus the 0.01 PyTorch weight-decay default), and sigma_s^2/d ~ 1e-10; empirically ||grad||_1 = Theta(sqrt(d)) ||grad||_2 with sqrt(d) = 11136

The 125M GPT-2 scale matches ours, but the run is 50000 steps at batch 640 versus our ~1010 steps at 524288 tokens, and the measurement is purely diagnostic - no arm is compared, so nothing here predicts a bpb change. Its only usable content is a weak 'do not spend budget tuning AdamW epsilon' signal, since the theory-implied epsilon = sigma_s^2/d ~ 1e-10 is already smaller than typical defaults. Internal validity 2: the full-gradient and noise quantities are approximated over 100 mini-batches for the LM run, not computed exactly.

comparator: Llama-architecture models, 1B training tokens, cosine schedule with 5% warmup, lr 1e-3 -> 1e-5, AdamW; sigma = 0.02 with lambda = 0.1 (GPT2/HuggingFace default) versus gamma-init configurations
effect: the paper states 'sigma-initialization achieves lower test loss with smaller models' and that 'its performance plateaus as the model size increases, resulting in significantly higher loss compared to gamma-initialized models at larger scales'; model sizes swept are 50M, 100M, 200M, 400M, 800M at 1B training tokens
locator: section 4.1 'Scaling law', Figure 2 (right panel); Appendix B Table 3
notes: Highest-transfer claim in this paper and the reason it is registered as 'opposes'. Our 124M model at ~0.53B tokens sits at the very size/data corner where the paper's own figure says the DEFAULT init wins and the proposed intervention loses. So gamma-init should not be launched here on this paper's authority - if anything the paper predicts it will hurt. Transfer 3: the swept sizes bracket ours and the intervention is a one-line change in train.py, but it is a figure-only claim with no tabulated numbers, single seed, and a Llama architecture without our SSSL windows, value embeddings or Muon.
statement: At a fixed 1B-token budget across models from 50M to 0.8B parameters, the conventional fixed-sigma initialization achieved lower test loss than the width-scaled gamma initialization at the smaller model sizes, with gamma-init only overtaking as model size grew.

comparator: same 0.8B Llama-architecture model and identical token budgets, three complexity configurations including the sigma = 0.02 / lambda = 0.1 default
effect: 0.8B-parameter models trained on 0.2B to 1.4B tokens: the small-complexity curve (gamma = 1, lambda = 1) lies left of the large-complexity curve (gamma = 0.5, lambda = 0.1); no numeric loss gap is tabulated
locator: section 4.1 'Scaling law', Figure 2 (left panel)
notes: Transfer 2 and in direct tension with the preceding claim, which is deliberate - the controller should see the contradiction. The token budgets here (0.2B-1.4B) bracket our ~0.53B, but the model is 0.8B rather than 124M, and the size sweep in the SAME figure says the effect reverses sign at small model size. Figure-only, single seed, no error bars, so internal validity 2. Note the paired lambda = 1 is a very large weight decay by our standards and interacts with Muon's own update normalization in ways this paper does not test.
statement: A small-complexity configuration (large initialization rate together with large weight decay) shifted the test-loss-versus-tokens curve leftward relative to a large-complexity configuration, indicating better sample efficiency at fixed data.

comparator: the 0.9B small-complexity configuration (gamma = 1) which did not require the extra normalizations
effect: for the 2.4B model the authors adopted gamma = 0.58 rather than gamma = 1 and added embedding normalization plus sandwich normalization to suppress loss spikes; the 0.9B small-complexity model used gamma = 1, lambda = 1
locator: section 6.1 'Training Stability'; Table 1 header row; Appendix D
notes: Transfer 2 as a cost rider on the previous claim: any gamma-init experiment here must be paired with a spike watch, and if it needs sandwich/embedding norm to be stable then it is no longer a free one-line change but a throughput-costing architecture change, which at 300s charged seconds is likely net-negative. The authors also note in Table 1 that gamma = 0.58 slightly beat gamma = 1 at 2.4B, i.e. the optimum is interior and scale-dependent. Internal validity 2: reported as engineering narrative, not as a controlled ablation.
statement: Small-complexity configurations increased loss-spike instability as model scale grew, forcing the authors to back off the initialization rate and add two extra normalization mechanisms to train their largest model.

comparator: 180M-parameter Llama-architecture models trained on a 40B-token Memory3 subset, lambda swept over {0, 0.1, 1} crossed with gamma over {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1}
effect: at lambda = 1, gamma = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8, 1 all converge to comparable small parameter norm; at lambda = 0 and lambda = 0.1, larger gamma converges to smaller complexity
locator: section 5.1 'Influence of initialization scale and weight decay', Figure 4
notes: Transfer 2 and practically the most useful part of this paper for us: it says weight decay, not init scale, is the knob that actually determines where the parameter norm lands, and weight decay is a pure scalar with zero throughput cost. That makes lambda a cheaper thing to sweep than an init-scale change. Caveats: measured on parameter norm, not on loss; 180M models but on 40B tokens (~76x our token budget), so the norm may not have converged at all by our step 1010; and our Muon branch normalizes updates on 2D matrices, which changes how weight decay interacts with the effective step size in a way this paper does not model. Figure-only, no seeds.
statement: With a large weight-decay coefficient, models initialized across a wide range of initialization rates converged to comparable small parameter norms, whereas with small or zero weight decay the final norm depended strongly on the initialization rate.

comparator: identical encoder-only models with independently initialized self-attention matrices, same datasets and epoch budget
effect: 4-layer models: Wikipedia 0.984 -> 0.812 (73% speed-up), Red Pajama 1.106 -> 0.907 (69%), Jigsaw 2.782 -> 2.758 (26%); 24-layer models: Wikipedia 0.192 -> 0.166 (44%), Red Pajama 0.209 -> 0.189 (34%)
locator: section 4.2 'Enforcing symmetry at initialization improves the training of encoder-only models', Table 1
notes: Transfer 1 because the demonstrated setting is bidirectional/masked-LM training, which is not our objective. The intervention itself is free (an initialization change, zero throughput cost), which is why it is worth registering at all. Internal validity 2: one run per cell, no seeds, no error bars, and 'speed-up' is defined against the other arm's own final loss rather than a fixed target.
statement: Initializing the query and key matrices so that their product is symmetric lowered final loss and accelerated convergence for encoder-only (bidirectionally trained) transformers.

comparator: the same 12-layer BERT-base-uncased architecture trained in encoder-only versus decoder-only mode on identical data
effect: Theorem 2.3 gives E[||delta w_col||^2] / E[||delta w_row||^2] > 1 under an autoregressive objective; empirically decoder-only models show high directionality and near-zero symmetry while encoder-only models show the reverse, replicated on Jigsaw, Wikipedia and Red Pajama
locator: section 2.4, Theorem 2.3 (equations 17-18) and Theorem 2.4; section 4.1 and Figure 3; section 6 Discussion
notes: Registered as 'opposes' so the symmetric-init lever is NOT ported to our decoder-only model on the strength of the encoder result. The paper's own theory predicts the opposite structural prior for autoregressive training, and section 6 explicitly leaves the decoder-side analogue unbuilt ('it is important to explore strategies for leveraging the directionality structures of decoder-only models'). Transfer 2: it is a well-supported reason to reject a cheap-looking lever, which is usable information. Internal validity 3: the theorems rest on four stated modelling assumptions (partial embedding alignment, i.i.d. init, early-token predictiveness, symmetric bidirectional error), but the empirical structure measurement is broad, covering many pretrained model families.
statement: Autoregressive training was shown theoretically and measured empirically to induce column-dominant directional structure in the query-key matrix rather than the symmetric structure induced by bidirectional training, and the authors list exploiting the directional structure as unaddressed future work.

comparator: non-symmetric initialization of the same architecture on the same dataset
effect: speed-ups fall from 26-73% at 4 layers to 0-35% at 12 layers; the 12-layer Jigsaw arm is worse with symmetry (1.430 versus 1.419) at 0% speed-up; 24-layer recovers to 14-44%
locator: section 4.2, Table 1 (4-layer, 12-layer and 24-layer blocks)
notes: Registered as 'opposes' because our model is depth 8, i.e. between the 4-layer arm where the effect is large and the 12-layer arm where it is zero or negative on one of three datasets. Non-monotonicity across 4 -> 12 -> 24 layers with single runs and no error bars is itself evidence that these differences may be seed noise. Given our measured counterbalanced resolution of 0.000174 bpb, the 12-layer Jigsaw delta of 0.011 nats would be resolvable here, but the paper cannot tell us its sign reliably at n=1. Transfer 2.
statement: The benefit of symmetric query-key initialization was largest for the shallowest models and shrank or reversed with depth, including one deeper configuration where symmetric initialization gave a higher final loss.

comparator: no filtering on Nemotron-CC, at four filtering rates (3%, 10%, 30%, 100%), compute-optimal training across the swept compute range; replicated on DCLM-RefinedWeb
effect: fitted F_opt(C) = 4e-5 x C^0.25 (percent of tokens retained versus training FLOPs); the probability-optimal rate shifts from top 3% below 1e21 FLOPs, to 10% around 1e22, to 30% beyond 1e23. Per-benchmark compute multipliers for the filtering method itself range 1.8x (Winogrande) to 10.4x (ARC-Easy), average 4.7x
locator: section 6.2 'Optimal filtering rate depends strongly on scale', Figure 10
notes: Transfer 1: prepare.py is FROZEN, so no filtering rate is ours to set. Recorded because it is the strongest evidence in this batch that data composition effects are strongly SCALE-DEPENDENT and that small-compute regimes want much narrower data than large ones - our run is around 3e17-4e17 FLOPs, below the bottom of their swept range, where the fit implies filtering far more aggressive than anything they tested. That is a caution against importing any large-scale data-composition result into this regime. Internal validity 3: careful multi-scale scaling-law fits with bootstrap uncertainty, but the outcome metric is downstream Core accuracy at compute-optimal training, not bits-per-byte at fixed wall clock, and the authors note the shift is 'much more gradual' when training fixed-size models for increasing token counts (Appendix D.5), which is closer to our setting.
statement: The compute-optimal fraction of pretraining tokens to retain after benchmark-targeted filtering increases as a power law in training compute, so smaller-compute runs are best served by much more aggressive filtering.

comparator: Pre-LN baseline, LLaMA-style RMSNorm+SwiGLU, Adam, lr 1e-3 (<=350M) / 5e-4 (1B), identical schedule; single run per cell
effect: LLaMA-130M/2.2B tokens: perplexity 26.73 (Pre-LN) -> 25.76 (LNS); LLaMA-1B/8.9B tokens: 17.02 -> 15.71
locator: section 5.1, Table 1
notes: Transfer 3, not 4: the intervention is one scalar multiply per norm and is directly implementable in train.py with zero parameters and negligible FLOPs, and the smallest demonstrated scale (130M) matches our 124M. Discounted because their 130M model is deeper (LLaMA-130M ~12 layers) than our depth-8 stack, and the whole mechanism is about deep layers going dead; at L=8 the scale factor only ranges 1.0 to 0.354, so the effect size should be much smaller. No seeds or error bars are reported anywhere in the paper, and their token budget (2.2B) is ~4x ours.
statement: Scaling each pre-LayerNorm output by 1/sqrt(layer_index) (LayerNorm Scaling) lowers validation perplexity versus plain Pre-LN at 130M-1B parameters under identical architecture, hyperparameters and schedule.

comparator: Pre-LN OLMo-7B, 20B tokens; crossover point not quantified
effect: Qualitative: 'LayerNorm Scaling exhibits slightly slower convergence at the early stages of training'; final OLMo-7B loss 2.69 (Pre-LN) -> 2.50 (LNS) only after the full 20B-token run
locator: section 5.3.1, Figure 6 (OLMo-7B loss curves)
notes: This is the single most decision-relevant fact in the paper for us and it cuts AGAINST adoption: our entire run is ~1010 steps / ~0.53B tokens, i.e. plausibly still inside the early phase where LNS is behind. Transfer 3 because the phenomenon is about training-horizon position, which is exactly our binding constraint, but the observation is at 7B and read off a figure with no crossover step reported. Blocker: nobody measured where the crossover is at 124M.
statement: LayerNorm Scaling converges more slowly than Pre-LN in the early phase of training and only overtakes it later in the run.

comparator: Pre-LN baseline at 130M/2.2B and 250M/3.9B tokens, single run per cell
effect: LLaMA-250M: LNS alone 20.35, LNS + Scaled Init 20.79, Scaled Init alone 20.98, Pre-LN 21.92; LLaMA-130M: 25.76 vs 25.80 vs 26.04 vs 26.73
locator: section 6 Ablation Study, Table 6
notes: Transfer 3 because it is a pure config interaction we can honour for free, and our train.py may already carry a 1/sqrt(2L)-style output-projection init that would silently cancel the lever. Score not 4 because the differences (25.76 vs 25.80) are far below anything our 0.000174 bpb resolution would separate at n=1 after conversion, and no seeds are reported.
statement: Combining LayerNorm Scaling with Scaled Initialization is worse than LayerNorm Scaling alone, so the two depth-scaling mechanisms must not be stacked.

comparator: Pre-LN 26.73 at LLaMA-130M / 2.2B tokens
effect: LLaMA-130M perplexity: after LN 25.76; after Attn/FFN 26.53; before LN 26.97; LNS only after Attn 26.89; LNS only after FFN 26.43; after residual 1358.11 (divergence)
locator: section 6 Ablation Study, Table 8
notes: Transfer 3: this is an implementation-placement fact at almost exactly our parameter count, and the divergence entry means a careless placement wastes a whole 300s run rather than costing a few thousandths of a bpb. Single run per cell, no seeds.
statement: The depth scaling factor must be applied to the LayerNorm output; applying the same factor after the residual connection diverges, and other insertion points give no gain.

comparator: Pre-LN baseline at 130M/2.2B and 250M/3.9B tokens
effect: LLaMA-130M: Pre-LN 26.73, +LayerScale 27.93, +SkipInit 27.41; LLaMA-250M: 21.92, 23.45, 22.29
locator: section 6 Ablation Study, Table 6
notes: Transfer 3 because learnable residual gates are a cheap-looking lever someone will propose for a 124M model, and this is direct evidence at 130M and 250M that they are worse than doing nothing. Uncertainty: single runs, and their LR was not re-tuned per variant, which usually disfavours variants that change effective residual scale.
statement: Learnable per-branch residual scalars (LayerScale, SkipInit) degrade language-model perplexity relative to plain Pre-LN, while fixed depth-dependent scaling helps.

comparator: Same model with QK norm (RMSNorm with learned scale on Q and K), Muon, constant LR + 500 warmup, 5000 steps
effect: ~10% faster training wall-clock vs QK norm at 1B params, 2048 ctx, 196608 tokens/batch, 4xGH200, bf16
locator: section 4, paragraph 'QuacK gives a performance boost over QK norm'
notes: Directly relevant: our config HAS QK-norm, and at 300 charged seconds a 10% throughput win is ~100 extra steps, which by our own token law is worth far more than the resolution floor. Transfer 3 not 4 because their step is a 1B model at 2048 ctx where norm kernels are a different fraction of the step than in our 124M/depth-8/~297ms step, and the 10% figure is a single informal observation with no profiling breakdown, no seeds, and no separation of the norm removal from the LR-modulation bookkeeping they added.
statement: Replacing QK-norm with query/key learning-rate modulation removes two RMSNorm computations per attention block and was observed to train about 10% faster.

comparator: 1B Qwen3-style MHA, Muon, 5000 steps, base LR in {3e-4, 3e-3, 3e-2}
effect: Qualitative from Figure 2: 'QK norm is overall the most performant'; QuacK 'similar but slightly worse' than QK norm in MHA; magnitude not tabulated
locator: section 4, Figure 2 (MHA row) and paragraph 'QuacK maintains stability and strong performance'
notes: Registered as opposing evidence to the throughput claim above: dropping QK-norm buys ~10% steps but costs some loss, and the paper never reports the size of that loss cost, so the net sign at our operating point is unknown. Transfer 3 because the architecture (MHA + Muon + QK-norm) is the closest match in this batch; internal validity 3 because losses are only shown as figures, with one seed per configuration.
statement: With multi-head attention, QK norm remained the most performant logit-stability intervention; the learning-rate-based substitute was slightly worse on validation loss.

comparator: 1B model, MHA and MLA, Muon, 5000 steps, three base LRs
effect: At eta=3e-4 all interventions within a small band with QK norm 'marginally better'; the interventions only separate at eta=3e-3 and eta=3e-2
locator: section 4, paragraph 'Higher learning rates are better', Figure 2 left column
notes: This bounds the whole family for us: if our run is not near its stability edge, swapping QK-norm for anything else is expected to be a wash on loss and is then purely a throughput trade. It also implies the real lever is raising the base LR until instability appears, then paying for stability. Transfer 3: same optimizer family and a short (5000-step) horizon, but 8x our parameter count and 8x our step count.
statement: At a low base learning rate all attention-logit interventions (QK norm, QK clip, fixed Q/K LR downscaling, QuacK) performed similarly, because no instability is encountered.

comparator: Same 1B model with a single global LR of 3e-2 (diverges) and QK norm (stable) as reference
effect: At base LR eta=3e-2, decreasing only the Q/K learning rates by a factor eta_Q/K fully stabilizes pretraining; the unmodified run 'never got below 4.5 loss after 1.5k steps'
locator: section 1, Figure 1
notes: Transfer 3: implementable as a per-parameter-group LR in our existing Muon/AdamW split with zero throughput cost, and it is the cheapest way to test whether a higher base LR is available to us in the ~1010-step regime. Demonstrated only at 1B/5000 steps and only as loss curves; no per-seed variance.
