statement: Reducing the learning rate of the query and key weights alone is sufficient to fully stabilize pretraining at a base learning rate that otherwise diverges.

comparator: Same ~100M model, Frobenius vs spectral norm inside the same LR rule
effect: 'The benefits of using the spectral norm are very small'; magnitudes not reported, sweep over tau with both norms at ~100M params
locator: section 3, Figure 3 (~100M parameter model)
notes: The only ~100M-scale evidence in the paper, i.e. our parameter count, which is why it is registered at all. Transfer 2 because it only tells us which cheap variant to pick if we adopt the rule at all; the difference is qualitative, read off a figure, and any effect described as 'very small' at 100M is likely under our 0.000174 bpb resolution.
statement: When modulating query/key learning rates by weight norm, using the spectral norm gave only very small benefits over the Frobenius norm.

comparator: Qwen3-0.6B from scratch on FineWeb-EDU, AdamW, batch 256 x seqlen 1024, 10000 steps, 2.6B tokens, 3 schedules x 3 peak LRs, exactly matched token budgets
effect: Final val loss gap (Type2 minus Type1) ranges from +0.017 to +0.743 across all 9 configurations; e.g. WSD at 3e-3: 3.015 vs 3.033; cosine at 3e-4: 3.221 vs 3.964
locator: Appendix C.5, Table 4 (and Remark 3.1)
notes: Best-controlled experiment in this batch and the closest to our scale (0.6B, 10k steps, 2.6B tokens, FineWeb-EDU). Transfer 3: it says do NOT trade our fixed 524288-token batch against LR decay, and it says the LR schedule is the lever with independent value. Not 4 because it is AdamW rather than our Muon hybrid, 10x our step count, and the largest gaps come from very small constant LRs that we would never run. One run per cell.
statement: Realizing a given eta/B trajectory through the learning-rate schedule consistently beats realizing the identical trajectory through a batch-size schedule at matched total tokens.

comparator: Static batch size at matched compute, Llama3-1B on FineWeb-edu, Muon-NSGD
effect: Relative improvement in best perplexity: 0.8% (cosine), 2.5% (WSD), 14.6% (constant LR)
locator: section 3.2, Figure 4
notes: Transfer 2, not 3: the theory-optimal schedule for a LINEAR-to-zero LR is exactly the static batch size (Table 2 row 'linear'), so if our schedule is linear decay there is nothing to win here; and the large 14.6% number belongs to a constant-LR run, which is not our schedule. Also 1B params on a much longer horizon, and the loader/packing that would have to emit variable batch sizes is inside frozen prepare.py.
statement: An increasing (variance-reducing) batch-size schedule at fixed compute improves best perplexity, but the size of the gain depends strongly on the learning-rate schedule shape.

comparator: Static batch size at the same precision, same model and data
effect: Qualitative: 'with half-precision training, the advantage of our batch size vanishes in comparison to the static batch size'; three-way comparison fp32 / fp32-bf16 mixed / bf16 at Llama3-1B on FineWeb-edu
locator: Appendix C.3, Figure 12
notes: Registered as opposing evidence because our run is bf16 autocast. Whether we count as 'mixed' (fp32 master weights, bf16 compute) or 'half' decides whether the whole batch-schedule family is live for us; the paper does not define the boundary. Transfer 3 because the confound is precision, which we cannot change without touching numerics, and it is directly on the path of any batch-schedule proposal. Internal validity 2: figure-only, no numbers, one run.
statement: The advantage of the optimal batch-size schedule over a static batch size vanishes under pure half-precision (bf16) training, while it survives under mixed and full precision.

comparator: Static batch size under fixed compute and under fixed iterations of 40000, Llama3-1B
effect: Advantage scales as X/B_static; 'practically significant even when the base batch size is increased 8x'; their 1x base batch is 128k tokens
locator: Appendix C.4, Figures 13-14; Corollary 3.3
notes: Directly bounds the lever for us: our batch is 524288 tokens = 4x their base, so we sit in the regime where the advantage is already shrinking, and the theory says it goes to zero as B grows. Transfer 3 because it is a quantitative argument against spending a run on batch scheduling at our token/step count, which is the useful direction. 1B params, figure-only evidence.
statement: The gain from a dynamic batch-size schedule is inversely proportional to the base batch size and vanishes as the batch grows, though it was still visible at 8x their base batch.

comparator: Static batch size, Llama3-1B on FineWeb-edu, Muon-NSGD
effect: Table 2 'linear' row: B_t^optim = B_static exactly; ablation at peak LR 0.003 / 0.01 (optimal) / 0.03 shows the dynamic schedule wins at every peak LR
locator: section 3.1, Theorem 3 and Table 2; Appendix C.2, Figure 11
notes: Transfer 3 as a decision rule rather than a lever: it tells us the batch-schedule family is a no-op under a linear-decay LR and is only worth anything under constant or WSD-like shapes, so it should be scored jointly with whatever LR schedule we run. Derivation is for a convex surrogate; the empirical support is 1B-scale figures.
statement: The compute-optimal batch-size schedule depends only on the shape of the learning-rate schedule, not on the peak learning rate, and for a linearly decaying learning rate the optimum is a constant batch size.

comparator: Parameter-matched MoE baseline, 0.92B trainable / 0.29B activated, 50B Nemotron-CC tokens, LLaMA-3 tokenizer
effect: Benchmark average 45.03 (vanilla Engram) vs 45.62 (MoE baseline); largest single-task drop BoolQ 55.93 -> 46.97
locator: section 4.2, Table 2 (0.92B trainable, 50B tokens)
notes: Registered as opposing evidence for our n-gram lever: the same mechanism that helps at 2.8B/100B tokens went NEGATIVE at ~1B, and the stated cause (table too small -> collisions) gets worse, not better, at 124M. Transfer 2 only: the metric is downstream benchmark accuracy, not loss/bpb, the backbone is MoE, and 50B tokens is ~100x our token budget. Single run per configuration.
statement: A hashed n-gram conditional memory module (vanilla Engram) underperformed the parameter-matched baseline at ~0.9B trainable parameters, attributed by the authors to hash collisions in a small embedding table.

comparator: Vanilla Engram at 0.92B trainable / 50B tokens
effect: Ordering by training-loss reduction relative to vanilla Engram: gated-longest-match + fallback > gated longest match > gated attention aggregation > attention aggregation; no numbers given
locator: section 4.3.3, Figure 5 (ablation of grafting mechanism)
notes: Useful as a design rule if we extend our n-gram path: prefer one longest-match lookup plus a fallback over attending across matched orders, because the selected memory is more specific and the fallback removes the hit-token bias. Transfer 2: the rule is cheap and implementable, but the evidence is loss curves in a figure with no numbers, at 8x our scale, and the coverage-bias argument is about matched vs unmatched tokens, which depends on our frozen tokenizer's n-gram statistics.
statement: Grafting only the longest matched n-gram through a gate outperformed attention-based aggregation over all matched n-grams, and adding a hashed fallback path for unmatched positions was better still.

comparator: Same recipient model and token budget, only the memory bank size varied, 0.92B / 50B tokens
effect: Memory size 30k -> 300k -> 3M entries improves the loss curve at every point; hit-rate growth slows but does not saturate
locator: section 4.3.4, Figure 5 (right); Appendix B.4, Figure 10
notes: Transfer 2: capacity of the n-gram table is a real knob we control, and this says bigger is monotonically better in loss up to 3M entries. Heavily discounted because their entries are frozen 35B-model hidden states (not learned rows), the recipient is 8x our size, and at 124M / ~1010 steps a large table is under-trained and adds parameter-init and memory-bandwidth cost that this paper never pays.
statement: Increasing the number of stored n-gram memory entries monotonically lowered training loss throughout training, with hit rate still rising at the largest bank tested.

comparator: MoE baseline of the same trainable/activated size, 0.92B trainable
effect: 0.92x training throughput and 0.95x inference throughput vs the MoE baseline, with 0.97x inference memory; ~12B frozen memory offloaded
locator: section 4.3.5, Figure 4 (efficiency analysis)
notes: Relevant because our host is CPU-contended and any per-token Python-side lookup would be far more expensive than their fused path; an 8% throughput loss at 300s is ~80 steps, which by our token law is a real bpb cost that must be beaten. Transfer 2: the number is measured on a different stack (offloaded 12GB bank, large model) and tells us the shape of the cost, not its value on our box.
statement: Adding an exact hash-indexed n-gram memory lookup path cost about 8% of training throughput even though the memory bank was much larger than the model.

comparator: Aggregate next-token loss on the same checkpoints; three 1B runs (Transformer, Hybrid, Pure RNN) on a matched mixture and budget under WSD
effect: Max Transformer-Hybrid separation ~0.06 nats under aggregate 'All tokens' vs ~0.12 nats under the Top-10 ∩ No-Copy filter, about twice as large
locator: section 6, Figure 7 (1B development runs)
notes: Interesting for our measurement problem, not our objective: our evaluator and BPB accounting are FROZEN, so this cannot change what we are scored on. Transfer 2 as a side diagnostic only, and only if per-token NLL is already available without touching prepare.py. Also note the amplification is architecture-family-sized (attention vs recurrence); it is not evidence that a filter would resolve a sub-0.000174 bpb knob difference.
statement: Filtering validation loss to open-class non-copy target tokens roughly doubled the measured loss separation between architectures compared with aggregate loss, at negligible extra cost.

comparator: Paired per-token NLL on matched prefixes; Olmo 3 7B vs Olmo Hybrid 7B for the natural-token analysis, 1B matched runs for the filtered curves
effect: On Copy-5 positions the Pure RNN is about 0.10 to 0.20 nats worse than the two attention-based models; the raw hybrid advantage over the transformer shrinks with n and approaches zero for long repeated spans
locator: section 4.1 (Figure 4B-C) and section 6 (Copy-5 filter)
notes: Bears directly on our confirmed span-vs-n-gram substitution result: it says local/visible-prefix copying is precisely the regime attention is good at, so removing attention span there is only safe if some other exact-recall path (our n-gram memory) covers it. Transfer 2: this is an observational analysis of released checkpoints at 7B (plus 1B re-scoring), with no intervention we can rerun, and the tags are acknowledged noisy proxies (Appendix E).
statement: On target positions that continue a repeated n-gram visible in the prefix, attention-based models beat a recurrence-only model, and the hybrid's advantage over the transformer collapses toward zero.

comparator: Olmo 3 7B vs Olmo Hybrid 7B, paired per-token NLL at identical prefixes, prose/code/markup
effect: Raw paired loss gap 0.0384 nats on content words vs 0.0238 nats on function words, a difference of 0.0146 nats (about 61% larger); ordering survives regression controls
locator: section 4.1, Figure 2 (aggregate raw panel)
notes: Transfer 1: it is a decomposition of an architecture gap we are not considering (no recurrent mixer in our stack), measured on two frozen 7B checkpoints, and it prescribes no intervention. Recorded so that the content/function decomposition is not mistaken for a lever.
statement: The measured loss advantage of a hybrid over a matched transformer concentrates on open-class content words and is smaller on closed-class function words.

comparator: StaticHybrid with a 1:3 full:SWA ratio, 1.5B model, 32K continual-pretraining data distribution
effect: Averaged full-attention ratio ~0.13 across 22 layers vs the 0.25 ratio of a static 1-full-per-3-SWA hybrid; layers 1, 2, 3 and 22 prefer SWA while layers 8, 11 and 14 use full attention more; counted over 400M tokens
locator: section 4.4, Figure 5 ('Ratios of Full Attention across Layers')
notes: Suggests a cheap static test for us: make the SSSL span depth-dependent (short at the first and last layers, longer in the middle) instead of uniform, which costs nothing at runtime. Transfer 2: the measurement comes from a 1.5B model continually pretrained at 32K context, a completely different length regime from ours, and routing preferences learned there need not hold at depth 8 / short context. Internal validity 2: one model, one data distribution, no seed variation.
statement: When each token at each layer is free to route between full attention and sliding-window attention, the learned full-attention usage is strongly layer-dependent and averages far below the usual static hybrid ratio.

comparator: SWA-ZS, SWA-CPT, StaticHybrid (1:3) and FullAttn at 1.5B, 4K pretraining context
effect: Qualitative: 'As the contexts of most instances are within the sliding window size (i.e., 1024), the performance of SwiAttn is similar to the baselines, including both full attention and SWA models'
locator: section 4.2, paragraph 'Commonsense Reasoning' (Table 1)
notes: Transfer 3 because it is the mechanism behind our own confirmed short-window win: when the predictive dependency lies inside the window, paying for longer attention buys nothing and only costs throughput. It says the safe span is set by where the dependencies actually are, not by the sequence length. Discounted from 4 because the evidence is benchmark accuracies at 1.5B rather than validation loss, and 'similar' is not quantified.
statement: On tasks whose contexts fit inside the sliding window, sliding-window attention, static hybrid and full attention performed similarly.

comparator: 1.5B model, 4K context, 240B pretraining tokens + 20B continual pretraining tokens
effect: Average 41.5 (SWA-CPT) and 41.7 (SWA-ZS) vs 50.6 (StaticHybrid) and 52.9 (FullAttn); the dynamic hybrid recovers FullAttn's 52.9, a 27.5% relative improvement over SWA-CPT
locator: section 4.2, Table 2 (in-context retrieval)
notes: Opposing evidence to unbounded span shrinking: some fraction of positions genuinely need out-of-window recall, and pure SWA gives that up. Transfer 2: measured with retrieval benchmarks at 1024-token windows and 4K contexts on a 1.5B model, and our objective is aggregate val_bpb where such positions are a small minority; still, it names the failure mode our n-gram memory has to be covering.
statement: Sliding-window-only attention lost heavily to full attention and to hybrids on in-context retrieval tasks whose evidence lies outside the window.

comparator: FullAttn baseline at 1.5B; training-time cost of the dual-branch scheme is not reported as a speedup
effect: Reported speedups are inference-side (over 4x prefill at 32K, up to 12x decode); the authors state 'lack of a hardware-efficient implementation for computing the two branches during the prefill stage'
locator: section 3.4 / Figure 2(a) (both branches computed during CPT) and the Limitations section
notes: Registered so the ~0.13 full-attention ratio is not read as a training-time FLOP saving. At 300 charged seconds, a scheme that computes both branches during training strictly loses steps, so only a STATIC per-layer span schedule derived from the routing observation is worth testing here. Transfer 2: the constraint is architectural and would apply to us, but their kernel situation is not ours.
statement: The dynamic full/sliding routing scheme computes both attention branches during training and has no hardware-efficient implementation, so its efficiency gains are inference-side only.

comparator: MiMo-7B-RL and GLM-4.5-Air 106B-A12B under DAPO and GSPO, 200 RL steps, batch 128, LR 1e-6, 128 H20 GPUs
effect: CE-loss MTP 47.7 average vs Detach 58.9 (largest gap -29.2 on AIME24); adaptive coefficient (OCC) 61.7, +2.8 over Detach; per-step time 8.07s (OCC) vs 8.11s (Detach) vs 45.06s (full-model MTP backprop, 5.6x slowdown)
locator: section 3.2 (Regime 2, Eq. 5-6) and section 4.2, Table 1
notes: Transfer 1 and recorded explicitly as a boundary so this paper is not cited as support for multi-token prediction in pretraining. The whole degradation argument depends on E[<g_RL, g_CE>] ~ 0, which follows from zero-mean advantages in RL; in pretraining the auxiliary CE gradient and the main CE gradient are strongly correlated, so the sign of the argument does not carry over. The only architecture-agnostic residue is the idea of setting an auxiliary-loss coefficient from a running estimate of gradient inner product over gradient norm at negligible cost, which has zero pretraining evidence here.
statement: The finding that a cross-entropy multi-token-prediction auxiliary loss degrades the main model, while an adaptively weighted one helps, was established only in reinforcement-learning post-training and rests on the advantage estimates being zero-mean.

comparator: Chinchilla baseline and Muennighoff et al. effective-data forms, fit over 157 Llama-2-architecture FineWeb runs, 15M-1B params, unique budgets 50M-6B tokens, epochs 1-16.
effect: One-parameter additive penalty reaches R^2_multi = 0.9503 vs 0.5825 for the exponential-decay effective-data form; four-parameter form reaches R^2 = 0.9971 (fitted P = 0.02305 +/- 0.00121 for the 1p form at weight decay 0.1).
locator: section 4 (Equations 6-8) and section 5, figure 4; appendix D.3 table 13
notes: Transfer 3 not 4: model sizes bracket our 124M and the fitted law is a closed form we can evaluate, but the fit is over full-convergence single-GPU runs with cosine-to-10% schedules and 512-token sequences, not 300s-truncated runs. Directly relevant because final_epoch=2.0 puts us at R_D=1. Blocker: the law predicts loss at end of a fixed token budget; it says nothing about a wall-clock-bounded budget.
statement: Excess loss from repeating training data is well described by an additive penalty term P * R_D^delta * (N/U_D^gamma)^kappa added to the Chinchilla law, rather than by an effective-data rescaling.

comparator: Same-N single-epoch Chinchilla prediction on FineWeb; fit spans 15M-1B params and 50M-6B unique tokens.
effect: P = 0.02305 nats; evaluated at R_D=1 and N/U_D ~ 0.47 (124M params over ~265M unique tokens) the penalty term is ~0.0108 nats/token, i.e. roughly 0.0035 bpb at ~4.4 bytes/token.
locator: section 4, Equation 6; appendix D.3 table 13 (standard study, lambda=0.1)
notes: Transfer 3: the arithmetic is my extrapolation of their fitted coefficient to our operating point, not a measured point in their grid (their smallest U_D is 50M and their grid uses R_D in {0,1,3,7,11,15}, so R_D=1 IS in-grid). The implied ~0.0035 bpb is ~20x our 0.000174 resolution, so 'stop at 1 epoch and take fewer tokens' vs 'take 2 epochs' is a measurable trade here. Uncertainty: MAD on P is +/-0.00121 (5%); the bytes/token conversion is mine and depends on the frozen tokenizer.
statement: At a capacity-to-unique-data ratio near N/U_D ~ 0.5 and one repetition (two epochs), the fitted one-parameter overfitting penalty is on the order of 0.01 nats/token, small but non-zero.

comparator: Identical model/data grid with all other hyperparameters (LR, warmup, batch size) held constant; 126 runs at lambda=1.0 vs 157 at lambda=0.1.
effect: One-parameter penalty coefficient P falls from 0.02305 (lambda=0.1) to 0.00681 (lambda=1.0); the exponential-decay tolerance R* rises from 7.756 to 12.731.
locator: section 6, figure 7; appendix D.3 tables 13 and 14
notes: Transfer 2: the mechanism is a one-line change we can make, but the benefit only pays off past the crossover compute budget (see the opposing claim below) and our budget is far below it. Also they only test two weight decay values, so the shape between 0.1 and 1.0 is unknown.
statement: Raising AdamW weight decay from 0.1 to 1.0 reduces the fitted repetition-overfitting coefficient by roughly 70%.

comparator: Same scaling grid, lambda=0.1 vs lambda=1.0, all other hyperparameters fixed.
effect: Crossover at C ~ 3.2e18 FLOPs for U_D=250M; below it lambda=0.1 wins (at C=3e18, ppl 23.38 vs 22.93 but BPB 1.46 vs 1.47). Strong WD raises the fitted entropy floor E from 1.8383 to 2.0422 nats and increases B by ~6x.
locator: section 6, figures 6 and 8; table 2; appendix D.2 table 12
notes: Transfer 3 and stance opposes: our run is ~6*124e6*530e6 ~ 4e17 FLOPs, an order of magnitude BELOW their U_D=250M crossover, so this paper predicts strong weight decay is NET HARMFUL at our operating point despite the attractive 70% penalty reduction. Registered as opposing evidence against the naive 'we repeat data so crank weight decay' reading of the previous claim.
statement: Strong weight decay (lambda=1.0) incurs a single-epoch loss premium at every compute budget and only overtakes standard weight decay past a crossover compute budget.

comparator: Three prescriptions (Chinchilla, effective-param, theirs) each trained and evaluated at matched (U_D, C).
effect: At U_D=250M, C=5e18: their law recommends 700M params / 5 epochs and achieves ppl 22.90 and OLMES BPB 1.45, vs Chinchilla's 280M / 12 epochs at ppl 25.31 / BPB 1.52.
locator: section 5, figure 5 and table 1
notes: Transfer 2: our epoch count is fixed at 2.0 by frozen accounting and our budget is wall-clock not FLOPs, so the epoch axis is not ours to move. What DOES carry over is the direction 'at fixed data, prefer capacity over repetition', which argues for spending the nearly-free GPU FLOPs on width/depth rather than on more passes. Prescriptive validation is one run per cell, no seeds.
statement: Under a fixed unique-data budget there is a compute level beyond which spending compute on model capacity beats spending it on more epochs, reversing the Chinchilla/effective-data recommendation.

comparator: AdamW with vs without bias correction, 160M-param 12-layer nanoGPT-style model, hidden 768, SlimPajama, 2.5B tokens, batch 256, averaged over 3 seeds (main sweep); appendix B beta sweep is single-seed.
effect: Reported as 'performance is identical' / 'indistinguishable for every learning rate and every choice of beta' at (beta1,beta2)=(0.95,0.95); no numeric gap is stated, only figures.
locator: section 2, figure 1 (right panels); appendix B, figure 6
notes: Transfer 3 and the effect is ZERO, so this is a 'do not spend a run on it' claim, not a lever. Effect field carries no decimal because the paper reports only figures. Score not 4 because their token budget implies roughly 19k steps whereas we run ~1000, and the bias-correction transient is exactly an early-training effect (see the boundary claim below).
statement: With a warmup-cosine learning-rate schedule and the LM-optimal beta1=beta2 setting, removing Adam bias correction leaves final validation perplexity unchanged across the whole learning-rate sweep.

comparator: Closed-form factorization of the Adam step; validated against the 160M SlimPajama sweep.
effect: At the torch default (0.9, 0.999) rho creates 'a very gradual warm-up effect, slowly increasing the effective learning rate across thousands of iterations' and dampens the peak of an explicit schedule; at (0.95, 0.95) it is a spike that decays within ~100 steps (figure 7 plots the first 100 steps).
locator: section 3, Equation 3 and figure 2; appendix B figure 7
notes: Transfer 3, and this is the operationally interesting part for us: a warmup transient measured in 'thousands of iterations' is <1% of their run but would be a LARGE fraction of our ~1010 steps. If any AdamW group here runs beta2=0.999, bias correction is silently reshaping the whole first tenth of training. Blocker: they never run a short-horizon budget, so the size of that distortion at 1000 steps is untested.
statement: Adam bias correction acts as a multiplicative modulation of the effective learning rate, rho(t) = sqrt(1-beta2^t)/(1-beta1^t), whose duration and shape depend strongly on (beta1, beta2).

comparator: Same 160M SlimPajama setup, constant LR instead of warmup-cosine.
effect: Stated as 'bias correction always performing worse' with the gap growing over beta in {0.9, 0.95, 0.975, 0.9875}; no numbers reported, figures only, and the appendix sweep is single-seed.
locator: section 2 figure 1 (constant-LR panels); appendix B figure 6
notes: Transfer 2 and internal_validity 2: single seed for the beta sweep, figure-only reporting, and we always run a schedule so the regime where the effect exists is not ours. Registered as a boundary condition on the neutrality claim rather than as a lever.
statement: With a constant (unscheduled) learning rate and beta1=beta2, including bias correction is worse than omitting it, and progressively worse for larger beta.

comparator: Global causal attention vs sliding-window span-50 attention on the same synthetic reconstruction task; figure-only loss values.
effect: On a 2500x2500 banded target (band width 50, d_k=25, 100K Adam steps), local attention reaches lower training loss and its max |QK^T| grows far more slowly than global attention's.
locator: section 3 and section 3.1, figure 2c-2d (synthetic banded-attention task)
notes: Transfer 3: this is the mechanistic argument UNDER the campaign's already-measured SSSL short-span win, so it is corroboration of a known lever rather than a new one. It also predicts the direction: the shorter the span the model must express, the less logit pressure. Effect has no decimal because the paper reports curves only; internal_validity 3 because the task is synthetic and hand-constructed.
statement: Softmax attention parameterized by O(n*d) degrees of freedom cannot represent a banded (dense-local) attention pattern requiring O(n^2) entries, and compensates by inflating pre-softmax logits; sliding-window local attention does not have this failure mode.

comparator: 6.5M-param GPT-2-style decoder, 6 layers, d=192, PG-19, 2^19 tokens/batch, bf16, single A40; three stabilization methods at matched steps.
effect: At sequence length 8192 after 50K steps, FlashAttention + QK-norm reaches validation perplexity ~112.17, more than 2.5x worse than LS-attention or fp32 FlashAttention (~38.5 and ~36).
locator: section 5.3, figure 5a
notes: Stance OPPOSES because our config uses QK-norm. Transfer 2 not higher: 6.5M params, n=8192 (we are far shorter), a 10K SentencePiece vocab, and a single seed per arm; the paper is comparing QK-norm against a mechanism that removes the instability at its source rather than against a no-QK-norm baseline, so this is not clean evidence that QK-norm is costing us anything. Register the contradiction; do not act on it without an in-house A/B.
statement: QK-normalization stabilizes long-sequence transformer training but converges to a markedly worse optimum than a long/short attention decomposition at equal step count.

comparator: Same 6.5M-param model, PG-19, only the head-type allocation changed.
effect: 1 global + 5 local heads reaches ~36 validation perplexity vs ~42 for 6 local heads, after 50K steps at n=8192.
locator: section 5.5, figure 6 (ablation)
notes: Transfer 3: this is directly a knob on an SSSL-style layout (how many heads/layers keep full context) and it is one of the few ablations here run at a genuinely small model. Discount: 50K steps and n=8192 vs our ~1000 steps and much shorter effective context; single seed; perplexities read off a figure.
statement: Replacing the single global attention head with an all-local head configuration degrades validation perplexity, so at least one full-context head carries real value.

comparator: FlashAttention-2 baseline vs LS-attention, bf16, same 6.5M model, forward pass only.
effect: Batch-forward time per sequence drops 7.14% at n=2048 (0.56 -> 0.52 ms) but 36.25% at n=8192 (3.31 -> 2.11 ms), with 1 global of 6 heads.
locator: section 5.4, table 1
notes: Transfer 2 and stance boundary: this is forward-pass inference timing, not training step time, and the asymptote is H/l which caps the win. Relevant as a caution: at our sequence lengths the throughput payoff from shrinking attention spans is in the single-digit-percent range, so any SSSL span change must be justified by loss, not by speed.
statement: Replacing most global heads with local span-limited heads reduces attention wall-clock, but the saving is small until sequence length is large.

comparator: Self-reported scope limit; supported by figure 3a where n=512 shows no instability at H=2 or H=6 over 50K steps.
effect: No number; stated as 'for shorter sequences, LS-attention may not offer significant advantages' and instability is 'more severe when training on longer sequences'.
locator: section 7 (Limitations)
notes: Registered as opposing/limiting evidence on the whole paper's transfer to us: our n_embd is 512 and our sequences are not in the n >> d regime that drives their effect, which caps how much of the LS-attention story should be believed here.
statement: The authors state that the advantages of decomposed long/short attention are pronounced only when sequence length greatly exceeds embedding dimension, and may not appear for shorter sequences.

comparator: Non-shared deep stacks (64 copies of a 12-layer block) where 1/sqrt(L) suffices and off-diagonal cosine similarities are near zero; 10 seeds, 10 optimizer steps, batch 1, seq 128.
effect: Under 1/sqrt(N) the residual-stream norm grows with N and can explode in early optimization; under 1/N it stays approximately invariant across N=1..64. Post-training cosine similarities between loop-step increments remain positive, concentrated in 0.3-0.6 for early/middle steps.
locator: section 3.2 Theorem 1; section 5.1 findings (i)-(iii), figures 2 and 3
notes: Transfer 3: looping a depth-8 stack is a MECHANISM that buys effective depth for zero extra parameters and costs only FLOPs, which the campaign has measured to be comparatively cheap. The residual-scaling rule is the thing you must get right before the mechanism can be evaluated at all. Discount: the init-time diagnostic is 10 steps at batch 1, and the theory abstracts attention away entirely (stated in Limitations).
statement: Weight-tied (looped) transformer stacks require 1/N residual-branch scaling rather than 1/sqrt(N), because shared weights make loop-step increments positively correlated so they accumulate constructively.

comparator: L=12 looped transformer, 183.5M tied params, FineWeb-Edu 10B tokens, 20,000 steps, 0.5M-token batch, AdamW (0.9,0.95), WSD schedule with 500 warmup and 1,000 decay steps, base LR swept over 8 values.
effect: A reduction of 0.025 nats at N=8 (best-over-LR-sweep comparison).
locator: section 5.2 findings (i), figure 5a-5b
notes: internal_validity 2 because each language-modeling configuration is a SINGLE seed (stated explicitly in Limitations); the 0.025-nat gap is a best-of-sweep difference with no seed error bar. transfer 3: architecture and scale are close to ours (183M, FineWeb-Edu) but 20,000 steps vs our ~1010, and looping multiplies step time by N which is the exact thing that costs us steps.
statement: At loop count 8, linear (1/N) residual scaling reaches a lower minimum validation loss than sqrt residual scaling.

comparator: Same family swept over LR grid {5, 7.5, 10, 12.5, 15, 20, 30, 40} x 1e-4; divergence criterion final val loss > 4.
effect: Optimal LR constant across N in {1,2,4,8} at L=12, 24 and 48; consistent with the predicted eta proportional to N^0. Base LR 1.25e-3 at L=12; at L=48 with N=8, base LRs above 2e-3 diverge.
locator: section 5.2 findings (ii) and section 5.3, figure 5a-5d
notes: Transfer 3: the practical payoff is that if we try looping we do NOT need to re-tune LR per loop count, which is decisive at 300s/run where a sweep is unaffordable. Single seed throughout; the depth correction m_L^{-1/2} is applied on top and is not separately ablated.
statement: Under 1/N residual scaling the optimal base learning rate is nearly invariant across loop counts, whereas under sqrt scaling the optimum shifts with loop count.

comparator: L=12 baseline tuned at eta_0 = 1.25e-3, AdamW, FineWeb-Edu 10B tokens.
effect: Reported qualitatively: 'a single base learning rate is near-optimal across all three depths' after applying m_L^{-1/2}; no per-depth loss numbers are given in the main text.
locator: section 5.3 findings (ii); appendix 8.2 table 3
notes: Transfer 2: our depth is fixed at 8, so a depth-transfer rule only matters if we sweep depth; and 2607.07884 in this same batch argues the exponent in such rules is data-dependent, so treat m_L^{-1/2} as a starting guess not a law. Single seed, no numeric effect reported.
statement: Applying a global depth correction of (L/12)^{-1/2} to hidden, pre-LN and bias learning rates makes a single base learning rate near-optimal across unique depths 12, 24 and 48.

comparator: Same run with eta_min swept; all else fixed. 8 V100s, block size 1024, batch 480 blocks.
effect: Measured fit loss = 3.145 + 110 * eta_min for large eta_min, on GPT-2-small / OpenWebText, 2k warmup + 7k stable (eta=6e-4) + 1k cosine decay, 10k steps total.
locator: section 3.3, figure 2b
notes: Transfer 4: 124M params, nanoGPT lineage, and a directly measured coefficient we can port. The slope 110 nats per unit LR means an eta_min change of 1e-5 moves loss ~1.1e-3 nats (~4e-4 bpb) which is above our 0.000174 resolution. Caveat: their stable phase is 7k steps vs our ~1000 total, so the equilibrium assumption underlying the linearity is much weaker at our horizon. Single-seed as far as reported.
statement: For a GPT-2-small pretraining run, final validation loss is a linear function of the final (end-of-decay) learning rate over the range where thermal equilibrium holds.

comparator: GPT-2-small / OpenWebText 10k-step WSD run with eta_min swept, peak eta = 6e-4.
effect: Lowest loss occurs around eta_min ~ 5e-5 > 0; too-small eta_min raises loss because thermal equilibrium breaks down when eta decays too fast. Theory says reaching eta_min=0 optimally would take infinite time.
locator: section 3.3 (discussion of figure 2b) and section 4.3 'Implications for LLM'
notes: Stance opposes because decay-to-zero is the modded-nanogpt default lineage this campaign inherits. Transfer 4: same parameter count, same codebase lineage, and it is a one-line schedule change. Strong caveat: the non-monotonicity is attributed to insufficient annealing time, and our annealing time is ~10x shorter than theirs, which would push the optimal eta_min HIGHER still, not lower.
statement: Decaying the learning rate all the way to zero is sub-optimal; the loss-minimizing final learning rate is strictly positive.

comparator: Grid over decay schedules eta_t = b*eta/(1+t/t_h); compared against linear and cosine decay indirectly via the 1-sqrt literature.
effect: Toy verification: with a=2, eta=0.1, sigma_g=0.1, n=10000 quadratic directions, the predicted optimum (b, t_h) = (0.5, 10) matches the empirical minimum of the phase diagram; loss is more sensitive to t_h than to b.
locator: section 4.1 Equation 3 and Remark 2; section 4.3, figure 3a-3c
notes: Transfer 3: the discontinuous halving at decay onset is cheap to test and contradicts standard continuous cosine practice, but the direct verification is on an isotropic quadratic toy, not on the LM. The anisotropic experiment (figure 3d) shows flat directions need t_h ~ 1/a, i.e. much longer decay, which is exactly the regime we cannot afford.
statement: The loss-minimizing learning-rate decay schedule has the form eta_t = (eta/2) / (1 + t/t_h), i.e. a 1/t decay that starts at half the stable learning rate rather than continuously from it.

comparator: Their own GPT-2-small WSD runs on OpenWebText with 3k-step decay phases.
effect: Stated as: Delta_anneal ~ 0 'when the decay phase is no smaller than 3k steps', for early-training GPT-2-small.
locator: section 6, Equation 6 and the surrounding text
notes: Stance opposes and transfer 4: our ENTIRE run is ~1010 steps, so no achievable decay phase reaches their 3k-step threshold. This says the annealing deficit is a first-order, not negligible, term for us, and that schedule shape should be a live lever rather than a settled one. It also warns that results tuned on longer runs about decay shape may not port.
statement: The 'insufficient annealing' correction to final loss is negligible only when the decay phase is at least a few thousand steps.

comparator: GPT-2-small / OpenWebText, stable phases of 1000*i steps for i=0..5, 3k-step cosine transition to a common eta_min.
effect: Validation-loss curves for stable eta in {3e-4, 6e-4, 1.2e-3} with matched eta_min=6e-4 roughly align when plotted against learning-rate sum; smaller eta gives slightly lower loss at equal sum, implying a slightly negative entropic force.
locator: section 5.3, figure 4; section 6, Equation 6
notes: Transfer 3: an actionable reparameterization - at fixed step count, raising the stable LR raises the LR sum and should lower loss provided eta_min is held and the decay is adequate. Caveat the authors state themselves: their training is early-stage due to compute limits, so the entropic correction may grow later; and our decay is nowhere near their 3k steps so Delta_anneal will not stay negligible.
statement: Final loss is largely determined by the learning-rate sum (which controls the slow 'river' component) plus the final learning rate (which controls the fast 'valley' component), with only small corrections.

comparator: 1D quadratic analysis, SGD and SignGD (SignGD is Adam with beta1=beta2=0); validated against the GPT-2-small eta_min sweep.
effect: For SGD mean thermal loss = sigma_g^2 * eta / 4 and for SignGD = sqrt(pi/32) * sigma_g * eta; sharpness a cancels because sigma is proportional to a^{-1/2}. Empirically the fitted slope 110 implies about 5e6 'valley' directions, ~4% of GPT-2-small's 124M parameters.
locator: section 3.1 (thermal loss paragraph) and table 1; section 3.2
notes: Transfer 2: derived for SGD/SignGD, and we run Muon on 2D matrices where the update is orthogonalized rather than signed, so the sharpness-cancellation argument is not established for our optimizer. Useful mainly as the theoretical basis for the linear-in-eta_min claim above.
statement: In the stable phase the equilibrium thermal loss is independent of the sharpness of the direction, so the loss reducible by annealing does not depend on how long the stable phase ran.

comparator: Prior width-only spectral condition and prior depth results (Yang et al., Bordelon et al., Dey et al.), unified by varying block depth.
effect: Hidden-weight condition alpha_l * ||W^(2)||_R * ||W^(1)||_R = Theta(1/L); with the standard muP init this forces alpha_l = Theta(1/L). Block depth 1 recovers the looser alpha_l = Theta(1/sqrt(L)).
locator: section 3.2 Condition 3.1 (C1.2, C2.2, C2.3) and the discussion following it; section 4.1 Equation 10
notes: Transfer 3: our attention and MLP branches are both multi-matmul, so the 1/L branch multiplier is the applicable rule, and it is a pure init/forward-scaling change with zero throughput cost. Derived on a linear residual MLP with a one-step update; generalization to nonlinearity is argued in an appendix, not proven. Note this AGREES with 2606.18524's 1/N loop rule and DISAGREES with the common 1/sqrt(depth) default.
statement: For residual blocks whose main branch has two or more stacked linear transformations, muP under joint width-depth scaling requires block multipliers of order 1/L, not 1/sqrt(L).

comparator: GPT-2-style models on OpenWebText, GPT-2 tokenizer, seq 1024, head dim 64, ffn 4n, Muon-Kimi (momentum 0.95) on matrices + AdamW elsewhere, no weight decay; base model (n,L)=(256,4); batch 240, 1221 iterations = 300M tokens, 120 warmup, cosine to 3e-5, grad clip 1.
effect: Best validation loss at L=8: 3.952 (SP) vs 3.938 (muP), a gain of 0.014 nats. At L=256 the gap widens to 3.753 vs 3.678 (0.075 nats). Width axis at n=512: 3.819 (SP) vs 3.811 (muP).
locator: appendix D.3.3, tables 10 and 11
notes: Transfer 3 and the highest-value part of this batch on setup grounds: 1221 iterations at 300M tokens with Muon-on-matrices + AdamW-elsewhere is very close to our 1010 steps and our optimizer split. Stance boundary because the honest reading is that at OUR depth (8) muP buys ~0.014 nats (~0.005 bpb) - real but modest - and the headline benefit is a scaling-transfer property we do not need at fixed size. Each table cell appears to be one run; no seed variance reported.
statement: With LayerNorm present, the width-depth muP parameterization for Muon-Kimi buys only a small validation-loss improvement over standard parameterization at moderate depth, and the gain grows with depth.

comparator: Same GPT-2-style Muon-Kimi setup with and without LayerNorm layers.
effect: With LayerNorm, SP's optimal base LR transfers across L=4..128 (table 10). Without LayerNorm, SP produces NaN divergence at several (L, eta) cells and its optimum wanders; muP stays stable up to L=256.
locator: section 5.2 Discussion; appendix D.3.4, figure 2 and tables 12-13
notes: Transfer 3 and important as a deflationary claim: because we already run QK-norm and normalization, the expected payoff from adopting muP-style depth corrections here is smaller than the muP literature implies. This is the mechanism explaining the previous claim's small 0.014-nat gap at L=8.
statement: LayerNorm and QK-Norm substantially mask the scaling pathology of standard parameterization, so at practical depths SP appears to transfer learning rate acceptably; removing LayerNorm breaks SP transfer and stability.

comparator: Derived against the spectral update condition; SP counterpart is eta_base for all layers (shown in gray in table 1).
effect: eta_l = Theta(1/sqrt(n_in)) for hidden weights; implemented as eta_hidden = eta_base / sqrt(r_n) with r_n = n / n_base, while input and output weight LRs stay eta_base.
locator: section 4.2, Equations 14 and 15; table 1
notes: Transfer 3: this is a concrete per-group learning-rate rule for exactly our optimizer split (Muon on matrices, AdamW on the rest) and costs nothing to apply. Whether our Muon implementation uses the 0.2*sqrt(max(fan)) RMS matching or the plain orthogonalized update must be checked first - the rule is derived for the RMS-matched variant.
statement: Muon-Kimi's RMS-matched update ΔW = -eta * 0.2 * sqrt(max(n_in, n_out)) * U V^T yields an RMS-operator-norm update of order eta*sqrt(n_in) for hidden layers, which fixes the required hidden learning-rate scaling to eta_base / sqrt(width ratio).

comparator: SP choices listed in the same table.
effect: alpha_0 = Theta(1), alpha_{L+1} = Theta(1/n_in); output initial variance sigma_base^2 under muP vs sigma_base^2/r_n under SP; output LR stays eta_base.
locator: section 4.1, Equations 8-9; table 1 (purple vs gray entries)
notes: Transfer 2: relevant to output-head and value-embedding scaling, but our width is fixed so r_n = 1 and the width-dependent parts collapse to the base values; only the residual/branch part (the 1/L claim) actually changes anything at our fixed size. Included because it defines what 'the rest of the parameterization' must be for the 1/L claim to be applied coherently.
statement: Under the width-depth spectral condition the output (unembedding) layer needs block multiplier of order 1/n_in with initialization variance held at the base value, differing from standard parameterization on both counts.

comparator: Same kernel with an artificial loop around the float computations; measured with Nsight Compute on an RTX 4060 Ti, input 1024x197x768.
effect: Forward pass 4.89-4.91 ms across 1x, 2x, 4x, 8x FLOPs (2.9T to 23.6T); backward pass 1.03 s at every loop count (11.2T to 89.2T FLOPs), with SM throughput 1.97% and HBM throughput 1.01%.
locator: section 3, Insight 2, table 2
notes: Transfer 3: directly corroborates this campaign's own nsys finding that the 297ms step is small-GEMM and tiny-kernel bound rather than FLOP bound, which is the premise behind 'spend FLOPs freely'. The specific kernel (KAT group-wise rational) is irrelevant to us; the methodology and the conclusion are what transfer. High internal validity - the FLOPs-scaling control is clean.
statement: A training kernel can be entirely memory-stall bound rather than compute bound: multiplying its floating-point work 8x leaves wall-clock time unchanged.

comparator: Standard KAT group-wise-rational backward kernel vs the FlashKAT Triton rewrite, same shapes, RTX 4060 Ti.
effect: Backward-pass kernel time drops from 1.03 s to 7.33 ms (140.5x); 'Stall Long Scoreboard' cycles fall from 981.51 to 2.31; HBM throughput rises from 1.01% to 92.05%.
locator: section 4.2-4.3 and section 5.1, table 3, figures 2 and 3
notes: Transfer 3: this campaign has an open throughput problem in the n-gram / value-embedding path (small GEMMs plus ~194k tiny fill kernels), which is structurally the same pattern - many threads accumulating into a few shared rows. The fix (reduce in shared memory per block, then one write) is portable to a Triton rewrite of that path. Not 4 because it is a vision architecture and the benefit here depends entirely on whether our hot kernel actually uses atomics.
statement: Accumulating gradients for a small set of shared parameters via global-memory atomic adds is the dominant source of backward-pass memory stalls; block-level reduction sums remove it.

comparator: KAT vs FlashKAT at matched parameter counts (5.7M/22.1M/86.6M), DeiT training recipe, H200.
effect: Mean absolute error on dA falls from 8.84e-2 to 8.42e-4 and on dB from 9.63e-2 to 9.81e-4; ImageNet-1k top-1 unchanged (KAT-T 74.6 vs FlashKAT-T 74.6; KAT-S 81.2 vs 81.4; KAT-B 82.3 vs 82.2) with 72.0x/86.5x/84.5x training-throughput gains.
locator: section 5.3, table 5; section 5.2, table 4
notes: Transfer 2: the accuracy-neutrality is the useful part - it says such a kernel rewrite is a pure throughput win with no loss cost, which is exactly the shape of intervention this campaign wants. Discounted because it is ImageNet classification, and because the rounding-error argument matters most in low precision (we run bf16 autocast, so it is at least directionally relevant).
statement: Replacing atomic-add gradient accumulation with block reduction sums reduces gradient rounding error by orders of magnitude at unchanged final accuracy.

comparator: Toto 1.0's AdamW baseline, but the architecture, loss (pinball vs Student-T NLL) and data mix all changed simultaneously.
effect: No isolated ablation is reported; the paper argues the case and selects NorMuon for all internal matrix-shaped parameters, with AdamW for input/output projections, biases and norms. Swept optimum: eta = 0.65, mu = 0.96, beta2 = 0.999, weight decay 2e-8.
locator: section 2.3, Equation 5
notes: internal_validity 1: there is NO controlled Muon-vs-NorMuon comparison anywhere in this paper; the choice is justified by argument plus a TPE sweep on a 10m proxy. Transfer 2: NorMuon is a small patch on our existing Muon and the row-norm imbalance argument is optimizer-general, but the motivating regime (sign-valued pinball gradients) does not apply to cross-entropy, which is the paper's own stated reason for needing it.
statement: Muon's orthogonalized update still leaves per-row L2 norms varying by orders of magnitude; NorMuon normalizes each row against an EMA of its own squared magnitude, reinstating a per-neuron second-moment mechanism.

comparator: Standard Newton-Schulz coefficients inside Muon; adopted without ablation in this paper.
effect: No number reported; described as 'a quintic iteration with coefficients optimized for faster convergence of the singular values to unity at low precision', used together with Nesterov momentum.
locator: section 2.3, final paragraph
notes: Transfer 3 because it is a coefficient swap in code we already run and it interacts directly with a measured fact on this system: cutting Newton-Schulz from 5 to 3 iterations costs +0.002645 bpb while saving only ~0.2% of step time, i.e. orthogonalization QUALITY is worth far more here than orthogonalization COST. Polar Express is the quality-preserving-at-fewer-iterations move that fact points at. internal_validity 1: this paper provides no evidence at all for the claim, only adoption; the evidence would have to come from the Polar Express paper itself.
statement: Replacing the standard Newton-Schulz orthogonalization inside Muon with the Polar Express quintic iteration gives faster convergence of singular values to unity at low precision.

comparator: Same proxy with QK-Norm or with neither, inside a TPE search over ~17 dimensions.
effect: No margin reported: 'the best configuration uses PerDimScale (over QK-Norm)'. Sweep options were PerDimScale, QK-Norm, or neither, on a 10m proxy (L=12, d_model=256, h=4) trained 30,000 steps under WSD, optimizing MASE/CRPS on GIFT-Eval validation.
locator: section 4.2 Round 1; section 2.4 (Attention changes)
notes: Stance opposes (we run QK-norm) but transfer 1: this is time-series forecasting with a quantile/pinball objective, alternating time-axis and variate-axis attention, and the comparison is a single TPE-selected configuration inside a joint search rather than a controlled A/B. Below the usable threshold; logged only so the QK-norm contradiction count is honest. Note it points the same direction as 2505.15548 and 2606.20027 in this batch.
statement: In a structured architecture sweep, learned per-dimension query scaling was selected over QK-Norm.

comparator: 1-sqrt decay shape and other decay lengths, swept from a stable-phase checkpoint on the 10m proxy.
effect: Linear decay won; final schedule decays linearly over 10,500 steps, 1.7-2.6% of the 400,000 and 600,500 total steps.
locator: section 4.2 Round 4; section 4.3 table 1
notes: Stance opposes because it contradicts 2505.10559 in this same batch, which derives 1/t as optimal and reports that 1-sqrt beats linear. Transfer 2: the sweep is on a time-series forecasting proxy with a pinball loss, so the loss geometry is different; but the finding that a very short decay tail suffices is directly load-bearing for us, where the entire run is ~1010 steps and a 3k-step decay is impossible. Single configuration selection, no seeds.
statement: A linear learning-rate decay tail occupying under 3% of total training steps was selected over a 1-sqrt shape in a sweep started from a checkpoint inside the stable phase.

comparator: The upstream unit_scaling library, which targets single-GPU eager mode.
effect: Required rewriting autograd scaling functions to eliminate graph breaks and caching distributed state before compilation; unit scaling had to be disabled in attention and MLP activations because its scale factors depend on sequence length, then compensated with alpha_res-attn-ratio = sqrt(S/log S) and alpha_res = 0.75.
locator: section 4.4 (torch.compile compatibility, FSDP2, Data/Tensor parallelism, Sequence-length invariance)
notes: Transfer 2 and stance boundary: this is an engineering-cost warning on the muP direction that 2603.00541 recommends. We are single-GPU so FSDP2/TP do not apply, but we DO run torch.compile, and graph breaks in the parameterization would cost step time, which at 300s costs val_bpb directly. No measurements given, only an experience report.
statement: Unit-scaled muP implementations attach scaling metadata to parameter tensors, and torch.compile, FSDP2 and tensor parallelism each destroy or invalidate that metadata unless explicitly worked around.

comparator: Data-agnostic rules eta ~ L^{-1} (plain chain), L^0 (block-depth-1 residual), L^1 (block-depth-2 residual), swept against the derived data-dependent rule.
effect: eta_L / eta_L0 = (L0/L) * r^{2(1/L - 1/L0)} with r = mu_yx/mu_xx; the effective power-law exponent p_eff = 1 - 2(1/L - 1/L0) ln r / ln(L/L0) depends on the data. Empirically, transferring with eta ~ L^{-1} gives too small an LR when r < 1 and too large when r > 1 (training loss after 30 gradient-descent steps).
locator: section 2 Equation 5; section 3 Equations 11-13 and figure 2
notes: Stance opposes: this is a direct challenge to the fixed-exponent depth rules asserted in 2606.18524 (m_L^{-1/2}) and 2603.00541 (alpha ~ 1/L) in this same batch, and the campaign wants that contradiction visible. Transfer 2: the model class is a scalar linear chain trained with plain gradient descent on l2 loss, three abstractions away from a 124M transformer under Muon.
statement: Even in a depth-L scalar linear network, the optimal depth-wise learning-rate scaling contains a data-dependent correction that no data-agnostic power law reproduces.

comparator: Their own figure 2 sweeps at fixed 30-step horizon.
effect: Stated qualitatively: transfer under L^{-1} scaling 'from an intermediate depth to large depth may still suffice despite being suboptimal, whereas transferring the learning rate from a small depth (e.g. L=2,4) to large depth would likely fail'.
locator: section 3, penultimate paragraph and figure 2
notes: Transfer 2 and boundary: relevant only because 2603.00541's muP base model is (n,L)=(256,4) - a small source depth - which is exactly the case this paper flags as unreliable. Useful as a caution on borrowing their tuned base LR rather than as a lever of its own. Qualitative, no numbers, toy model.
statement: The authors note the data dependence of optimal LR scaling is weak at large L, so transferring from an intermediate depth may suffice, while transferring from a very small source depth would likely fail.

comparator: Vanilla Mamba-2-780M and Gated DeltaNet-1.3B pretrained from scratch on 50B tokens of Long-Data-Collections at 16K sequence length, 4x A100, matched configuration.
effect: Mamba-2-780M average 31.8 vs 31.0 with log-linear attention; Gated DeltaNet-1.3B 32.8 vs 32.6 with log-linear. Their own DLA reaches 34.2 and 34.8 respectively.
locator: section 4.2, table 1
notes: Transfer 1, below the usable threshold: 780M-1.3B params, 50B tokens, 16K context, linear-attention/SSM backbones we do not use, custom chunked-scan kernels, and NO language-modeling loss or perplexity is reported anywhere - only downstream accuracies, which are a noisy proxy for val_bpb. Logged as a single cautionary data point that bolt-on memory hierarchies are not free; everything else in this paper is inference-efficiency and long-context retrieval, which are out of scope.
statement: Adding hierarchical multi-state (log-linear) memory to a linear-attention backbone did not uniformly help and slightly reduced average zero-shot commonsense accuracy relative to the vanilla backbone.

comparator: raw GPT baseline, 9 layers, hidden 512, 8 q heads / 4 kv heads, MLP expansion 2, 6000 steps at 524,288 tokens/step, FineWeb, Muon on matrices + Adam elsewhere, seed 1337
effect: val BPB 1.251 -> 1.209 with +26M params; TN-gram variant 1.208 with +19M
locator: section 5 'Accuracy-Efficiency Tradeoff', Table 1 (L=9 columns)
notes: Operating point is unusually close to ours (same batch tokens/step, same width, 8-9 layers, Muon+Adam, BPB reported directly), which is why transfer is 3 not 2. Two big caveats: main tables use vocabulary size 1024 (a toy vocab; the frozen tokenizer here is far larger) and 6000 steps vs our ~1010, so the absolute BPB level is not comparable. Single seed (1337). Effect size (0.042 BPB) is 240x our 0.000174 resolution, so even a heavily discounted version would be measurable.
statement: Inserting an Engram-style hashed n-gram memory module into two layers of a 9-layer d=512 GPT lowered validation BPB from 1.251 to 1.209 at the cost of 26M extra parameters.

comparator: Engram at same n-gram order N=5, tensor rank R=1800, matched-or-lower added parameter count (48M vs 60M)
effect: 18 layers: TN-gram val BPB 1.071 vs Engram 1.070, i.e. TN-gram higher by one thousandth; CORE 0.120 vs 0.115
locator: section 5 'Accuracy-Efficiency Tradeoff', Table 1 (L=18 columns)
notes: Registered as opposing evidence against 'use the tensorized variant to get a loss win'. The tensorization is a parameter-efficiency and downstream-score story, not a BPB story, once depth grows. Transfer 2: the mechanism is implementable but the added complexity buys nothing on the exact metric we optimize, and the 9L-vs-18L reversal means the sign is depth-dependent (we are at depth 8, i.e. their 9L side).
statement: The CP-factorized TN-gram memory did not improve validation BPB over hash-based Engram at 18 layers, reporting 1.071 against Engram's 1.070, and improved only a downstream aggregate score.

comparator: same TN-gram/Engram model swept over N in {2,...,7}, 9-layer d=512 backbone, 6000 steps
effect: most of the validation-loss gain achieved by N=5; 'only marginal improvements and sometimes degradations thereafter'; parameter count grows roughly linearly with N
locator: section 5 'Effect of n-gram Order', Figure 2 (left)
notes: Bounds the search: no reason to sweep n-gram order above 5, and order 2 alone is the weakest setting (at N=2 the tensorized variant is worse than plain hashing because there is no cross-order structure). Transfer 3 because the backbone and batch size match ours closely; discounted from 4 because vocab is 1024, which makes higher-order contexts far denser than they would be under our frozen tokenizer, so real saturation could occur at a lower N here.
statement: Validation loss from an explicit n-gram memory improves with maximum n-gram order up to N=5, with only marginal and sometimes negative changes beyond that.

comparator: Engram with K hash heads vs TN-gram with CP rank R, same 9-layer d=512 backbone and token budget
effect: increasing Engram hashing heads gives 'modest improvements in validation loss' with diminishing returns; increasing CP tensor rank R gives 'a more consistent reduction'
locator: section 5 'Effect of Tensor Rank', Figure 3
notes: Registered as opposing evidence against the cheap knob 'just add more hash heads to the n-gram memory'. Internal validity 2 because the comparison is read off a figure with no tabulated numbers and no seeds. Transfer 3 because it directly constrains a knob that exists in our n-gram lever and it was measured at our width/batch.
statement: Scaling explicit n-gram memory capacity by adding hashing heads yields only limited validation-loss improvement, whereas scaling a shared latent rank improves it consistently.

comparator: full TN-gram with RMSNorm + learnable scale + order-absorption, 9-layer d=512 backbone
effect: each removal increases validation loss; removing the learnable per-order scales {s_k} has a larger effect than removing the order-absorption vectors; removing both is worst; the no-RMSNorm variant is consistently worse across all n-gram orders
locator: section 5.1 'Ablation of TN-gram components', Figure 4 (right)
notes: This is a signal-scale claim about how retrieved memory is injected into the residual stream: normalize then rescale with a learned per-order scalar. Cheap to implement and orthogonal to which memory you use. Internal validity 2: figure-only, no numbers, single seed. Transfer 3: same width, same optimizer split, and the intervention is a two-line change.
statement: Removing RMS normalization of the n-gram token-space vector, or the learnable per-order scalars, each increases validation loss in an explicit n-gram memory module.

comparator: hash-based Engram at equal n-gram order
effect: no wall-clock number reported; authors describe unquantified overhead vs hash-based Engram and defer the fix to 'customized CUDA kernels'
locator: section 6 'Limitations and future work'
notes: Directly relevant blocker: at 300 charged seconds an unquantified per-step overhead converts into lost steps. Our own profiling already flagged the n-gram value-embedding GEMMs plus ~194k tiny fill kernels as the step-time bottleneck, so a mechanism that adds MORE small elementwise ops in the same place is likely to lose on wall clock even if it wins per step. Transfer 3 as a blocker, not as a gain.
statement: The authors state their tensorized n-gram memory is not optimized for wall-clock speed and adds factor gathering, Hadamard products, normalization and scaling on top of a hash lookup, expecting the overhead to need custom CUDA kernels.

comparator: SP, muP, and single-change interpolants; depth-12 GPT on FineWeb-Edu, widths 128-2048, head dim fixed 64, AdamW, WSD schedule, 10,000 steps at ~1M tokens/step
effect: SP+Embd matches muP on loss degradation R(inf), predictability error E and robustness exponent kappa; plain SP has predictability error E roughly 3x larger than muP
locator: section 4.3 'A Step by Step Journey from SP to muP', Figure 3 (orange arrow, SP+Embd)
notes: Internal validity 4: full LR x weight-decay x width x parameterization grid, ~160,000 H100 hours, one-change-at-a-time ablations. Transfer 3 not 4: their runs are 10x our step count and 2x our batch, and they scan width rather than fixing 124M, so the concrete optimal embedding LR does not port; the DIRECTION (embedding/first-layer LR deserves its own, relatively large value) does. In our train.py embeddings are on AdamW while 2D matrices are on Muon, so this is a live, cheap, one-scalar knob.
statement: Training standard parameterization with a width-independent (Theta(1)) embedding-layer learning rate matches muP on all three of their transfer metrics, while giving muP a Theta(1/n) embedding learning rate degrades it.

comparator: muP with Theta(1) embedding LR throughout, same width and step budget
effect: persistent end-of-training loss difference of ~0.1-0.2 nats when the embedding LR is slowed early; further training closes much but not all of the gap
locator: section 5 'The Importance of Embedding Layer Learning Rate', Figure 4(a)
notes: The 'early training is where the embedding LR matters' finding is the part that transfers hardest to a ~1010-step run: essentially our entire run IS the early phase, so an embedding LR that is too small never gets a chance to be compensated. 0.1-0.2 nats is enormous relative to our 0.000174 bpb resolution, but it is measured at their 10k-step scale with a deliberately crippled setting, so treat the magnitude as an upper bound, not a prediction. Transfer 3.
statement: Reducing the embedding-layer learning rate from Theta(1) to Theta(1/n) partway through training leaves a residual loss gap of about 0.1 to 0.2 at the end of training, with earlier switches producing larger gaps.

comparator: same parameterization at lambda=0; depth-12 GPT, 10,000 steps at ~1M tokens/step, FineWeb-Edu
effect: R(inf) rises monotonically with lambda from about 0.01 to about 1 at large lambda, across parameterizations, in the fixed-step regime
locator: section 6 'The Effect of Weight Decay and Compute Optimal Training', Figure 5a
notes: Deliberately registered as OPPOSING the 'raise weight decay' direction that arXiv 2602.11137 and 2606.06888 both push. The contradiction is real and should stay visible: this paper measures a fixed-step, effectively single-pass regime with LARGE token budgets, whereas the pro-weight-decay results come from repeated-epoch / data-constrained regimes. Our run does two passes over a fixed dataset at ~1010 steps, which sits between the two, so the sign of the weight-decay lever here is genuinely unresolved and is an experiment, not a settled direction. Transfer 3.
statement: In the fixed-step training setting, weight decay consistently hurts asymptotic performance: the loss-degradation metric increases monotonically with the weight-decay coefficient across all parameterizations.

comparator: same muP model and LR sweep with warmup fraction varied; depth-12 GPT, 10,000 steps
effect: 1-5% warmup: noisy loss curves across widths, extrapolation meaningless; 10% warmup: smoother, optimal log-LR aligns across widths; authors adopt a conservative 20% throughout
locator: Appendix F 'The Effect of Learning Rate Warmup on Learning Rate Transfer', Figure 21
notes: At our ~1010 steps, 10-20% warmup means 100-200 steps of warmup, which is a large fraction of a 300s run and directly trades against the annealing budget (see the annealing-ratio claims from 2512.13705). Transfer 3: the knob is free to change and the metric they used (curve smoothness / optimum alignment) is a proxy for the single-seed noise we already struggle with. Note their claim is about transfer reliability, not about final loss, so it is worded no stronger than that.
statement: Learning-rate warmup durations of 1-5% of total steps produce training instabilities and noisy loss curves across widths, while 10% warmup gives noticeably smoother curves and consistent optima.

comparator: muP and SP baselines at matched width and step budget
effect: no loss number given; 'negligible effect' for decreasing LN LR, 'worsens instability' for increasing it
locator: section 4.3 'A Step by Step Journey from SP to muP' (LayerNorm paragraph), Figure 3 and Figure 18
notes: Boundary claim: it tells us where NOT to spend an experiment. Norm-gain learning rate is a knob we could tune, and this says the upside is near zero and the downside is instability. Transfer 2 because no number is attached and the finding is about width-scaling exponents rather than a fixed-width value; our depth-8 model has few norm parameters so the prior for a measurable effect is weak anyway.
statement: Lowering the LayerNorm-parameter learning rate to Theta(1/n) in muP has a negligible effect, while raising it to Theta(1) in SP worsens training instability.

comparator: same parameterization with a trainable embedding, widths 128-2048, 10,000 steps
effect: muP frozen-embedding remains worse across all widths even when compared per trainable parameter; SP frozen achieves LOWER loss than unfrozen at small widths, converging at large widths
locator: Appendix G 'Effect of Freezing the Embedding Layer', Figure 22
notes: Two-sided. The SP-small-width branch is the interesting one for us: at small width the embedding dominates parameter count and freezing it can be parameter-efficient. Our 124M model with value embeddings puts a lot of capacity in embedding-like tables, so 'freeze / partially freeze embeddings and spend the parameters elsewhere' is at least a coherent capacity experiment. Transfer 2: their SP result is at widths far below ours and no number is tabulated; the authors themselves defer explanation to future work.
statement: Completely freezing the embedding layer at initialization hurts final loss in both SP and muP, hurting muP substantially more, and the gap persists even after correcting for the reduced trainable-parameter count.

comparator: AdamW-only baseline over the same 20k decay steps with identical LR schedule, batch size, grad clip, weight decay and 66.9% SFT data blend
effect: +4.58 pp absolute on a 13-task reasoning average; no validation loss or BPB number reported for the switch
locator: section 3.2 'Optimizer ablation: AdamW -> Muon'
notes: Internal validity 2: single-variable claim asserted by the authors, but n=1, and the metric is a downstream aggregate, not loss, on a decay phase whose data blend is 66.9% SFT. Transfer 2 and the DIRECTION is inverted for us: we already run Muon on 2D matrices throughout, so what this paper actually supports testing is the complement, AdamW (or reduced Muon) early plus Muon late. At ~1010 steps a phase split is implementable but each phase is tiny. Also note our system already measured that Newton-Schulz iteration count is a fraction of a percent of a 297ms step, so the Muon-side cost is not the obstacle; the question is purely whether the update rule helps at different points in the run.
statement: Replacing AdamW with Muon for only the final 20k decay steps of a 560k-step 1.3B pretraining run, with all other hyperparameters frozen, raised the 13-task reasoning average by 4.58 percentage points.

comparator: none reported (no 1/sqrt(d_head) control run)
effect: no number; adopted as a design choice with all other components (Pre-RMSNorm, SwiGLU) inherited unmodified
locator: section 3.1 'Model Architecture'
notes: Internal validity 1 by construction: this is an adoption, not a measurement. Included only because it is a one-line change at our operating point (head_dim 128, so 1/d_head vs 1/sqrt(d_head) is a factor of ~11 change in logit scale, which interacts with our QK-norm and would need the LR re-checked). Transfer 2: implementable and cheap, but with zero evidence attached and a known interaction with QK-norm, this is a speculative experiment, not a supported direction. Cross-check against 2605.21486, which found attention scaling changes made LR transfer BRITTLE in both directions.
statement: The authors adopt muP attention-logit scaling of 1/d_head (rather than 1/sqrt(d_head)) as their only muP-compatibility architecture change, but report no ablation isolating its effect.

comparator: none; single uncontrolled training curve, attribution is the authors' interpretation
effect: a 'first drop' in the WikiText-2 loss curve coincident with the batch-size increase from ~1.78M to ~3.56M tokens/step; no controlled number
locator: section 5.2 'Training Loss', Figure 2
notes: Internal validity 1: one curve, no control, and the authors hedge with 'likely'. Registered because it corroborates the independent batch-size claim from 2512.13705 and because our batch is fixed at 524,288 tokens/step, which those fits put BELOW the optimal batch at the loss level we reach. Transfer 2: batch is changeable in train.py, but at 300 charged seconds doubling batch halves step count, and step count dominates val_bpb at fixed wall clock, so this can only pay if the per-step gain beats the token law.
statement: Increasing the batch size mid-run from about 2M to about 4M tokens produced a visible drop in the training loss curve, which the authors attribute to replicating the stabilizing effect of a reduced learning rate.

comparator: the same run's checkpoint immediately before the long-context phase
effect: 'small bump' in WikiText-2 perplexity; 13-task average 52.36 -> 52.49
locator: section 5.2 'Training Loss'
notes: Registered as opposing evidence for any claim that late-phase architecture/context changes are free on loss. For this campaign the objective IS val_bpb, so a change that trades perplexity for downstream score is a strict loss. Transfer 1: 1.3B, 560k steps, context stretch from 3712 to 16384 is not available under a frozen packing pipeline. Internal validity 1: n=1, no control.
statement: A 10k-step long-context extension phase increased WikiText-2 perplexity while the 13-task downstream average rose from 52.36 to 52.49.

comparator: WSD schedule at fixed batch 640 and max LR 2e-4, 1B MoE, annealing ratio swept, Delta_loss measured against the best ratio
effect: R_opt = lambda_T * T^alpha_T with alpha_T approx -9.46e-1 and lambda_T approx 5.987e5 for 1B MoE, fitted over T in {30k, 100k, 300k} steps
locator: section 'Across Steps Transferability', Observation 4, Equation 14, Figure 8
notes: The direction is what transfers: fewer total steps => spend a LARGER fraction of the run decaying. Naively evaluating the fit at T=1010 gives a nonsensical ratio far above 1, so this must be used as a monotone direction only, not as a formula: our step count is ~30x below the smallest fitted T. Internal validity 2: single-seed curve fits, MoE-only for this particular law, and the authors explicitly scope transfer claims to within-architecture. Transfer 2. Companion observation from the same section: entering annealing too early risks overfitting, and Delta_loss between ratios SHRINKS as steps grow, i.e. schedule choice matters MORE at our short horizon.
statement: The optimal WSD annealing (decay) ratio follows a power law in total training steps with a near-inverse exponent, so shorter runs have a larger optimal decay fraction.

comparator: 500M Dense and MoE models, batch size 512, sequence length 8192, 24k steps, annealing ratio swept per max LR
effect: R_opt = lambda_eta * eta_max^alpha_eta with lambda_eta approx 5.996e3, alpha_eta approx 7.09e-1 for Dense models; lambda_eta approx 4.675e4, alpha_eta approx 1.056 for MoE
locator: section 'Across LR_max Transferability', Observation 1, Equation 13, Figure 5 (left and middle)
notes: Actionable coupling: LR and decay fraction must be tuned together, so a single-knob LR sweep at fixed decay fraction is systematically mis-specified. Transfer 2: fitted at 24k steps and 4M-token batches, 24x our step count; the exponent is unlikely to be quantitatively right at 1010 steps, but the coupling direction should hold. Internal validity 2: fits from smoothed single-run curves (50-step moving average), Huber objective, no seed replication for these particular fits.
statement: The optimal annealing ratio follows a power law in the maximum learning rate, increasing as the peak learning rate increases.

comparator: Dense ladder (50M/100M/500M/1B) at batch 512, seqlen 8192, 24k steps, max LR 4e-5; MoE ladder at max LR 2e-4
effect: R_opt stable across model sizes at fixed max LR / steps / batch; Delta_loss gaps between ratios grow larger with model size
locator: section 'Across Model Transferability', Observation 2, Figure 6
notes: Useful because it licenses tuning the decay fraction on a cheaper proxy and porting it. Transfer 2: their smallest dense model (50M, hidden 512, 14 layers) is architecturally near ours, but every fit uses >=24k steps and 8192-token sequences, so the transfer claim is about size, not about horizon, and our horizon is the out-of-range axis.
statement: The optimal annealing ratio converges to the same value across model sizes for both Dense and MoE families, while the loss penalty for choosing a wrong ratio grows with model size.

comparator: same model size, max LR and scheduler with only batch size varied, Dense and MoE, The Pile
effect: B_opt = lambda_B / L^alpha_B with lambda_B approx 2.711e7, alpha_B approx 2.710 for Dense (4.390e7 and 3.430 for MoE); measured B_opt approx 293 sequences of length 8192 for a 500M Dense model and approx 366 for 700M MoE
locator: section 'Across Batch Sizes Fitting', Observation 2, Equation 11, Figure 3
notes: Boundary because the implication cuts against us: 293 sequences x 8192 = ~2.4M tokens is ~4.6x our fixed 524,288 tokens/step, and the fitted law says B_opt GROWS as loss falls. If the law ported, our batch would be below B_opt at the loss levels we reach, meaning step-based curves would NOT be batch-invariant and our gradient is noisier than optimal. But raising batch at fixed 300s directly costs steps, and step count dominates val_bpb here, so this is a tension to test rather than a lever to pull. Internal validity 2: fits on smoothed single runs, different tokenizer and data (The Pile), loss units not directly comparable to our BPB.
statement: For a fixed model, batch sizes above an optimal batch size B_opt produce nearly identical step-based loss curves under the same learning-rate schedule, and B_opt follows an inverse power law in the loss level.

comparator: same model, same total steps and max LR, only the schedule shape changed; 3 random seeds
locator: section 'Across Schedulers Fitting', Observation 3, Table 1, Figure 4
notes: One of the few results in this batch with reported seed variance (3 seeds). Internal validity 3. Transfer 2: it is a claim about curve-fit predictability, not about which schedule wins, and MAPE under 1% on a loss around 2-3 nats is still ~0.02 nats of absolute slack, which is two orders of magnitude coarser than our 0.000174 bpb resolution. Use it to justify cheap schedule-shape screening, not to predict a winner.
statement: A loss-curve model fitted on a cosine-schedule run predicts the WSD-schedule run's loss curve and vice versa, with mean absolute percentage error under 1% at 50M, 100M and 500M dense scales.

comparator: same architecture, data and all other hyperparameters, sweeping weight decay over up to 11 values (0 to 10.0); Llama-2 on FineWeb-Edu, OLMo-2 on OLMo-Mix-1124, single epoch, AdamW, warmup-cosine
