locator: section 4.1, Figure 1(a,b,c) and Appendix B Figure 7
notes: Internal validity 3: a real one-variable sweep with 10-11 weight-decay values at two model families, but n=1 seed per point and the optimum is read from a curve. Transfer 3: the metric is exactly ours (pretraining validation cross-entropy), the regime (short training relative to model size) is on our side of their pivot, and weight decay is a free scalar in train.py. Discount: their 20 TPP is ~4x more tokens per parameter than our ~1010 steps x 524288 tokens over 124M params with 2 epochs, so we sit even further into the short-training regime where the trend says WD should be even higher. Directly CONTRADICTED by arXiv 2605.21486 Figure 5a, which finds weight decay monotonically hurts asymptotic loss in a fixed-step setting.
statement: At the 20 tokens-per-parameter compute-optimal ratio, the weight decay minimizing pretraining validation loss was larger than the standard default of 0.1 in every model group tested.

comparator: same OLMo-2-1B model and data at 210B tokens (140 TPP), WSD schedule, weight decay swept over {0, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0}
effect: OLMo-2-1B-140x validation cross-entropy 2.6088 at wd=0.1 vs 2.6208 at wd=0.3 and 2.7064 at wd=1.0
locator: section 4.1 and section 4.3, Figure 1(c)
notes: This is the boundary of the previous claim and is registered separately so the pivot stays visible: the sign of the weight-decay lever flips with training duration. It also gives a usable magnitude: the wd=0.1 to wd=0.3 gap is 0.012 nats, i.e. small but far above our measurement floor once converted. Transfer 3 for the boundary logic; our operating point is on the SHORT side of the pivot, so the pro-high-WD branch is the one to test, but the existence of the pivot means the effect cannot be assumed monotone.
statement: At 140 tokens-per-parameter (overtrained), the default weight decay of 0.1 gave lower pretraining validation loss than the larger values 0.3 and 1.0.

comparator: same OLMo-2-1B-20x model at each weight decay value, 30B tokens, single epoch
effect: train-val gap (validation loss minus training loss on the training data) decreases monotonically as weight decay increases, across the 11-value sweep for OLMo-2-1B-20x
locator: section 5.3 'Weight decay reduces overfitting on training data', Figure 6, Equation 3
notes: Mechanistically the most relevant claim in this paper for us, because our run makes TWO passes over a fixed dataset and sits near an overfitting boundary; the n-gram memory lever in particular has already been measured on this system to behave as a memorizer. If repetition-driven memorization is what caps our val_bpb, weight decay is the cheapest counter-lever and costs zero throughput. Transfer 3: the metric and mechanism port; the magnitudes come from a single-epoch 1.5B run, so they do not.
statement: Increasing weight decay during pretraining monotonically decreased the train-val loss gap, indicating less overfitting to the pretraining data.

comparator: same OLMo-2-1B-20x and Llama-2 models across the weight-decay sweep, pseudo-rank measured during training
effect: weight decay 1.0 reduces W_QK pseudo-rank by roughly a factor of 2 while W_VP stays close to full rank; at the default 0.1 both matrices are near full rank; for Llama-2 the W_VP rank is stable up to wd=1.0 and then collapses, correlated with a significant performance drop
locator: section 5.2 'Weight decay reduces the rank of attention matrices', Figure 5, Figure 26, Figure 28
notes: Gives a diagnostic and a safety rail for the high-weight-decay experiments: monitor W_VP rank, and treat its collapse as the upper bound on usable weight decay. Transfer 2: rank measurements at 1B-1.5B with 16-22 layers and head dim different from our 128; our model also has QK-norm, which changes the QK conditioning story that this rank claim rests on. Corroborates the independent theory result in arXiv 2510.06954 that key-query matrices undergo rank collapse as an intrinsic training dynamic.
statement: Larger weight decay monotonically reduces the effective rank of attention matrices, with the query-key product far more sensitive than the value-output product, and a value-output rank collapse coinciding with a significant performance drop.

comparator: Llama-2-0.5B-20x and Llama-2-1B-20x sweeps over 10 weight-decay values from 0 to 10.0
effect: weight decay values in {0, 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01} are nearly indistinguishable on pretraining loss; wd=10.0 substantially degrades it; the useful range is roughly [0.1, 3]
locator: section 4.1, Figure 1(a), Appendix B Table 3
notes: Bounds the search box for any weight-decay experiment on our system to roughly [0.1, 3] and says the sub-0.1 half of the axis is dead, which saves runs. Transfer 3: the flatness below 0.1 is the kind of finding that survives scale changes better than the optimum location does. Single seed per point.
statement: Very small weight decay values below 0.1 have little effect on pretraining loss, while extremely large values such as 10 substantially degrade pretraining performance.

comparator: a strongly regularized AR baseline with per-cell tuned (epochs, weight decay, learning rate) held fixed across both recipes; DCLM 100M unique tokens, Llama-style decoder with QK-norm and interleaved local/global attention, GPT-2 tokenizer, AdamW, WSD, five seeds
effect: 1.4B: mean validation loss 3.347 -> 3.317; seed-42 table: 72M 3.615903 -> 3.613621, 257M 3.422107 -> 3.404833, 1.4B 3.339578 -> 3.308170; average gain grows from roughly 0.006 at 72M to about 0.03 at 1.4B; hyperparameters r_min=0, r_max=0.5, lambda=0.4
locator: section 3.4 'Validation loss improvements', Figure 1(a), Appendix A.7 and A.8 Table 7
notes: Internal validity 4: five seeds, matched-seed comparison, tuned baseline rather than a strawman, and it replicates on code data (Stack-V2, gains 0.008 to 0.020). Transfer 3, with two concrete blockers. (1) It needs a [MASK] token; the paper added one to the GPT-2 vocab, which our frozen prepare.py forbids, but the masking happens on the input tensor inside the training step, so a reserved/unused id or an extra learned embedding row in train.py is a plausible in-scope workaround. (2) It costs a SECOND forward pass per step, i.e. real throughput; our profiling says GPU capacity in this scope is comparatively cheap and ~94% of charged time is the frozen packing loop, which is exactly the condition under which spending extra FLOPs for no extra data can pay. Magnitude warning: at 72M the gain is only ~0.002-0.006 nats, so at our 124M the expected effect is small and needs the control-variate/paired protocol to resolve.
statement: Adding an auxiliary next-token-prediction loss computed on a randomly [MASK]-corrupted copy of the same input lowered validation loss at every model scale from 72M to 1.4B and on every matched seed, in a data-constrained repeated-epoch regime.

comparator: strongly regularized AR baseline at the same model size and 100M unique tokens, averaged over five seeds
effect: average gain approximately 0.006 loss at 72M rising to approximately 0.03 loss at the two largest models (664M, 1.4B)
locator: section 3.4 point (1) and 'Validation loss improvements' paragraph, Figure 1(a)
notes: Registered as the boundary on the previous claim, because it is the part that most limits us: our 124M sits at the small end of their ladder where the measured gain is smallest. 0.006 nats converts to roughly 0.002 bpb at typical bytes-per-token ratios, about 12x our 0.000174 resolution, so it is measurable but only just, and only if the extra forward pass does not cost more steps than the gain is worth. Transfer 3 because the scaling trend itself is well-measured and tells us the expected effect size at our exact scale.
statement: The validation-loss gain from masked-input regularization grows with model capacity at fixed unique data, from about 0.006 at 72M parameters to about 0.03 at 1.4B.

comparator: multi-epoch AR at wd=0.1 with tuned epoch count, same 100M unique DCLM tokens and same architecture; recipes compared at 140M, 257M and 664M
effect: 257M AR validation loss 3.88 (wd=0.1, tuned epochs) -> 3.42 (jointly tuned epochs/wd/lr); dLLM 3.60 -> 3.48 when the AR-tuned large weight decay is ported to it
locator: section 3.1 'Weight Decay Transfers Across AR and dLLM Pretraining', Figure 2, Appendix A.8 Table 4/7
notes: A 0.46-nat swing from regularization alone in a repeated-data regime is the largest regularization effect in this batch. Transfer 3: the mechanism (repeated data plus underregularization equals memorization) applies to our final_epoch 2.0 run and the fix is free at inference and at training throughput. Discount: their repetition is 8-32 epochs versus our 2, so the magnitude will be far smaller for us, and the joint sweep confounds three knobs at once so it does not attribute the gain to weight decay alone.
statement: Jointly tuning epochs, weight decay and learning rate reduced 257M multi-epoch autoregressive validation loss from 3.88 to 3.42 on 100M unique tokens, eliminating the previously reported advantage of diffusion language models in the data-constrained regime.

comparator: grid search over epochs, weight decay and learning rate at each (model size, unique-data budget) cell, DCLM, WSD schedule with 1% warmup and 10% warmdown, dropout 0.1
effect: at 100M unique tokens best (epochs, wd, lr) is (32, 0.4, 1e-2) for 72M, (32, 0.8, 3e-3) for 140M, (16, 1.6, 1e-3) for 257M and 664M, (16, 3.2, 1e-3) for 1.4B; for the 72M model the best wd falls to 0.2 at 200M unique tokens and 0.1 at 300M and 400M unique tokens
locator: Appendix A.6 'Strongly Regularized Baseline Search', Table 5 and Table 6
notes: Critical calibration for us and the reason this is a boundary rather than a support claim. Their weight decays of 0.4-3.2 come with 16-64 epochs of repetition. Our run makes only 2 passes, which by their own trend puts us at the LOW end of the weight-decay axis, i.e. near or below the 0.1 default rather than at 1.0. So this paper simultaneously supports 'repetition demands regularization' and argues AGAINST simply importing the large weight-decay values that arXiv 2602.11137 found at 20 TPP. Transfer 3: the trend is measured across five model sizes and four data budgets with a real grid.
statement: In their tuned sweeps the best weight decay increases with model size and with the number of epochs over the same data, and decreases as the unique-data budget grows at fixed model size.

comparator: cosine annealing at otherwise identical settings, 72M to 1.4B, DCLM 100M unique tokens
effect: no number reported; stated as 'WSD performs better across all model sizes we tested' versus the cosine annealing used by the prior work they build on
locator: Appendix A.3 'AR Training Recipe'
notes: Internal validity 2: the comparison is asserted in an appendix sentence with no table and no seeds. Transfer 3 anyway because the schedule is a free change, our regime is the same data-constrained repeated-pass regime, and their 10% warmdown fraction is a concrete, testable setting that also sits inside the annealing-ratio window implied by arXiv 2512.13705's step law. Note the direct tension with that paper: 2512.13705 says shorter runs want a LARGER decay fraction than 10%.
statement: The authors report that a warmup-stable-decay schedule with 1% warmup and 10% warmdown performed better than cosine annealing across all model sizes they tested in the data-constrained setting.

comparator: strongly regularized 1.4B baseline evaluated on the same 10M-token DCLM eval set
effect: 6.61% of validation tokens have loss gap >= 1 favouring MIR versus 5.41% favouring the baseline; of the top 0.1% MIR-better positions, 62.6% are word or subword continuations, 16.3% non-English or transliterated text, 11.6% punctuation
locator: section 3.4 'Where MIR helps: Token-level analysis', Figure 3
notes: Matters because it predicts WHERE the gain would show up in our BPB accounting: broadly distributed, on common target tokens made hard by messy prefixes, which is the bulk of a FineWeb-like validation set rather than a tail we might not sample. Transfer 2: measured only at 1.4B, and the tail statistics depend on the tokenizer and the eval distribution, both frozen and different for us.
statement: A token-level analysis at 1.4B shows the masked-input-regularization gain comes from a broad set of validation positions rather than a few outliers, concentrated on continuation problems with noisy or unusual prefix context.

comparator: vanilla single-stream residual Transformer, 10B-total MoE backbone with GQA and 144 experts top-8, matched data budget, AdamW, context 8192
effect: Pile validation loss 2.029 (vanilla residual) -> 2.004 (mHC N=4) at +0.6% training FLOPs; going to N=16 dense only reaches 1.998 at +18.8% FLOPs
locator: section 4.5 'Ablation Study', Table 2 rows (1) and (2)
notes: Transfer 2, not 3: every number comes from a 10B-parameter MoE trained on a multilingual/code/math mixture at 8192 context, roughly 80x our parameter count and a different sparsity regime, and the residual-stream mechanism interacts with depth (they have far more layers than our 8). The FLOPs-cheap N=4 variant is the only version worth considering here, and the N=4 -> N=16 numbers show the mechanism saturates fast: 0.006 loss for 32% more FLOPs is a losing trade at 300 charged seconds.
statement: A multi-stream hyper-connection residual architecture at N=4 improved validation loss from 2.029 to 2.004 while adding only 0.6% training FLOPs.

comparator: dense mHC at N=16 without temporal augmentation, 10B MoE, Pile validation loss, matched data budget
effect: dense mHC at N=16: 1.998 (no conv) -> 1.989 (one causal conv branch) -> 1.984 (three branches with different kernel sizes)
locator: Appendix D 'Effect of multi-scale temporal components', Table 12; also section 4.5 Table 2 row (4)
notes: This is the most portable piece of the paper: a short depthwise causal convolution applied to a sublayer output before it is written back to the residual stream is a small, dense-model-compatible addition, and it is the same primitive the Engram/n-gram papers use (kernel size 3 depthwise causal conv on the gated memory value). Transfer 2 because the isolated effect (0.014 loss) was measured only inside a 16-stream hyper-connection MoE at 10B, where the authors argue the benefit exists specifically BECAUSE large-N write-back is information-bottlenecked; a single-stream depth-8 model may have no such bottleneck. Convolutions also add small kernels, which our profiling says is exactly where our step time already goes.
statement: Adding causal convolution branches to the sublayer write-back signal improved validation loss, with one branch giving 1.998 to 1.989 and three multi-scale branches giving 1.984.

comparator: mHC at its standard N=4 configuration, same backbone
effect: per-sublayer per-token I/O: 34C for mHC N=4, 73.5C for xHC (N=16,k=4) which is about 2.2x, 130C for dense mHC at N=16, reduced to 51C by the Flash variant and 40C by its four-sublayer version; FLOPs overhead only 3.0% at 28B
locator: section 5.1 'Efficiency Analysis', Table 4
notes: Registered as opposing evidence for any 'FLOPs are cheap so add residual-stream capacity' reasoning on this system. Our scope has nearly free GPU capacity in the FLOPs sense but our measured 297ms step is dominated by small GEMMs and ~194k tiny fill kernels, i.e. exactly memory-traffic and launch-bound work. Transfer 3 as a methodological blocker even though the numbers come from 10B-28B MoE: the accounting (count residual-state reads/writes per sublayer, not FLOPs) is the right way to pre-screen any multi-stream or extra-branch mechanism before spending a run on it.
statement: For hyper-connection-family residual architectures the dominant runtime cost is memory traffic rather than arithmetic FLOPs, with the proposed variant reading and writing 73.5C bytes per token per sublayer versus 34C for the N=4 baseline despite adding only 3.0% FLOPs.

comparator: Muon applied to all matrix parameters (not run), and xHC with Gram-Schmidt retained under Muon
effect: no isolated loss number for the optimizer split; removing Gram-Schmidt changed validation loss from 1.983 to 1.984 at the 10B ablation scale but caused training instability at 18B where conv-to-main-branch cosine similarity exceeded 0.7
locator: section 4.6 'Compatibility with Muon Optimizer'; Appendix D Table 11
notes: Relevant to our Muon-on-2D-matrices-plus-AdamW-elsewhere split: this is direct evidence that matrices whose output dimension is much smaller than their input dimension are poor Muon candidates and should be routed to AdamW. If we add any gating, routing or per-order-scale projection (as the n-gram memory papers require), the parameter-group assignment is a real decision, not a detail. Transfer 2: asserted as a practical adaptation rather than ablated, and our system has already measured that the Newton-Schulz orthogonalization itself is a fraction of a percent of step time, so this is about update quality, not cost. Note the second-order finding: Muon's orthogonalization made a forward-pass Gram-Schmidt step unnecessary, i.e. Muon can substitute for some explicit conditioning tricks.
statement: When training the multi-stream residual architecture with Muon, the authors applied Muon only to backbone attention and MLP projection matrices and kept the highly unbalanced routing and mapping projections on AdamW, and also removed a Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization step that was needed under AdamW.

comparator: xHC default with temporal augmentation only after MoE FFN layers, 10B MoE, Pile validation loss
effect: validation loss 1.983 (MLP-side only) vs 1.985 (adding attention-side), i.e. 0.002 worse, at extra computation and complexity
locator: Appendix D 'Attention-side Temporal Feature Augmentation', Table 11
notes: Placement claim: the authors reason that attention already mixes across tokens so a local causal convolution adds nothing there, whereas the token-independent MLP sublayer is the clean injection point. Registered as opposing the naive 'apply it everywhere' variant. Transfer 2: 0.002 loss is within plausible single-run noise at their scale and no seeds are reported, and our model uses SSSL sliding-window attention whose locality profile differs from their global/GQA attention, which is exactly the property the argument rests on.
statement: Applying the temporal convolution augmentation after attention sublayers as well as after MLP sublayers was slightly worse than applying it only after MLP sublayers.

comparator: pure sliding-window attention and full attention baselines on the same Qwen3-4B checkpoint, LongMemEval / LongBench V2 / Ruler, 128k prompts, vLLM float16, greedy decoding
effect: no loss number; accuracy on long-context benchmarks, odd-layer full attention 'vastly outperforms' even-layer for Qwen3-4B; retrieval behaviour appears concentrated in specific layers, and needle-in-haystack accuracy barely improves unless interleaved layers are enabled
locator: section 4.2.1 'Interleaving FA and SWA Layers', Table 1 row 13 vs row 11; section 3.1.2
notes: The rest of this paper is inference-time adaptation of already-pretrained models (FA Decode, Keep First k sink tokens, SFT recovery, vLLM latency) and is transfer 0 at our operating point: no pretraining loss is measured anywhere, all interventions target 128k-context serving. This single claim is registered at transfer 1 only because it is an existence argument that layer-wise attention-span heterogeneity has large effects, which is adjacent to our confirmed SSSL span lever (halving the short-window span from 2^10 to 2^9 was a measured SOTA win here). But their sensitivity arises from a train/inference MISMATCH on an FA-pretrained model, a mechanism that cannot exist when the span pattern is fixed from step 0, so it is not evidence for any particular pattern in our from-scratch run.
statement: When converting a full-attention pretrained model to sliding-window attention, which layers retain full attention matters greatly, with odd-numbered full-attention layers vastly outperforming even-numbered ones on the same model.

comparator: the authors' own v1 single-phase run over a 142M-token technical corpus for two epochs; 8 layers, hidden 512, GQA 8/2, head dim 64, vocab 16384, AdamW, cosine, 131,072 tokens/step, ~3519 steps total, single NVIDIA L4
effect: final pretraining loss 2.16 (three-phase curriculum with 25% and 10%/20% replay) vs 3.35 (single-phase over the full technical corpus), described as ~36% relative reduction 'at no token budget premium'
locator: section 6.4 'Loss trajectories', Table 5 and Figure 2; section 6.1
notes: Internal validity 1: the two runs see DIFFERENT data mixtures, so the losses are not on a common measure and the 36% figure is not a controlled effect; single seed; no held-out BPB. Transfer 1: prepare.py is frozen, so data ordering, mixture weights and replay fractions are all out of scope for this campaign regardless of the result. Included only to record that the paper's headline result is a data-ordering result and therefore not actionable here, despite the architecture (8 layers, d=512, ~1000-3500 steps, 131k-524k tokens/step) being the closest match in this entire batch.
statement: A three-phase pretraining curriculum with replay reached a final pretraining loss of 2.16 versus 3.35 for a single-phase run at the same token budget on a 42M-parameter 8-layer d=512 model.

comparator: identical architecture, tokenizer, SFT corpus and optimizer, varying only the Phase-1 bootstrap corpus (42M tokens of subtitle dialogue vs 64M tokens of web prose) with replay fractions adjusted
effect: mC4-ES bootstrap vs OpenSubtitles-ES bootstrap: P2 final loss 2.71 vs 3.00 (-0.29), P3 final loss 1.88 vs 2.16 (-0.28), SFT final loss 1.65 vs 1.82 (-0.17), but conversational gate 6/10 vs 7/10
locator: section 6.6 'Ablation: bootstrap-corpus register', Table 6
notes: Registered as opposing evidence for treating loss as a universal proxy, matching the analogous inversions in arXiv 2602.11137 and 2511.19496. Transfer 1: for THIS campaign the objective is literally val_bpb, so a loss/behaviour inversion is not a problem we have; and the intervention is a data swap under a frozen pipeline. Internal validity 2: the ablation does hold architecture and optimizer fixed, but corpus sizes differ (42M vs 64M tokens), replay fractions were changed to compensate, and the behavioural metric is a 10-item hand gate, single seed.
statement: Swapping the bootstrap corpus produced uniformly lower validation loss at every post-bootstrap phase but a worse score on the authors' held-out conversational benchmark.

comparator: standard ViT-Base (12 layers, 12 heads, head dim 64, token dim 768) with skip connections, ImageNet-1k, 300 epochs, drop path disabled for fairness
effect: skip 80.3% (AdamW) / 80.1% (SOAP); skipless 61.4% (AdamW) / 77.0% (SOAP); skipless + proposed init 78.1% (AdamW) / 80.8% (SOAP), the last exceeding the skip baseline by 0.5%
locator: section 6.1 'Supervised learning with Skipless ViT', Table 1
notes: Registered as opposing evidence against any 'remove the residual stream to save memory traffic or fuse layers' idea. Transfer 1: the entire paper is vision (supervised ViT plus DINO self-supervised ViT with segmentation and object-discovery probes); there is no language-modelling experiment, no loss-vs-compute comparison, and the one configuration that beat the baseline required SOAP, a second-order optimizer that is not in our stack. The 300-epoch budget is also the opposite of our 300-second regime.
statement: Removing all skip connections from a ViT-Base collapsed ImageNet-1k validation accuracy from 80.3% to 61.4% under AdamW, and even with a purpose-built conditioning initialization the AdamW result recovered only to 78.1%.

comparator: standard random Q/K initialization within the same skipless ViT-Base; the authors note the hyperparameters (alpha, beta, c) are 'not highly sensitive'
effect: no isolated ablation number; at random init logits are diffuse so the attention matrix approaches the rank-1 uniform matrix with condition number growing as tau/Delta and worsening with sequence length n; the identity term bounds the condition number instead
locator: section 5.2 'Initialization for W^Q W^K', Proposition 1 and Equation 11; section 6.1 (alpha=2, beta=0.6, c=3)
notes: Internal validity 2: the conditioning argument is proved for a stylized setting and the empirical support is entangled with the V/O orthogonal initialization and with skip removal, never isolated in a standard residual network. Transfer 1: no language-model evidence at any scale, and our model already applies QK-norm, which independently controls logit scale and largely addresses the diffuse-logit failure mode this init targets; the paper itself credits the technique to prior work (mimetic init) rather than establishing it. Recorded so the direction is visible, not because it is ready to run.
statement: Initializing the query-key product as a random matrix plus an identity term makes the initial attention logits diagonally dominant and the attention operator better conditioned, which the authors argue theoretically and use to enable skipless training.

comparator: the same models' own attention-parameter trajectories; a one-layer tanh transformer on a synthetic anchor-function task and a two-layer GeLU transformer on WikiText, both AdamW, LayerNorm deliberately omitted in the WikiText model
effect: no loss number; effective rank of outer parameters falls steadily during stage 1 while attention parameter norms remain close to initialization, then attention effective rank drops precipitously after the plateau; the condensation condition is satisfied for essentially all coordinates within the first 200 training steps
locator: section 5.1.1 and Figure 1(b,c); section 5.2 'Real Task' and Figure 3
notes: Transfer 1 and it should stay there: one- and two-layer models, binary-classification theory, layer normalization explicitly removed, no validation loss reported, and the authors' own limitations section says the analysis 'precludes insights' beyond binary settings. Registered because IF a version of this two-stage dynamic held in our depth-8 model, a ~1010-step budget could end before the attention parameters have done much learning at all, which would make QK-side initialization scale or a separate QK learning rate a structural lever rather than a knob. That is a hypothesis this paper does not test at our scale.
statement: In small transformers the outer parameters (value and MLP matrices) condense into low-rank structure first while query and key matrices stay near their initialization, and the attention parameters only begin to change after the training loss enters a plateau.

comparator: the same models at initialization and during stage 1; theory derived under gradient flow with small non-degenerate initialization and a binary classification objective
effect: no numeric loss effect; effective rank of the key-query parameters drops sharply in stage 2 in both the synthetic and WikiText experiments, consistent with the theorem
locator: section 4.4 'Key-Query Dynamics', Theorem 3 'Asymptotic rank collapse'; section 5.1.1 Figure 1(c)
notes: Registered because it partially corroborates and partially complicates the weight-decay rank story in arXiv 2602.11137: that paper attributes reduced query-key rank to weight decay and reports near-full-rank matrices at the default 0.1, while this paper predicts the collapse happens anyway from the training dynamics. If both hold, weight decay accelerates a collapse that would occur regardless, which weakens 'low rank' as the mechanistic explanation for weight decay's benefit. Transfer 1: one/two-layer models, no LayerNorm, binary classification, gradient flow, no measured language-modelling effect.
statement: The key-query matrices undergo an asymptotic rank collapse as an intrinsic outcome of gradient training, not only as a consequence of explicit regularization.

comparator: SGD and AdamW on the identical AT pipeline, WRN-34-20 (192.9M params), CIFAR-10, single RTX 4080S
effect: 52h45m (Muon) vs 51h59m (SGD), ~1.5% wall-clock overhead over 100 epochs
locator: section 3.4 'Training Time', table 6
notes: Transfer 2: corroborates the already-measured local fact that Newton-Schulz orthogonalization is a fraction of a percent of our ~297ms step, but the measurement is on a convnet on CIFAR-10 with an adversarial inner loop (10 APGD steps) that inflates the denominator, so the ratio is optimistic for us. Single run per cell, no seeds. Does not contradict our 5->3 NS-iteration result.
statement: Under adversarial training of WRN-34-20 for 100 epochs, total wall-clock training time with Muon is only slightly above SGD and AdamW (52h45m vs 51h59m / 52h06m on the l1+linf norm setting), i.e. the orthogonalization overhead is ~1.5% of end-to-end training time.

comparator: SGD and AdamW, ResNet-50 on ImageNet, 100 epochs, 2000 validation samples
effect: union robust acc 16.21 (Muon) vs 20.17 (SGD); Muon/AdamW needed lr 1e-4 while SGD used 1.0
locator: section 3.4 'Results on ImageNet', table 8
notes: Transfer 1: vision classification with adversarial inner loop, and the authors themselves say the comparison is HP-budget-limited, not a verdict on Muon. Registered as opposing evidence only for the general claim 'Muon is uniformly better than the tuned baseline' — it says nothing directly about a 124M LM. Only 2000 eval samples.
statement: Under a shared tuning budget, Muon underperformed SGD on ImageNet adversarial training (union robust accuracy 16.21 vs 20.17 best-checkpoint), which the authors attribute to Muon being more sensitive to learning rate, warmup and weight decay at scale rather than to the method failing.

comparator: unbounded spectral growth under adaptive (AdamW-style) updates; theoretical, not measured
effect: ||W_t||_2 <= max(||W_0||_2, (1+eps_bar)/lambda)
locator: section 2.2, theorem 2.1; appendix B, algorithm 2 and table 9
notes: Transfer 2: theorem is architecture-agnostic and applies to any 2D block updated by Muon, so it applies to our Muon-on-matrices setup. Actionable implication is that the ceiling requires lambda>0 on Muon-updated matrices; the paper does not measure a loss effect, and the ceiling is called 'a structural property rather than a tight robustness certificate' by the authors. No language-modeling evidence.
statement: Muon's polar (Newton-Schulz) update combined with decoupled weight decay lambda gives a spectral-norm stability ceiling ||W_t||_2 <= max(||W_0||_2, (1+eps_bar)/lambda) for all t, a structural bound that adaptive optimizers do not admit.

comparator: the conventional-transformer baseline curve in figure 3/4; no matched-seed A/B, no held-out eval reported
effect: Engram LR = 5x backbone LR; zero-init embeddings; gradient-norm switch point at step 3,250 crossing 0.05
locator: section 4.2 and section 4.3, figure 5
notes: Transfer 2 only for the recipe details (zero-init + LR multiplier on an n-gram memory table), which are implementable in train.py. Internal validity 1: single run, no seeds, no validation metric (training loss only), different tokenizer (syllabic, vocab 2,843) and language mix, and the baseline is not characterized. The step-3,250 activation is a red flag for our ~1000-step budget: the memory may not have populated before our run ends.
statement: In TOBA-LM the Engram n-gram memory module is trained with a learning rate five times higher than the backbone and its memory embeddings are zero-initialized; the module's gradient norm stays near zero until an abrupt overshoot past 0.05 at step 3,250, which coincides with the sharp loss drop.

comparator: none (no placement ablation is run)
effect: placement after block 3 of 36; additive residual fusion with sigmoid gate; 2-gram and 3-gram parallel lookups
locator: section 2.2 (eqs 3-7) and section 5.1
notes: Transfer 2: the placement/fusion recipe is directly implementable at our depth 8 and is a mechanism-level variation on our existing n-gram lever. But the paper runs NO placement ablation, so the choice is unjustified; internal validity 1. Depth-36 backbone means 'after block 3' is 1/12 of the way in, which at depth 8 would be under one block.
statement: TOBA-LM places the Engram memory module after the third transformer block (not at the embedding input), with parallel 2-gram and 3-gram lookup pathways fused additively as h' = h + Engram(h) under a sigmoid gate g = sigma(W_g h).

comparator: a 'conventional transformer architecture' baseline that is not specified (no matched parameter count, tokenizer, LR, or data schedule reported)
effect: loss 1.7996 at 12,973 steps vs >70,000 steps for baseline; '80% step efficiency'
locator: section 4.2, figure 3 and figure 4; section 5.2
notes: Transfer 1: 1.2B params, 1,024-token context, syllabic tokenizer over Indonesian/Batak/Minang Wikipedia — none of that matches our operating point, and the effect is training loss on a different tokenizer so it is not comparable in BPB. Internal validity 1: the baseline is uncontrolled and the 500,000x768 table adds parameters the baseline does not have. Registered because Engram is the operator-flagged priority mechanism; treat the magnitude as unusable.
statement: TOBA-LM reports reaching training loss 1.7996 in 12,973 steps with the Engram module while the conventional-transformer baseline had not reached comparable loss after more than 70,000 steps, described as an 80% reduction in training steps.

comparator: observational within one nanoGPT 110M run on FineWeb; no baseline arm
effect: ~4,000 of ~1.3e5 tokens per step at exactly zero loss (~3%)
locator: section 4.3 'Large Language Models'
notes: Transfer 1: the model scale (110M nanoGPT on FineWeb) is very close to ours, but the observation is reported for long training and the collapse mechanism requires the residual probability mass to fall below the bf16/fp32 absorption threshold — implausible at ~1000 steps where per-token loss is still ~1 bpb. Useful mainly as a reason NOT to spend budget on z-loss/logit-control at our horizon.
statement: During GPT training on FineWeb, roughly 4,000 of the ~1.3e5 tokens in each step reach exactly zero loss (Softmax Collapse), concentrated on template-predictable tokens such as '.', 'org', 'example', ',' and 'last'.

comparator: the same LM training run with the loss computation cast to float64 vs the standard bf16-autocast + fp32-loss recipe
effect: mean logit 183 (fp32 loss) vs 498 (fp64 loss) after 1e5 steps
locator: section 4.3 'Large Language Models', figure 13; figure 1(a) for the classification contrast
notes: Transfer 2: directly opposes the intuition that raising loss-computation precision above our bf16-autocast/fp32-loss default helps language modeling; the authors attribute the inversion to Zipfian token imbalance creating a large output-embedding global mean. Not scored higher because the effect is measured at 1e5 steps and on logit magnitude, not on val loss, and no seeds are reported.
statement: In language-model training, computing the loss in float64 did not reduce logit growth relative to standard bf16 training with fp32 loss; after 1e5 steps the mean logit was 183 under float32 loss but 498 under float64 loss, the opposite of the MLP/CNN/ViT result where float64 removes the instability.

comparator: Wortsman et al.'s reported divergence, which they claim reproduces at 2.4M params with lr 0.1
effect: failed reproduction at 19M and 150M GPT-2; authors note no independent reproduction in three years
locator: appendix A.4 'Discussion on output logit divergence in LLMs'
notes: Transfer 3: 19M/150M GPT-2 in PyTorch is essentially our regime, and this directly undercuts a common justification for logit-control interventions (z-loss, QK-norm-for-stability) at small scale in PyTorch. It is negative evidence (a non-reproduction), so it bounds the expected payoff of stability tricks rather than predicting a bpb gain.
statement: The authors could not reproduce the widely cited output-logit-divergence phenomenon of Wortsman et al. when training GPT-2 models of 19M and 150M parameters, in either PyTorch or the original JAX/Flax NanoDo codebase configured to match the paper.

comparator: the paper's own zero-weight-decay full-batch Adam setting where spikes do occur
effect: ||w||_inf ~< 1/lambda; float32 absorption requires a logit margin of approximately 16
locator: appendix A.3.1 'Weight Decay' and A.3.2 'Mini-Batch'
notes: Transfer 2: applies to our AdamW arm and argues weight decay is already buying numerical safety we should not remove; but it is a cited theoretical bound (Xie & Li) plus qualitative reasoning, and all the paper's own spike experiments use zero weight decay and full-batch Adam on CIFAR-10/modular arithmetic. Our large-batch (524288-token) setting is closer to full-batch than typical, which is the direction that makes spikes MORE likely.
statement: Explicit decoupled weight decay bounds parameter magnitude by ||w||_inf ~< 1/lambda, which keeps output logits in a finite range and is identified as one of the two dominant reasons Softmax-Collapse-driven loss spikes almost never appear in standard training recipes (the other being mini-batch noise).

comparator: log-spaced 80-point LR grid, 3 seeds per depth, weighted least squares with 95% CIs; SGD without momentum
effect: fitted alpha_hat = -1.44 / -1.35 / -1.45 vs theory -1.5; across all 9 architecture-dataset cells the range is -1.18 to -1.57, mean -1.38
locator: section 3.5 proposition; section 4.4, figure 3(c), table 1
notes: Transfer 2: gives a concrete LR-rescaling rule for any depth change we make (a transformer block counts as TWO depth units because it has two residual additions). But all evidence is image classification with SGD-no-momentum, the optimum is a one-epoch TRAINING-loss minimizer not a val minimizer, and our optimizer is Muon+AdamW. Only actionable if we vary depth, which we currently do not.
statement: For transformers, the maximal-update-optimal learning rate scales as eta* = Theta(L_tr^{-3/2}) in effective depth, and grid-searched one-epoch optima on CIFAR-10 fit exponents of -1.44 (ViT), -1.35 (BEiT) and -1.45 (CCT) against the theoretical -1.5.

comparator: the same depth sweep and LR grid with SGD (no momentum) as baseline, CIFAR-10
locator: section 4.5 'Optimizers' (ablations, table 3 in appendix E.1)
notes: Transfer 2: bounds how much of the L^{-3/2} rule survives under an adaptive optimizer, which matters because our AdamW arm is adaptive and Muon is spectrally normalized (likely to flatten the exponent further, untested). Vision-only; the ablation is not run on transformers.
statement: Switching the optimizer from SGD to Adam reduces the magnitude of the fitted depth-LR exponent by 10-12% (CNN -1.339 -> -1.207; ResNet -1.435 -> -1.269), so adaptivity partially but not fully compensates for depth scaling.

comparator: same depth sweep and 80-point LR grid on ImageNet subset
effect: alpha_hat -1.131 (Pre-LN) vs -1.178 (Post-LN), 4.0% difference
locator: section 4.5 'Normalization and regularization'
notes: Transfer 2: tells us not to expect an LR-retune requirement from norm-placement changes. Vision transformers on image classification, one-epoch training-loss optimum, 3 seeds; the claim is about the SCALING EXPONENT only and says nothing about which placement gives lower loss.
statement: Pre-LN and Post-LN ViTs yield essentially the same depth-LR exponent (-1.131 vs -1.178, a 4.0% difference), indicating normalization placement has minimal effect on depth scaling.

comparator: no comparison against a converged-run optimal LR is reported
effect: one-epoch training-loss minimizer used as the empirical proxy for eta*
locator: section 4.1 'General Protocol' and its footnote 3
notes: Transfer 3 because our whole run IS the early-training regime (~1010 steps, final_epoch 2.0), so a proxy that is questionable for long runs is unusually well matched to us; conversely this means the paper's law is being validated in exactly our regime. Internal validity 2 because the proxy is asserted, never validated against a long-run optimum, which the authors acknowledge only by citation.
statement: The optimal learning rate used throughout is the one-epoch training-loss minimizer, adopted explicitly as a proxy on the muP argument that optimal learning rates are primarily governed by early-training dynamics.

comparator: same Transformer-Medium (90M) recipe on WikiText-103, four attention variants, standard attention as baseline
effect: val PPL 26.980 (QUEST) vs 27.376 (QKNorm-DS) and 27.441 (standard); ~1.4% relative vs QKNorm-DS
locator: section 4.4, table 10
notes: Transfer 3: directly opposes our current QK-norm choice at a model size (90M) and family (decoder LM) close to ours, and is a genuine drop-in in train.py (l2-normalize K, set softmax_scale=1.0, drop the query norm). Scored 3 not 4 because no seeds/variance are given for the LM table, the metric is PPL on WikiText-103 rather than BPB on FineWeb, and the runs are far longer than 1000 steps. Risk flag: unnormalized queries with softmax_scale=1 changes logit magnitude under bf16 and interacts with our fa3 sliding-window kernel.
statement: On WikiText-103 with a 90M-parameter Transformer, normalizing only the keys with no 1/sqrt(d) scaling (QUEST) gives lower validation perplexity than standard attention, QNorm and QKNorm-DS: 26.980 vs 27.441 / 27.233 / 27.376.

comparator: ViT-Tiny / DeiT recipe, ImageNet-1K, 300 epochs, means over 3 independent training runs
effect: top-1 71.6 (QKNorm-DS) and 71.9 (QKNorm) vs 72.6 (standard) and 73.4 (QUEST)
locator: section 4.1.1, table 1 (means over 3 runs; per-run statistics in table A1)
notes: Transfer 2: the mechanism (QK-norm removes per-token control of softmax sharpness and thus costs expressivity when the model is small) is architecture-general and we run a small model with QK-norm, but the evidence itself is image classification. The paper's own framing is that QKNorm was justified for LARGE ViTs where training diverges — a stability argument that does not apply at 124M.
statement: On ImageNet with a ViT-Tiny trained for 300 epochs, QKNorm variants underperform standard attention (QKNorm-DS 71.6, QKNorm 71.9 vs standard 72.6 top-1), which the authors attribute to QKNorm constraining every token in every head to the same attention sharpness.

comparator: standard attention and QKNorm-DS under the identical DeiT recipe
effect: standard attention crashed at ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 (100 epochs); QUEST reached 79.7 and 74.9 top-1
locator: section 4.1.1 and appendix A.1, figure A6; table 2 ('training crashed' rows)
notes: Transfer 2: supports that key-only normalization is not a stability regression relative to full QK-norm, which is the main risk of swapping our QK-norm out. Evidence is vision at 86M-303M; the mechanism argument (breaking the query-key norm cross-play in the VJPs) is in appendix A.1 and is analytic, not measured on an LM.
statement: Normalizing only the keys also stabilizes query norms and maximum attention logits, which the authors give as the reason QUEST trains stably where standard attention diverges (ViT-B/16 and ViT-L/16 DeiT runs crashed with standard attention).

comparator: standard attention C=1/sqrt(D_H); QKNorm-HS (learnable C in R^H); QKNorm-DS (learnable C_q, C_k in R^{D_H})
effect: A = softmax(Q Kbar^T) with C=1 and Kbar the l2-normalized keys; no learnable per-head or per-dim scale
locator: section 2.1 (QUEST definition) and appendix A.2, algorithm A1 lines 16-18
notes: Transfer 3: this is the exact implementation detail needed to try it here, and the absence of any learnable scale means the change is parameter-neutral. Caveat for our head_dim=128: with C=1 and unnormalized queries the logit magnitude is set entirely by ||q||, which is initialized larger at larger head_dim — the paper never sweeps head_dim, so an LR/init interaction is untested.
statement: QUEST removes the 1/sqrt(D_H) scaling entirely (C=1) and adds no learnable scale, so attention rank-order is determined purely by query-key cosine similarity while the query norm controls per-token softmax sharpness.

comparator: standard attention, same 44M Transformer recipe on WikiText-103
effect: val PPL 32.966 (QUEST) vs 33.073 (standard); 5.0%-corruption test PPL 61.062 (QUEST) vs 60.944 (standard)
locator: section 4.4, table 10, rows 'Transformer Small (44M)'
notes: Transfer 3: this is the size closest to a small LM and it bounds the expected effect DOWNWARD — a sub-1% relative PPL change is near or below what our 0.000174 bpb counterbalanced resolution can distinguish once converted. The paper reports no seeds for the LM table, so the 44M gain may be noise. Register alongside the 90M win as the honest uncertainty band.
statement: On the smaller 44M Transformer, QUEST's clean-data validation perplexity on WikiText-103 is 32.966 against 33.073 for standard attention, and it is worse than standard attention on the most heavily corrupted test split (61.062 vs 60.944).

comparator: standard Adam on a 2-layer, 64-dim, 4-head transformer on synthetic text classification
effect: +35% time per epoch; -16% total time to a fixed accuracy target
locator: section IV-C 'Computational Efficiency'
notes: Transfer 1: a 35% per-step tax is fatal at a fixed 300 charged seconds, where step count dominates val_bpb, and the offsetting argument depends on an epochs-to-target-accuracy framing that does not exist in our fixed-budget setting. Internal validity 1: the perturbation is applied only to the first n_qubits=4 parameters (section III-A2 and eq. 2), so the reported gains cannot plausibly come from the stated mechanism.
statement: Superpositional Gradient Descent requires approximately 35% more time per epoch than Adam due to quantum-circuit simulation, offset in the authors' setting only by needing fewer epochs (16% lower total time to reach 90% accuracy on a synthetic text-classification task).

comparator: AdamW at lr 2e-5, single epoch, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on GSM8K
locator: section IV-B, table I
notes: Transfer 0: instruction fine-tuning of a pretrained 1B model is outside the pretraining operating point entirely, and no seeds, no validation split and no LR retune of the AdamW baseline are reported. Registered so the direction controller does not re-surface this paper as an optimizer lever.
statement: The only language-model evidence is one epoch of GSM8K fine-tuning of Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, where mean loss fell from 0.2188 (AdamW) to 0.2098 (lambda=0.1) and 0.2097 (lambda=0.5).

comparator: ResNets of depth 6n+2 at several fixed base-channel widths, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (no rebound observed on CIFAR-100 within the tested depth range)
effect: non-monotonic test-loss-vs-depth curves with a rebound at larger depths; mean over 5 random seeds with 1-sd shading
locator: section 7.3, figure 3(a),(b)
notes: Transfer 2: our n_embd is fixed at 512, so this is a direct caution that a depth-only increase from 8 can lose rather than gain — it opposes any naive 'add layers' lever. Evidence is image classification with ResNets, and the mechanism (first-order descent signal at insertion layers) is argued theoretically rather than demonstrated on a transformer.
statement: On CIFAR-10, test loss as a function of depth at fixed width is non-monotonic: after an initial improvement it rebounds noticeably at larger depths, so the best depth depends on width and deeper is not better at fixed width.

comparator: same ResNet family at several fixed depths, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100
effect: width-scaling curves flatten past a moderate width; 5 seeds, 1-sd bands
locator: section 7.3, figure 3(c),(d)
notes: Transfer 2: relevant because at our operating point GPU capacity is comparatively cheap and widening is the obvious way to spend it, but the paper says the payoff has a saturation point whose location is architecture- and data-dependent and is not identified. Vision-only; no LM validation.
statement: Increasing width produces a substantial test-loss reduction only in the narrow-to-moderate regime, especially for deeper models; once width is sufficiently large the curves flatten and further widening yields only marginal improvement.

comparator: ResNets of varying depth and base channel width, trained under a shared optimization setup, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100
effect: monotone decay of absolute and width-normalized activation-gradient norm with depth; most of the reduction occurs early in deepening, then flattens
locator: section 7.2, figure 2(a)-(d)
notes: Transfer 1: mechanism-level and vision-only, measured on trained models at one layer; it is a proxy for the theory's Condition 1 rather than a loss measurement. Useful only as a rationale for why depth-only levers plateau, not as a predictor at 124M.
statement: The l2-norm of the average activation gradient immediately before the final linear layer decreases substantially as depth increases across all tested widths, and remains decreasing after width-wise normalization, indicating deeper models carry a weaker remaining first-order improvement signal.

comparator: standard Muon under the identical LLaMA/C4 seq-256 recipe with only optimizer hyperparameters tuned
locator: section 6.3.1, figure 20 and section 6.3.2, table 18
notes: Transfer 3: a pure optimizer-internal change to the Muon we already run, no throughput cost, validated at two scales on a decoder LM. Not 4 because the smallest scale tested here is 350M with 60k steps (we run ~1010), no seeds or variance are reported, and Stage-1 disables weight decay and gradient clipping. Relative gain is ~0.5% PPL, which is near our resolution once converted to bpb — needs n>=3.
statement: Symmetric two-way learning-rate scaling applied to Muon's orthogonalized direction improves C4 validation perplexity from 16.60 to 16.52 at 350M and from 13.72 to 13.64 at 1B, and combining it with post-NS Nesterov gives 16.51 and 13.58.

comparator: standard Muon at C4-LLaMA 350M, seq 256, 60k steps
effect: PPL 23.01 (momentum in orthogonalized space) vs 16.60 (momentum in gradient space); 16.70 (LR scaling pre-NS) vs 16.60
locator: section 6.3.1 'Operator order is constrained', figure 20 third block
notes: Transfer 3: a cheap correctness check on our Muon implementation (momentum must be accumulated pre-orthogonalization; any scale correction must be applied post-NS). The 23.01 figure is a large, unambiguous effect. Single scale, single run; weight decay and clipping disabled in Stage 1, and the paper notes weight-decay ordering was near-irrelevant in this specific setting.
statement: Muon's sub-operations are not freely permutable: accumulating momentum in the orthogonalized space instead of the original gradient space degrades C4-350M perplexity from 16.60 to 23.01, and applying LR scaling before Newton-Schulz instead of after worsens it to 16.70.

comparator: AdamW at 17.78 on the same C4-LLaMA 350M seq-256 recipe
effect: PPL 70.74 (no v_t, no NS) -> 16.86 (+NS) -> 16.76 (+LR scaling) -> 16.60 (+Nesterov); AdamW 17.78
locator: section 6.3.1 'NS orthogonalization is the core mechanism' and 'Scaling and Nesterov are secondary gains', figure 20 first block
notes: Transfer 3: consistent with our locally measured result that degrading the orthogonalization (5->3 NS iterations) costs +0.002645 bpb — the orthogonalization quality, not the momentum bookkeeping, is what carries Muon. Single seed, single scale for the decomposition; Stage 1 has weight decay and clipping off.
statement: Removing AdamW's second moment without adding Newton-Schulz orthogonalization is catastrophic (C4-350M PPL 17.78 -> 70.74), while adding NS orthogonalization recovers to 16.86, already better than AdamW; LR scaling and Nesterov then contribute only 16.86 -> 16.76 -> 16.60.

comparator: AdamW and 22 other optimizers under one measurement harness, LLaMA on C4 at seq 256
effect: Muon 30.48 ms/step vs AdamW 2.31 ms/step at 130M (~13x)
locator: section 6.2.1, table 13 (T ms columns) and 'Runtime' paragraph
notes: Transfer 2, stance opposes: 30 ms would be ~10% of our ~297 ms step, whereas we have MEASURED that the whole orthogonalization is a fraction of a percent here. The discrepancy is most likely implementation (unfused per-matrix NS, no compile, Muon applied without our AdamW hybrid split) plus seq-256 short steps making the optimizer share large. Do not adopt this number; it is registered so a future 'Muon is expensive' argument is traceable to a harness difference, not to our system.
statement: Isolated per-step optimizer runtime for Muon is reported as 21.01 ms at 60M and 30.48 ms at 130M, against 1.14 ms and 2.31 ms for AdamW at the same scales.

comparator: 24 optimizers, LLaMA architecture on C4, seq 256, 10k/20k/60k/100k steps by scale, only optimizer hyperparameters tuned
effect: Muon 28.26 / 21.81 best at 60M / 130M; APOLLO 16.43 / 13.53 best at 350M / 1B
locator: section 6.1 'Training protocol' and section 6.2.1 'Quality', table 13
notes: Transfer 3 and it cuts BOTH ways for us: our 124M sits exactly in the band where Muon led, which supports our current choice; but the same finding means any optimizer result we import from a larger-scale paper is untrustworthy here. Caveat: Stage 1 disables weight decay and gradient clipping, and the authors state in section 7.1 that many apparent improvements over AdamW shrink or disappear once the AdamW baseline is retuned.
statement: Optimizer ranking is scale-dependent: Muon has the best C4 validation perplexity at 60M (28.26) and 130M (21.81), but APOLLO becomes strongest at 350M (16.43) and 1B (13.53), so the authors weight the 350M and 1B results most heavily and state that small-scale rankings are unreliable predictors of behavior at scale.

comparator: AdamW baseline under an identical controlled-variable protocol at 60M/130M/350M/1B on C4
locator: section 6.2.1, table 13; section 6.2.2 Pareto analysis; section 7.2 'Selection guidance'
notes: Transfer 3: both are row/column-normalized cheap approximations to matrix preconditioning, implementable in train.py, and evaluated at 60M-130M which brackets our 124M. Blockers: single run per cell with no seeds, Stage-1 disables weight decay and clipping, and the runtime column is from their harness which already overstates Muon's cost relative to ours — so the runtime ARGUMENT for switching is weak here even if the quality is real.
statement: RMNP and Conda reach near-Muon short-context quality at a small fraction of Muon's per-step optimizer runtime: at 130M, Conda 21.91 PPL at 7.11 ms and RMNP 22.54 PPL at 4.63 ms, against Muon 21.81 PPL at 30.48 ms and AdamW 23.18 PPL at 2.31 ms.

comparator: the standard two-term Kaplan/Chinchilla form with model size treated as a single quantity
effect: alpha_m = 0.98 +/- 0.08, alpha_l = 1.2 +/- 0.3, alpha_D = 0.30 +/- 0.01; mean relative fit error 0.4%
locator: section 2, equation 3 and figure 2f (fitting details in appendix B)
notes: Transfer 2: implies that at fixed parameter budget N ~ m^2 * l the optimal aspect is m proportional to l, which our 512/8 config does not obviously satisfy — but the proportionality CONSTANT is not identified, so the law cannot say whether we are on the wrong side. The fit is on Chinchilla models trained near compute-optimal (~20 tokens/param); we run ~4 tokens/param, outside the fitted data regime, and alpha_l has 25% relative uncertainty.
statement: Fitting L = c_m/m^alpha_m + c_l/l^alpha_l + c_D/D^alpha_D + L_0 to ~200 reconstructed Chinchilla data points gives alpha_m = 0.98 +/- 0.08, alpha_l = 1.2 +/- 0.3 and alpha_D = 0.30 +/- 0.01, with 0.4% mean relative error between empirical and fitted loss.

comparator: the compositional-assembly and procedural-assembly (neural-ODE) alternatives, distinguished via a controlled toy model in sections 3-4
effect: mean middle-layer update angle ~ 1/depth; theta(delta h_l, delta h_{l+1}) typically large (weak inter-layer correlation)
locator: section 2, figure 2(c),(d),(e)
notes: Transfer 2: measured on real decoder LMs on FineWeb (our data family), and it argues that additional depth buys error averaging, not new function classes — consistent with the campaign's observed saturation of depth-style knobs. But it is measured on converged public checkpoints, not on 1000-step runs, and the authors explicitly cannot exclude other mechanisms producing the same signature.
statement: Hidden-state analysis on Pythia models evaluated on FineWeb shows the dataset-averaged per-layer angular update in the middle layers scales approximately inversely with depth, and neighbouring updates are weakly correlated, which the authors read as ensemble averaging rather than compositional or smooth-dynamics use of depth.

comparator: the middle layers of the same models; across Pythia sizes and other model families (appendix A)
effect: first/last layer update angles near pi/2 and depth-independent; middle-layer angles small and decreasing with depth
locator: section 2, figure 2(a),(c)
notes: Transfer 2: motivates treating the first and last blocks differently from the bulk (separate LR, separate init scale, or placing value/n-gram injections there) at our depth 8, where 'first and last' is a quarter of the network. Observational on converged checkpoints; no intervention is run, so the payoff of any asymmetric treatment is unmeasured.
statement: In Pythia models on FineWeb the first and last layers rotate hidden states by large angles close to pi/2 and change hidden-state norms substantially, independently of total depth, while the intermediate layers make small and progressively smaller updates.

comparator: two constructed ideal trajectories ('early stop' with zero middle angles, 'evenly in the middle' at 0.45 rad)
effect: 0.4% early-stop cluster (document-initial tokens) vs 99.6% evenly-updated cluster
locator: section 2, figure 2(b)
notes: Transfer 1: interesting for document-boundary handling (which touches our doc-mask lever) but the affected token fraction is 0.4%, far too small to move val_bpb by our 0.000174 resolution on its own. Registered to bound expectations, not as a lever.
statement: PCA of per-token layer-update trajectories in Pythia-410m separates two clusters: 0.4% of tokens stop updating early and correspond mostly to the first tokens of documents, while the remaining 99.6% are updated evenly through the middle layers.

comparator: fixed final-checkpoint k-means partitions plus an exogenous part-of-speech partition as a clustering-free control; recomputed at every checkpoint on a common covered-token set
effect: between-category share 0.03 (step<=16) -> peak 0.15-0.21 (steps 64-512) -> minima 0.057-0.065 at steps 4k-32k; within-token share minimum 0.66-0.68
locator: section 6 'The Pythia trajectory', figure 5 left and center
notes: Transfer 3: our entire ~1010-step run lies inside the overshoot-and-early-reallocation window, so this is one of the few papers whose measured DYNAMICS are indexed to our exact step range. Implication: at our horizon the model is still crystallizing coarse category structure, so levers that buy fine-grained/context-dependent capacity are being asked to pay off before their phase begins. Observational only — no intervention is run, so this ranks levers rather than predicting a bpb delta. Checkpoint-hygiene caveat: Pythia-2.8B was excluded after a stale-revision bug, and Pythia-1B is an outlier that never recovers.
statement: On Pythia checkpoints, the between-category variance share is dormant through step 16 (~0.03), multiplies severalfold between steps 32 and 64, and peaks at 0.15-0.21 within the first 64-512 steps — about 1.8-3.3x its final value — while the within-token share dips to its all-training minimum of 0.66-0.68.

comparator: the between-category term of the same exact decomposition, on the same models and token sets
effect: within-category loss share 0.59-0.64 (K=10), 0.43-0.53 (K=50), 0.46-0.48 (POS)
locator: section 4 'The loss-side anchor' (proposition 1(iii))
notes: Transfer 2: the decomposition is exact and computed on real LM checkpoints, and it says roughly half of next-token loss is fine-grained within-category choice — which is what an n-gram/local-recall memory would target. Scored 2 because it is measured on converged models, K is chosen by k-means, and the weakest cells (K=10, ten points per model) rest on cross-model consistency rather than any single correlation.
statement: An exact decomposition of cross-entropy from the same inference pass shows the within-category term carries 0.59-0.64 of the loss at K=10 across four models, 0.43-0.53 at K=50, and 0.46-0.48 under part-of-speech categories.

comparator: the neural-collapse prediction from classification that terminal training collapses representations; OLMo-2 criteria fixed before the run (3 of 4 passed; R4 failed its pre-set 1.3x bar at 1.21)
effect: 160M: 0.065 (step 4k) -> 0.114 (step 143k); CDNV best 3.1-4.9 at steps 256-1000, 4.8-9.0 at end; OLMo-2-1B between-category 0.201 at 1B tokens, min 0.083 at 21B, 0.124 at 1.3T
locator: section 6 'The Pythia trajectory' and 'Why recovery is the expected ending'; OLMo-2 replication under pre-registered criteria R1-R4
notes: Transfer 2: opposes importing neural-collapse-motivated interventions (e.g. objectives that push toward simplex-ETF geometry) into LM pretraining. For our 1000-step run the operative fact is the OPPOSITE end: CDNV minima at steps 256-1000 mean our run terminates near the maximal-collapse point, not the recovered one. Observational, no intervention, and the general-K information floor remains a conjecture (only the binary case is proved).
statement: Contrary to the classification picture of terminal neural collapse, in language models the between-category share partially recovers late in training (for example Pythia-160M from 0.065 at step 4k to 0.114 at step 143k) while validation loss improves throughout, and cluster-level CDNV is best early (minima 3.1-4.9 at steps 256-1000) and worse at the end (4.8-9.0).

comparator: warmup-cosine-decay, asserted from unshown 'experimental validation'
effect: no number reported for the WSD-vs-cosine comparison
locator: section 2.2.2 'Cosine Decay vs. WSD vs. FG-WSD'
notes: Transfer 1: the schedule swap is implementable, but the claim is stated without any number, without a scale, and is explicitly CONDITIONED on annealing-phase data quality — a condition we cannot satisfy because prepare.py is frozen and the data mix cannot change. Internal validity 1: no supporting table.
statement: The authors state that when data quality during the annealing phase is sufficiently high, warmup-stable-decay significantly outperforms warmup-cosine-decay, and they therefore adopt WSD as the base schedule.

comparator: vanilla WSD with the same 1T stable-phase tokens uniformly shuffled from a static 1:1 HQ/MQ mixture, 1B parameter model
locator: section 2.2.2 'Preliminary Experiments', table 2 and table 3
notes: Transfer 0: despite the 'scheduler' name, table 3 shows the learning rate is constant at 4.5e-4 across both stable stages — the only thing that changes is data ordering, which is out of scope under a frozen prepare.py. Registered explicitly so this is not mis-read as a learning-rate-schedule lever. Evaluation is few-shot downstream accuracy, not loss, single run.
statement: Fine-Grained WSD improves benchmark scores over vanilla WSD at 1B parameters and 1T stable-phase tokens (GSM8k 27.1 -> 34.3, CMath 34.5 -> 39.5, BBH 29.3 -> 31.6, MMLU 49.2 -> 50.6), but the intervention is a data-ordering change (progressively raising the high-quality data fraction in later stages) at an identical constant learning rate, not a learning-rate change.

comparator: GPT-2 models pre-trained with token vocabulary sizes swept from 32K to 2M
effect: 97.6% of tokens get >100 updates at 32K vocab vs 7.3% at 2,097,152 vocab, over 100M training tokens
locator: section 3.2 and appendix C, figure 9
notes: Transfer 3: our run sees ~530M tokens total (524288 x ~1010) with final_epoch 2.0, so any large n-gram/f-gram embedding table we add would sit deep in the sparse-update regime this measures — this is the strongest argument in the batch against scaling up a raw n-gram table at our horizon, and it points instead to parameterizing n-gram embeddings with a small network or hashing to a small table. Measured at GPT-2 scale on WebText; the exact token counts differ from ours.
statement: Directly backpropagating into a very large embedding table fails because of sparse updates: over 100M training tokens, 97.6% of tokens in a 32K vocabulary receive more than 100 updates, but only 7.3% do at a 2M vocabulary, and GPT-2 performance degrades accordingly.

comparator: the same GPT-2 architectures at smaller vocabulary sizes; BPC chosen over cross-entropy because it is vocabulary-insensitive
effect: non-monotonic BPC vs vocabulary size (improves then deteriorates) across three model sizes
locator: appendix C, figure 8
notes: Transfer 2: our tokenizer is frozen so vocabulary size is not a lever, but the mechanism (more embedding rows -> fewer updates each -> worse loss) is exactly what governs any added lookup table we CAN change. Also confirms BPC/BPB is the right vocabulary-insensitive metric. The turning point location is not identified numerically.
statement: Bits-per-character on the WebText validation set initially improves as vocabulary size increases but eventually deteriorates, for all three model sizes tested.

comparator: the same model with token embeddings only (baseline star in figure 5), WebText/WikiText-103, 128M-589M models
effect: perplexity gain saturates at maximum n-gram length 4; frequency cutoff rises from 7 (n=2) to 108 (n=8) at fixed 20M entries
locator: section 4.1.1, figure 5 (perplexity averaged over three seeds) and appendix D.1
notes: Transfer 3: bounds the n-gram order worth spending on in our n-gram lever at 3-5, evaluated at 128M-589M which brackets our 124M, and averaged over three seeds. Caveat: their table is frequency-ranked over the training corpus, so with a fixed budget longer n-grams crowd out shorter ones — the saturation is partly a budget-allocation artifact, which the authors state.
statement: Varying the maximum f-gram length from 2 to 8 at fixed table size (20M entries) shows perplexity improving up to length 4 and then plateauing with fluctuation, and average matched f-gram length likewise stabilizes after 4; the authors therefore fix the maximum at 5.

comparator: the 0.7B/1B/1.3B baselines without Scone on the OLMo corpus
effect: later convergence for Scone-enabled models; models trained 200B tokens, ~10x the compute-optimal token count for 1B
locator: appendix D.2 'Loss Curves over Training', figure 13
notes: Transfer 3 and stance opposes: capacity-expanding n-gram embedding layers pay off LATE, and our budget is ~530M tokens over ~1010 steps — the opposite end of the curve. This is the cleanest available warning that an n-gram-embedding win reported at 200B tokens may invert at our horizon, and it matches the locally recorded finding that the n-gram lever's help flips sign with operating point. Observational reading of loss curves; no early-stopping comparison is tabulated.
statement: Evaluation-loss curves show that models trained with Scone (n-gram contextualized input embeddings) converge later than the baseline, which the authors read as evidence that Scone effectively expands model capacity.

comparator: the same training with on-the-fly lookup
effect: qualitative: on-the-fly longest-match lookup causes GPU idle time; fixed by an offline pre-scan tagging pass
locator: appendix E 'Implementation Details'
notes: Transfer 2: our host is CPU-contended and the packing loop in the frozen prepare.py is already a large share of wall clock, so an on-the-fly longest-match n-gram lookup would land on the most expensive resource we have — and the paper's fix (offline pre-scan of the tokenized corpus) is exactly the kind of change prepare.py being frozen forbids. Any n-gram lookup we add must be GPU-side or precomputable outside the charged window. No timing numbers given.
statement: At training time f-gram lookup is a bottleneck because transformers process all token positions in parallel, causing GPU idle time while fetching the longest matching n-gram; the authors remove it by pre-scanning training sequences offline to tag the longest matching length for every token.

comparator: 1B, 1.3B and 1.9B dense baselines trained on the identical 200B-token corpus and architecture family
effect: average PPL 16.082 -> 15.125 (10M f-grams, 1.8B A_fgram) -> 14.581 (1B f-grams); 1.9B baseline 14.598
locator: section 4.2, table 2
notes: Transfer 1: the headline result is at 1B params / 200B tokens with an auxiliary f-gram model up to 1.8B parameters — three orders of magnitude past our budget, and the method's whole selling point (embeddings precomputed and offloaded so INFERENCE FLOPS stay fixed) is irrelevant when our objective is training-time loss under 300 charged seconds. The training-time cost is real and unquantified in the paper.
statement: On the OLMo evaluation mixture after 200B tokens, adding 10M f-gram embeddings learned by a 1.8B f-gram model improves a 1B baseline's average perplexity from 16.082 to 15.125, and 1B f-gram embeddings bring it to 14.581, surpassing the 1.9B baseline at 14.598.
